Initially created: 2025-12-05T09:42:48.215+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: Sīmǎ Guāng
by imperial command edited
Later Study Heaven Terrace
Cāo defeated Yuán Shàng
and obtained Jìzhōu.
He then resided in Yè.
Yè
was the seat of Wèijùn in the Hàn dynasty.
Wèi
was a great name;
he was then enfeoffed as the Duke of Wèi.
Moreover, a prophecy stated:
"The one who will replace the Hàn will be 'Dāngtúgāo'."
"Dāngtúgāo"
means Wèi.
Emperor Wén received the abdication from Hàn,
and the state was then named Wèi.
Emperor Shìzǔ Wén, the Eldest,
personal name Pī,
courtesy name Zǐhuán,
was King Wǔ Cāo's eldest son.
According to the posthumous naming system: "studious, diligent, and fond of asking questions" is called Wén.
Shìzǔ
is a temple name.
According to rites:
"Zǔ" (ancestor) is for those with merit, and "Zōng" (revered ancestor) for those with virtue.
According to the posthumous naming system: "objects and scenes in the four directions" is called Shì;
"receiving mandate and not moving" is called Shì.
"Pacifying the people and acting as their model" is called Huáng;
"clarifying unified virtue" is called Huáng;
"clarifying unity and conforming to the Way" is called Huáng.
"Virtue resembling heaven and earth" is called Dì;
"acting according to the Way without action" is called Dì.
In the first year of Huángchū
(gēngzǐ, 220), Wèi received the abdication from Hàn,
following the cycle of the Five Virtues,
with Earth succeeding Fire.
The color of Earth is yellow,
thus the era name was Huángchū.
He received the abdication in the tenth month of this year,
and only then changed the era name.
1 Spring,
first month,
King Wǔ arrived at Luòyáng;
on gēngzǐ,
he passed away.
King Wèi Cāo was posthumously named Wǔ.
He was hard to deceive with falsehoods.
"Xuàn"
means the eye has no fixed focus;
"hard to deceive with falsehoods"
means that people could not obscure his clarity.
He did not restrict himself to the humble or lowly,
but employed people according to their abilities,
and all found their use.
When facing the enemy in formation,
his demeanor was calm and composed,
as if he did not wish to fight;
but when the moment came to make a decision and seize victory,
his spirit and momentum were overflowing.
For meritorious service deserving reward,
he would not begrudge a thousand pieces of gold;
for those without merit who sought favors,
"Shī,"
pronounced shì chǐ fān.
he would not give a single fraction.
"Háo"
is the character "háo" (毫).
Those who committed offenses were certainly executed;
sometimes he would shed tears when facing them,
but ultimately granted no pardon.
His nature was refined and frugal,
not fond of extravagance.
Thus he was able to eliminate all the heroes,
almost pacifying the entire realm.
"Almost"
means
because
he could not conquer Wú and Shǔ.
"Shān,"
pronounced suǒ xián fān.
"Jī,"
pronounced jū xī fān.
At this time, the crown prince was in Yè,
and the army was in turmoil.
Many officials wished to keep the mourning a secret and not announce it.
Jiànyì Dàfū Jiǎ Kuí believed that the matter could not be kept secret,
and so announced the mourning.
Some said that the city guardians should be replaced,
all with people from Qiáo and Pèi.
The Cáo clan were from Qiáo in Pèiguó;
the shortsighted believed that people from their hometown were trustworthy.
"Shǒu,"
pronounced shì yòu fān;
same below.
"Now that the distant and near are unified,
people are eager to demonstrate their loyalty,
why must we exclusively appoint people from Qiáo and Pèi,
thereby discouraging the hearts of the palace guards!"
So they stopped.
The Qīngzhōu soldiers
beat drums and left together;
the Qīngzhōu soldiers were those who surrendered when Cāo defeated the Yellow Turbans in the third year of Chúpíng under Emperor Xiàn.
Those who did not follow were to be punished.
Jiǎ Kuí said:
"This is not permissible."
He wrote a long proclamation
ordering local authorities to provide them with provisions.
The Marquis of Yānlíng, Zhāng, came from Cháng'ān to attend.
Cāo had returned his army east from Hànzhōng,
and Zhāng had pacified Dài and welcomed Cāo to the west,
then Zhāng was kept in Cháng'ān.
"Yān,"
Lù Démíng says yè wǎn fān,
also yú jiàn fān;
Shīgǔ pronounces it yǎn.
Kuí sternly said:
"The state has an heir apparent.
The former king's seals and ribbons
are not something for your lordship to inquire about."
The news of the calamity reached Yè,
and the crown prince wept uncontrollably.
Zhōngshùzǐ Sīmǎ Fú admonished him, saying:
The Xù Hàn Zhì states: The Crown Prince's Zhōngshùzǐ,
with a rank of six hundred dàn,
whose duties were like those of a Shìzhōng.
"The lord king has passed away.
The world relies on Your Highness for its fate;
you must act above for the ancestral temple
and below for the myriad states.
How can you act with the filial piety of a common man!"
After a long while, the crown prince stopped,
saying:
"Your words are correct."
At that time, when the officials first heard of the king's demise,
they gathered and wept,
without any order.
Fú sternly spoke in the court:
"Now that the lord king has left this world,
the world is shaken.
We must promptly enthrone the successor
to stabilize the myriad states.
And yet you only weep!"
He then dismissed the officials,
prepared the imperial guard,
and managed the funeral arrangements.
Fú
was Yì's younger brother.
The officials believed that for the crown prince to ascend the throne,
an imperial edict was necessary.
This refers to waiting for an imperial edict from the Hàn emperor.
"The king died away from home,
and the world is fearful.
The crown prince should set aside his grief and ascend the throne
to secure the hopes of the distant and near.
Moreover, if a beloved son is at his side,
"beloved son"
refers to the Marquis of Yānlíng, Zhāng.
then the state will be in danger."
He immediately prepared the official positions and ceremonial rites,
completing everything in one day.
"Biàn"
is the same as "bàn";
the Shǔ version writes
"bàn."
By the Queen's order,
a proclamation enthroned the crown prince as king,
and a general amnesty was declared.
The Hàn emperor soon dispatched Yùshǐ Dàfū Huà Xīn to present an imperial edict,
conferring upon the crown prince the seal and ribbon of the Prime Minister,
the seal and ribbon of the King of Wèi,
and appointment as Pastor of Jìzhōu.
Thereupon, the Queen was honored as Queen Dowager.
2 The era name was changed to Yánkāng.
This was a Hàn era name change,
according to the Wèi Zhì.
3 Second month,
on dìngwèi shuò,
there was a solar eclipse.
4 On rénxū,
Tàizhōng Dàfū Jiǎ Xǔ was made Tàiwèi,
Yùshǐ Dàfū Huà Xīn was made Xiàngguó,
and Dàlǐ Wáng Lǎng was made Yùshǐ Dàfū.
5 On dīngmǎo,
King Wǔ was buried at Gāolíng.
Gāolíng
was west of the city of Yè.
Cāo's dying instruction said: "You all should frequently ascend the Tóngquè Terrace,
and look upon my western mausoleum and fields."
The Wèi Jì records Cāo's order saying: "Set the mausoleum on the western plain west of the temple of Xī Ménbào."
The King’s younger brother, Márquís Yānlíng Zhāng (曹彰), and others all proceeded to their fiefs.
Guàn Jūn (灌均), the Inspector of Línzī (臨菑) and Yèzhě (謁者),
played to the King's inclinations and reported,
“Márquís Línzī Zhí (曹植) got drunk and behaved outrageously and disrespectfully,
even threatening an envoy.”
The King demoted Zhí to Márquís Ānxiāng (安鄉侯),
and executed Dīng Yí (丁儀) of Péiguó (沛國), the Right Cìjiān Yuàn (刺姦掾).
Wáng Mǎng (王莽) established Left and Right Cìjiān to supervise the cunning and treacherous.
Guāngwǔ (光武) revived the dynasty,
and also appointed Cìjiān Jiàngjūn (刺姦將軍);
however, the Gōngfǔ Yuàn (公府掾) did not have such a position.
From the Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉) dynasties, the Gōngfǔ began to have positions such as Yíngjūn (營軍) and Cìjiān.
Yuàn (掾),
read as Yú-juàn.
Both he and his male dependents were executed,
thereby ending his lineage.
Yì (廙),
read as Yì-zhí,
also as Yáng-zhì.
Yú Huàn (魚豢) commented: The proverb says,
“The poor do not need to learn frugality;
the humble do not need to learn humility.”
This is not because human nature is inherently different,
but because circumstances make it so.
If Tàizǔ (太祖) had restrained Zhí and others in the past,
how could these worthy individuals have harbored ambitions?
Zhāng's (曹彰) resentment,
still came to nothing;
as for Zhí (曹植),
how could he have instigated trouble!
Instead, Yáng Xiū (楊脩) met with misfortune due to his being relied upon,
and Dīng Yí (丁儀) suffered clan extermination for playing to others' wishes.
Alas!
At first, four Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍) and four Shìláng (侍郎) were appointed.
Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍) was a Qín (秦) official position.
The Qín (秦) established Sànqí (散騎),
and also established Zhōng Chángshì (中常侍).
Sànqí (散騎) were cavalry who followed the imperial carriage;
Zhōng Chángshì (中常侍) were allowed to enter the forbidden palace: both were considered honorary appointments.
At the beginning of the Eastern Hàn (漢) dynasty, Sànqí (散騎) was abolished,
and Zhōng Chángshì (中常侍) were appointed from among eunuchs.
It was at this time that Sànqí (散騎) was first re-established,
combining it with Zhōng Chángshì (中常侍) into a single office,
called Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍),
responsible for offering remonstrance,
but not for managing affairs;
they wore sable tails and cicada pins on the right,
riding in scattered attendance.
Later, it became a prominent position.
From Wèi (魏) to Jìn (晉), Sànqí Shìláng (散騎侍郎), together with Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍), Shìzhōng (侍中), and Huángmén Shìláng (黃門侍郎), jointly deliberated on memorials to the Shàngshū (尚書);
it was abolished on the left bank of the Jiāng (江).

It refers to the offices of Zuǒ (左), Yòu (右), Zhōng Shàngfāng (中尚方), Zhōnghuáng (中黃), Zuǒ (左), Yòu Zàng (右藏), Zuǒ Xiào (左校), Zhēn Guān (甄官), Xī Guān (奚官), Huángmén (黃門), Yètíng (掖庭), Yǒngxiàng (永巷), Yùfǔ (御府), Gōudùn (鉤盾), Zhōngzàngfǔ (中藏府), Nèizhě (內者), and others.
Stored in the stone chamber.
At this time, when Shìzhōng (侍中) and Chángshì (常侍) were to be selected,
the King's former associates subtly urged the official in charge,
wishing to immediately employ them [themselves]
without considering others.
Sīmǎ Fú (司馬孚) said,
"Now that the heir King has just ascended,
we should promote the outstanding and virtuous talents from all within the seas.
How can you wish to seize this opportunity
to recommend yourselves?
If officials fail in their duties,
even those who obtain positions are not truly esteemed."
Thereupon, other selections were made.
Shàngshū Chén Qún (陳羣), believing that the Heavenly Court's selections did not fully utilize talented individuals,
"Heavenly Court"
refers to the Hàn (漢) court.
Cháo (朝),
read as Zhí-yáo.
established Zhōngzhèng (中正) in all zhōu (州) and jùn (郡) to determine their selections,
choosing the virtuous and discerning among the zhōu (州) and jùn (郡) to serve in this capacity,
to differentiate individuals
and rank them by their quality.
The Jiǔpǐn Zhōngzhèng (九品中正) system began from this.
Jiǔpǐn (九品) are Shàngshàng (上上), Shàngzhōng (上中), Shàngxià (上下), Zhōngshàng (中上), Zhōngzhōng (中中), Zhōngxià (中下), Xiàshàng (下上), Xiàzhōng (下中), and Xiàxià (下下).
Bié (別),
read as Bǐ-liè.
Summer,
fifth month,
on the day Wùyín (戊寅), the Hàn (漢) Emperor posthumously honored the King's ancestor, the Tàiwèi (太尉), as Tàiwáng (太王).
The King's ancestor was Hàn Tàiwèi Cáo Sōng (曹嵩).
The King appointed Zōu Qí (鄒岐), the Administrator of Āndìng (安定), as the Inspector of Liángzhōu (涼州).
Qū Yǎn (麴演) of Xīpíng (西平) banded with neighboring commanderies to revolt and resist Qí;
Zhāng Jìn (張進) of Zhāngyè (張掖) seized Administrator Dù Tōng (杜通);
Huáng Huá (黃華) of Jiǔquán (酒泉) refused to accept Administrator Xīn Jī (辛機);
all proclaimed themselves administrators in response to Yǎn;
Qū Yǎn (麴演) was the one who executed Hán Suí (韓遂);
his authority had long been established in the Liáng (涼) region, which is why Jìn (張進) and others responded to him.
Wúqiū Xīng (毋丘興), Administrator of Wǔwēi (武威),
Wúqiū (毋丘)
is a double-character surname.
was about to rescue him.
The people of the commandery all believed that the rebels' power was still strong,
and it was advisable to await a large army.
At that time, Generals Hǎo Zhāo (郝昭) and Wèi Píng (魏平) were first stationed in Jīnchéng (金城),
having received an imperial edict not to cross to the west.
Jīnchéng (金城) was separated from Wǔwēi (武威), Zhāngyè (張掖), and Jiǔquán (酒泉) by a river.
"Though the rebels are strong now,
they are all newly assembled,
and some were coerced,
so they may not be united in heart;
if we attack them taking advantage of the rift,
the good and bad will surely separate.
When they separate and return to us,
our strength will increase while theirs will diminish.
Having gained the benefit of augmented forces,
and with the potential for doubled morale,
leading an expedition against them,
their defeat is certain.
If we wait for a large army,
it will be a prolonged delay,
and the good people will have no refuge,
inevitably joining the wicked.
Once good and bad are united,
their separation will be difficult to achieve quickly.
Though there is an imperial edict,
it is permissible to disregard it and act expediently,
taking the initiative."
Zhāo (郝昭) and others followed his advice,
then dispatched troops to rescue Wǔwēi (武威),
causing three Hú (胡) tribes to surrender.
They joined Wúqiū Xīng (毋丘興) in attacking Zhāng Jìn (張進) in Zhāngyè (張掖).
Qū Yǎn (麴演), hearing of this,
led three thousand infantry and cavalry to meet him,
claiming to assist the army,
but actually intending to mutiny.
He lured and executed Yǎn (麴演),
displaying his head to the army.
Yǎn's (麴演) followers all scattered and fled.
He then joined the other armies in besieging Zhāngyè (張掖),
defeated it,
and executed Jìn (張進);
Huáng Huá (黃華), afraid,
begged for surrender.
According to Péi Sōngzhī's (裴松之) annotations,
Huá (黃華) was the same person who later, as Inspector of Yǎnzhōu (兗州), memorialized against Wáng Líng (王淩).
The event is recorded in volume seventy-five under Jiāpíng (嘉平) third year of Shàolíng Lìgōng (邵陵厲公).
Earlier, Mǎ Ài (馬艾), the Administrator of Dūnhuáng (敦煌), died in office.
The people of the commandery supported Gōngcáo (功曹) Zhāng Gōng (張恭) to act as Chángshǐ (長史).
Gōng (張恭) sent his son, Jiù (就), to the imperial court to request a new administrator.
Coincidentally, Huáng Huá (黃華) and Zhāng Jìn (張進) rebelled,
intending to combine forces with Dūnhuáng (敦煌).
They seized Jiù (就),
and threatened him with drawn blades;
Jiù (就) ultimately did not yield.
He secretly wrote to Gōng (張恭):
"Father led and encouraged Dūnhuáng (敦煌),
and your loyalty and righteousness are clearly evident.
How could you abandon this because Jiù (就) is in distress?
Now, the great army is about to arrive;
you should only hasten troops to flank the enemy.
I hope you will not, out of 'love for the lower stream,'
cause Jiù (就) to have regrets in the yellow earth."
The Analects say: A gentleman dislikes dwelling in the lower stream,
for all evils in the world flow to it.
This means that one should hate dwelling in the lower stream, not love it.
Another interpretation: Liú (流),
means "kind" or "class";
to be swayed by paternal love
and abandon the righteousness between ruler and minister
is the inferior insight of a common person,
hence it is called "love for the lower stream."
He separately dispatched two hundred iron cavalry and officials,
along the northern frontier of Jiǔquán (酒泉),
to the east to welcome Administrator Yǐn Fèng (尹奉).
Huáng Huá (黃華) wanted to save Zhāng Jìn (張進),
but looking west at Gōng's (張恭) troops,
he feared being attacked from the rear,
and thus could not go and surrendered.
Jiù (就) eventually returned safely,
Fèng (尹奉) was able to take up his post in the commandery,
and an imperial edict bestowed upon Gōng (張恭) the noble title of Guānnèi Hóu (關內侯).
Sixth month,
on the day Gēngwǔ (庚午),
the King led his army on a southern tour.
Autumn,
seventh month, Sūn Quán (孫權) sent envoys to offer tribute.
13 Shǔ general Méng Dá 屯上庸,
was at odds with his deputy commander, Zhonglángjiàng Liú Fēng.
Fēng harassed and insulted him,
so Dá led his subordinates and over four thousand families to surrender.
Dá had a graceful demeanor and talent,
and the King greatly esteemed and loved him.
He invited him to ride in the same carriage,
appointed Dá as Sànqí Chángshì and Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn,
and enfeoffed him as Píngyáng Tínghóu.
The three commanderies of Fánglíng, Shàngyōng, and Xīchéng were combined to form Xīnchéng.
The division of these three commanderies from Shǔ is mentioned in the previous volume, Han Xiàndì, Jiàn'ān 24th year.
He entrusted Dá with the responsibility for the southwest.
Xíngjūn Chángshǐ Liú Yè said:
At that time, Wèi Wáng led his army on a southern tour,
with Yè serving as Chángshǐ.
"Dá has a mercenary heart,
and relies on his talent while being fond of schemes;
he will certainly be incapable of gratitude or righteousness.
Xīnchéng is contiguous with Sūn and Liú.
Han-Zhōng of Shǔ,
and Yídū of Wú,
are both contiguous with Xīnchéng.
He will create trouble for the state."
The King did not listen.
This laid the groundwork for Méng Dá's defection from Wèi.
為,
read as yú wěi fān.
Shàngyōng Tàishǒu Shēn Dān rebelled against Fēng and surrendered.
Fēng was defeated
and fled back to Chéngdū.
Initially,
Fēng was the son of a man named Kòu from Luóhóu.
When Han-Zhōng Wáng first arrived in Jīngzhōu,
as he had no heir yet,
he adopted Fēng as his son.
Zhūgé Liàng feared that Fēng was too fierce and strong,
and after a change of era,
he would ultimately be difficult to control.
He advised Han-Zhōng Wáng to eliminate him on this occasion;
consequently, Fēng was given death.
14 The Dī king of Wǔdū, Yáng Pú, led his people to pledge allegiance.
15 On jiǎwǔ,
the King stopped at Qiáo,
and held a grand feast for the six armies and the elders of Qiáo in the eastern part of the city.
He provided music, dance, and various performances.
Officials and common people offered blessings,
and the event concluded at dusk.
Sūn Shèng said: The three-year mourning period
applies from the Son of Heaven down to commoners.
Therefore, even at the end of the Three Dynasties,
referring to the late period of the three dynasties.
Qín, Zhào, Hán, Wèi, Qí, Chǔ, Yān were the Seven Warring States.
they would remove the hemp staff on the day of the "reverse weeping."
麻 (má)
refers to the mourning band (dié).
When mourning a father, one carries a coarse staff.
According to the rites: one performs "reverse weeping" after the burial.
The Tán Gōng states: "Reverse weeping involves ascending the hall,
returning to the place where it (the deceased) resided."
The condolence of "reverse weeping"
represents the utmost grief;
to return and find it (the deceased) gone
is to have lost it,
and this is the most poignant.
衰 (cuī),
read as cāng huí fān.
The ancient system was altered,
as detailed in Volume 15, Wéndì's 7th year.
To abolish it in an instant
already indicated a decline of virtue in that era
and a weakening of custom for a hundred generations.
Wèi Wáng, by tracing the Han system,
abolished its grand rites,
and in a time of gravest sorrow
held feasts and entertainment.
At the beginning of establishing a legacy, he destroyed the foundation of kingly transformation.
The Shàng Shū says: "There are regulations and rules,
which are handed down to one's descendants."
墮 (duò)
is read as huī.
He openly accepted two daughters,
when Xiàndì abdicated,

The prophecy for the duration of the dynasty was cut short.
16 The King appointed Prime Minister Jìjiǔ Jiǎ Kuí as Yùzhōu Cìshǐ.
Yùzhōu administered Yǐngchuān, Rǔyīn, Rǔnán, Liángguó, Pèijùn, Qiáojùn, Lǔjùn, Yìyáng, and Ānfēng commanderies.

Many Cìshǐ were unable to govern their commanderies effectively.
攝 (shè)
means to control and oversee.
"The province originally used six articles of imperial edicts to investigate officials of 2,000 shí and below,
adopting the Han system.
One who has the talent for supervision,
not for tranquility, leniency, or benevolence,

Now, chief officials disregard the law,

If the province knows but does not rectify it,

All officials of 2,000 shí and below
who were indulgent or did not act according to the law

Externally, he trained the military;

Officials and common people praised him.
The King said:

"Wèi's succession to Hàn
is seen in diagrams and apocrypha;
the evidence is abundant.
According to the biography of Xiàndì,
Lǐ Fú cited Kǒngzǐ's jade tablet,
and Xǔ Zhī cited the Chūnqiū Hàn Hánzīt, the jade tablet prophecy, the Zuǒzhù Qī, the Xiàojīng Zhōnghuáng Chèn, and the Yì Yùnqī Chèn.
Those who urged him to ascend the throne at that time were
Xīn Pí, Liú Yè, Fù Xùn, Wèi Zhēn, Huán Jiē, Chén Jiǎo, Chén Qún, Sū Lín, Dǒng Bā;
followed by
Sīmǎ Yì, Zhèng Hún, Yáng Mì, Bào Xūn.
In winter,
10th month,
on yǐmǎo,
the Hàn Emperor announced sacrifices at the ancestral temple,
and sent Xíng Yùshǐ Dàfū Zhāng Yīn, holding the scepter, to present the imperial seal and ribbon, and the imperial edict,
abdicating the throne to Wèi.
The King submitted three petitions to decline,
but then a坛 (tán) was erected at Fányáng.
At that time, on his southern tour, he reached Yǐngchuān, Yǐngyīn Xiàn,
and built an altar at Fányáng Tíng in Qūlí.
The Shùzhēng Jì states: its location is 70 lǐ south of Xǔ.
To the east, there was a platform
seven zhàng high and fifty bù square;
to the south, there was an altar
two zhàng high and thirty bù square,
which was the altar for receiving the abdication.
In this year, Fányáng was renamed Fánchāng Xiàn.
On xīnwèi,
he ascended the altar and received the imperial seal and ribbon,
and ascended to the imperial throne.
Kǎoyì states: Chén Zhì says:
"On bǐngwǔ,
he reached Qūlí,
and the Hàn Emperor abdicated.
On gēngwǔ,
he ascended the altar and the throne."
Yuán Jì also says:
"On gēngwǔ, Wèi Wáng ascended the throne."
According to the Xiàndì Jì,
the abdication edict was first issued on yǐmǎo,
and he ascended the altar to receive the mandate on the 29th day.
Furthermore, the Wéndì Shòuchán Bēi is still extant today,
and also states that he received the abdication on xīnwèi.
Chén Zhì and Yuán Jì are mistaken.
Fàn Shū says:
"Wèi sent envoys to request the imperial seal and ribbon,
but Empress Cáo did not give it.
After several such requests,
the Empress then called the envoy,
threw the seal down to the steps,
and with tears streaming down, said: 'Heaven will not bless you!'
Those around her could not even look up."
This, however, is an event from the former Hàn's Empress Yuán,
and moreover, the imperial seal and ribbon could not have been in Empress Cáo's possession;
this statement is erroneous.
The era name was changed,
and a general amnesty was declared.
In the 11th month,
on guǐyǒu,
the Hàn Emperor was enfeoffed as Shānyáng Gōng.
Shānyáng Xiàn belonged to Hé'nèi Jùn.
He was to use the rituals and music of a Son of Heaven;
the Duke's four sons were enfeoffed as Lièhóu.
The Grand King (Tài Wáng) was posthumously honored as Tài Huángdì;
King Wǔ was honored as Wǔ Huángdì, with the temple name Tàizǔ;
the King's Grand Empress Dowager was honored as Huáng Tàihòu.
Han feudal princes were made Chóngdé Hóu,
and Han marquises (Lièhóu) were made Guānzhōng Hóu.
The officials and ministers were enfeoffed and promoted in varying degrees.
The Xiàngguó was changed to Sītú,
and the Yùshǐ Dàfū was changed to Sīkōng.
The offices of the Sāngōng were abolished in the 13th year of Jiàn'ān during Han Xiàndì's reign;
now they were restored.
The Emperor wanted to reform the calendar and system of weights and measures.
Shìzhōng Xīn Pí (辛毗) said:
"The Wèi (魏) clan follows the succession of Shùn (舜) and Yǔ (禹),
responding to Heaven and obeying the people.
As for Tāng (湯) and Wǔ (武),
they established the empire through warfare,
and only then reformed the calendar and system of weights and measures.
Confucius said: 'Follow the calendar of Xià (夏).'
The Zuǒ Shì Zhuàn (左氏傳) says: 'The Xià (夏) calendar was considered to have obtained the correct celestial alignment.'
Why must we seek to contradict it?"
The Emperor approved and followed his advice.
From then on,
everyone consistently regarded jiànyín (建寅) as the beginning of the year.
(The character "傳" (zhuàn)
is pronounced zhí liàn fān.)
Many suppressed or disparaged the previous dynasty.
However, Sànqí Chángshì Wèi Zhēn (衞臻) alone clearly articulated the meaning of the abdication and succession,
praising the virtues of the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
The Emperor repeatedly looked at Zhēn (臻) and said:
"The treasures of the world
should be shared with Shānyáng (山陽)."
The Emperor wished to posthumously enfeoff his Empress Dowager's parents.
Shàngshū Chén Qún (陳㣥) presented a memorial, saying:
"Your Majesty, with sagely virtue, responded to the auspicious moment and received the Mandate of Heaven.
By initiating new enterprises and reforming institutions,
you should serve as a perpetual model for later generations.
According to the texts of the classics and records,
there is no system for women to be granted land or titles.
In the rites,
a woman takes her rank from her husband.
The Lǐ Jì (禮記) states: 'Women have no rank of their own,
but follow their husband's rank.'
The Hàn (漢) dynasty followed this,
which was not an excellent institution of the former kings."
The Emperor said:
"This argument is correct;
do not implement it."
He then established this as a fixed regulation,
storing it in the imperial archives.
(Tái Gē (臺閣)
refers to the place in the Shàngshū (尚書) where precedents are stored.)
In the twelfth month of the 18th year [of Jiàn'ān (建安)],
construction of the Luòyáng (洛陽) palace began.
On the day wùwǔ (戊午),
the Emperor proceeded to Luòyáng (洛陽).
Péi Sōngzhī (裴松之) noted: "According to various records,
at this time, the Emperor resided in the Northern Palace,
using the Jiànshǐ Diàn (建始殿) for audiences with his officials,
and the gate was called Chéngmíng (承明).
Chén Sī Wáng Zhí's (陳思王植) poem
'Audience with the Emperor in the Chéngmíng (承明) Lodge'
refers to this.
It was not until the time of Emperor Míng (明帝)
that the Tàijí (太極) and Zhāoyáng (昭陽) palaces were built on the site of the Hàn (漢) Southern Palace's Chóngdé Diàn (崇德殿)."
The Wèi Lüè (魏略) states: "The Hàn (漢) dynasty followed the element of Fire.
Fire fears Water,
hence
'Luò' (洛)
removed
'water' (水)
and added
'zhūi' (隹).
The Wèi (魏) dynasty, in its cyclical order, represented Earth.
Earth
is the 'male' element of Water;
Water flows when it encounters Earth,
and Earth softens when it encounters Water.
Therefore, [the character] removed
'zhūi' (隹)
and added
'water' (水),
changing
'Luò' (雒)
to
'Luò' (洛)."
The Emperor said to Shìzhōng Sū Zé (蘇則):
"Previously, we defeated Jiǔquán (酒泉) and Zhāngyè (張掖),
and the Western Regions sent envoys to Dūnhuáng (敦煌),
presenting pearls an inch in diameter.
Can we try to purchase more?"
Zé (則) replied:
"If Your Majesty's transforming influence extends throughout the central plains,
and your virtue flows into the deserts,
then they will arrive without being sought.
To seek and obtain them
is not worthy of esteem."
The Emperor remained silent.
The Emperor summoned Dōng Zhōngláng Jiàng Jiǎng Jì (蔣濟) to be Sànqí Chángshì.
At that time, there was an imperial edict granting Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn Xiàhóu Shàng (夏侯尚), which stated:
"You are a trusted and important general,
specially entrusted with power.
You may exercise authority and bestow blessings,
killing or sparing lives."
Shàng (尚) showed it to Jì (濟).
When Jì (濟) arrived,
the Emperor asked him about what he had heard and seen.
He replied:
"I have not seen any other good things,
only words that lead to the ruin of a state."
The Emperor was indignant and his countenance changed as he asked for the reason.
Jì (濟) explained in detail,
and then said:
"Indeed, 'to exercise authority and bestow blessings'
is a clear warning in the Shū Jīng (書經).
The 'Hóng Fàn' (洪範) chapter of the Shū Jīng (書經) states: 'Ministers should not exercise authority and bestow blessings.
If ministers exercise authority and bestow blessings,
it will harm their families
and bring misfortune to their state.'
This is what the ancients were cautious about;
may Your Majesty examine it!"
The Emperor immediately sent someone to retrieve the previous edict.
The Emperor wanted to relocate one hundred thousand households of soldiers from Jìzhōu (冀州) to settle in Hénán (河南).
At that time, Luòyáng (洛陽) was being constructed,
so he wanted to relocate the soldiers' families from Jìzhōu (冀州) to settle it.
The people were starving,
and all the officials believed it was not feasible,
but the Emperor's intention was very strong.
Shìzhōng Xīn Pí (辛毗) and the court officials collectively sought an audience.
The Emperor knew they wanted to remonstrate,
and adopted a stern expression to await them,
so no one dared to speak.
Pí (毗) said:
"Your Majesty wishes to relocate the soldiers' families.
What is the plan for this?"
The Emperor said:
"Do you think my relocation plan is wrong?"
Pí (毗) replied:
"Indeed, I consider it wrong."
The Emperor said:
"I will not discuss this with you."
Pí (毗) said:
"Your Majesty, despite my unworthiness,
has placed me by your side,
appointing me to an office of consultation and deliberation.
Shìzhōng (侍中),
in the Zhōu (周) dynasty, held the responsibility of Cháng Bó (常伯),
remaining by the Son of Heaven's side,
ready to answer pressing questions and provide immediate responses,
picking up omissions and filling in deficiencies.
What I say is not for private gain,
but a concern for the state and the ancestral altars.
How can you be angry with me?"
The Emperor did not reply,
stood up and entered his private chambers.
Pí (毗) followed and pulled at his robe.
The Emperor then shook off his sleeve and did not return.
After a long while, he came out
and said:
"Zuǒzhì (佐治),
why are you so insistent with me?"
(Xīn Pí's (辛毗)
courtesy name was Zuǒzhì (佐治).
The character "治" (zhì)
is pronounced zhí lì fān.)
"Now, if we relocate them,
we will both lose the people's hearts
and have nothing to feed them with.
Therefore, I dare not but argue with all my might."
The Emperor then relocated only half of them.
The Emperor once went out hunting pheasants,
and looking at his officials, said:
"Hunting pheasants is delightful!"
Pí (毗) replied:
"For Your Majesty, it is indeed delightful;
for the people, it is indeed苦 (bitter)."
The Emperor remained silent,
and afterwards, went out less frequently.
In the first month of spring,
Kǒng Xiàn (孔羨), a Yìláng (議郎), was enfeoffed as Zōngshèng Hóu (宗聖侯)
to offer sacrifices to Confucius.
In the first year of Yuánshǐ (元始) of Emperor Píng (平帝) of Hàn (漢),
Kǒng Bà's (孔霸) great-grandson, Kǒng Jūn (孔均), was enfeoffed as Bāochéng Hóu (褒成侯)
to offer sacrifices to Confucius.
When Wáng Mǎng (王莽) was defeated,
the state was lost.
In the thirteenth year of Jiànwǔ (建武) of Emperor Guāngwǔ (光武),
Jūn's (均) son Zhì (志) was again enfeoffed as Bāochéng Hóu (褒成侯).
Zhì's (志) son, Sǔn (損),
was transferred to be enfeoffed as Bāotíng Hóu (褒亭侯) in the fourth year of Yǒngyuán (永元) of Emperor Hé (和帝).
This title was passed down through generations,
until it ceased to exist in the early years of Emperor Xiàn (獻帝).
The Wèi (魏) dynasty enfeoffed Kǒng Xiàn (孔羨), the 21st-generation descendant of Confucius, as Zōngshèng Hóu (宗聖侯),
with an estate of one hundred households.
The Jìn (晉) dynasty enfeoffed Zhèn (震), the 23rd-generation descendant, as Fèngshèngtíng Hóu (奉聖亭侯).
Later, the Northern Wèi (魏) enfeoffed Chéng (乘), the 27th-generation descendant, as Chóngshèng Dàfū (崇聖大夫).
In the 19th year of Tàihé (太和) of Emperor Xiàowén (孝文), he visited Lǔ (魯)
and again enfeoffed Zhēn (珍), the 28th-generation descendant, as Chóngshèng Hóu (崇聖侯).
The Northern Qí (齊) dynasty changed the enfeoffment of the 31st-generation descendant □ to Gōngshèng Hóu (恭聖侯).
When Emperor Wǔ (武帝) of Zhōu (周) pacified Qí (齊),
he changed the enfeoffment to Zōuguó Gōng (鄒國公).
Emperor Wén (文帝) of Suí (隋) maintained the old title of Zōuguó Gōng (鄒國公).
Emperor Yáng (煬帝) changed the enfeoffment to Shàoshèng Hóu (紹聖侯).
In the eleventh year of Zhēngguān (貞觀) of Emperor Tàizōng (太宗) of Táng (唐),
Lún (倫), a descendant of Confucius, was enfeoffed as Bāoshèng Hóu (褒聖侯).
In the third month,
Gōngsūn Gōng (公孫恭), the Grand Administrator of Liáodōng (遼東), was promoted to Chējì Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍).
Gōng (恭) was the second son of Gōngsūn Dù (公孫度)
and the younger brother of Kāng (康).
3 The five-zhù coins were restored for the first time.
In the first year of Chūpíng of Emperor Xiàn of Hàn,
Dǒng Zhuó had destroyed the five-zhù coins,
and now they were restored.
4 A rumor spread in Shǔ that the Hàn emperor had already been murdered.
Thereupon, the King of Hànzhōng issued mourning decrees and donned mourning attire,
and gave him the posthumous title Emperor Xiàomǐn.
From then on, people competed to speak of auspicious omens,
and urged the King of Hànzhōng to assume the imperial title.
The Former Army Commandant Fèi Shī submitted a memorial, saying:
At this time, Fèi Shī was the Former Army Commandant of Yìzhōu.
Fèi,
the pronunciation of the father is "fèi".
“Your Highness considers Cáo Cāo and his son to have usurped the throne by coercing the ruler,
which is why you have journeyed thousands of miles,
and gathered soldiers and commoners,
intending to punish the rebels.
Now, the great enemy has not yet been overcome, but you intend to establish yourself first;
I fear this will cause doubt in people's hearts.
In the past, Gāozǔ made a pact with Chǔ,
that whoever first defeated Qín would be king.
When he captured Xiányáng
and apprehended Zǐyīng,
he still had the humility to decline;
how much more so now, when Your Highness has not even left the courtyard,
do you wish to establish yourself!
Your foolish subject truly does not consider this a good move for Your Highness.”
The King was displeased,
and demoted Shī to Chief Clerk of Yǒngchāng Commandery.
He was an assistant to the governor of Yìzhōu,
in Yǒngchāng Commandery.
In the fourth month,
on the day Bǐngwǔ,
the King of Hànzhōng ascended the imperial throne south of Wǔdān.
The Shǔběnjì states: In Wǔdū, a man transformed into a woman,
with a beautiful countenance,
likely a mountain spirit.
The King of Shǔ married her,
but she was not accustomed to the climate,
became ill, and wished to return to her country.
The King of Shǔ kept her,
and she died not long after.
The King of Shǔ dispatched troops to Wǔdū to carry earth,
and buried her within the city walls of Chéngdū,
covering several acres of land,
ten zhàng high,
and it was named Wǔdān.
Péi Sōngzhī commented: According to Wǔdān Mountain, it is in the northwest of Chéngdū.
It is probably because the Qián trigram (northwest) symbolizes the ruler,
hence he chose that location to ascend the throne.
Dù Yòu said: Wǔdān Mountain is west of Shǔ Commandery.
He changed the era name to Zhāngwǔ.
He appointed Zhūgé Liàng as Chancellor
and Xǔ Jìng as Minister of Education.
Your servant Guāng says: Heaven gives birth to the teeming people,
whose nature is such that they cannot govern themselves.
They must mutually uphold a ruler to govern them.
If a ruler can suppress violence and eliminate harm to preserve their lives,
and reward good and punish evil to prevent chaos,
then they can be called a ruler.
Wēn Gōng’s explanation
is precisely the meaning of the Zǔ Zhōu Shū’s saying,
"If you soothe us, you are our lord;
if you oppress us, you are our foe."
The Bái Hǔ Tōng says: A jūn is
to gather;
it is he to whom the hearts of those below flock.
Within the four seas, the zhūhóu,
were not just ten thousand states.
Huáng Dì established left and right grand supervisors
to oversee the ten thousand states.
Yǔ assembled the zhūhóu at Tú Shān,
and there were ten thousand states bearing jade and silk.
Those with people and altars of soil and grain
were generally called jūn.
He who united the ten thousand states and ruled them,
established laws and regulations,
issued commands and orders,
and whom no one in the world dared to disobey,
was called a wáng.
When the wáng’s virtue declined,
a powerful state that could lead the zhūhóu to honor the Son of Heaven
was called a bà.
Therefore, since ancient times, when the world was without the Way,
and the zhūhóu contended for power,
there were indeed many occasions when there was no wáng for generations.
For example, the Gòng Gōng Shì between Fú Xī and Shén Nóng,
and Qín between Zhōu and Hàn,
were all called bà but not wáng.
This is what is meant by "no wáng for generations."
Also, for example, Yǒu Qióng during Xià,
and Gòng Hé during Zhōu,
were also without a wáng for generations.
When the Hàn dynasty arose,
scholars began to expound on the Five Phases’ generation and conquest cycles,
considering Qín a "surplus reign" (rùn wèi),
positioned between Wood and Fire,
ruling as a bà but not a wáng.
Thus, the debate over "legitimate" and "surplus" reigns arose.
Mèng Kāng says: Qín followed the Five Victories theory,
considering Zhōu to be Fire,
and conquered it with Water.
Hàn Confucians regarded Páo Xī as having succeeded Heaven to become wáng,
as the first of all wángs,
with his virtue beginning with Wood.
The Gòng Gōng Shì dominated the nine regions;
although possessing the virtue of Water,
it was between Wood and Fire,
not in its proper sequence,
hence it was a bà but not a wáng.
The Shén Nóng Shì succeeded Wood with Fire,
hence he was called the Yán Dì.
After the Shén Nóng Shì passed away,
the Huáng Dì Shì arose;
Fire gives birth to Earth,
hence he possessed the virtue of Earth.
Shǎo Hào,
son of Huáng Dì,
Earth gives birth to Metal,
hence he possessed the virtue of Metal.
When Shǎo Hào’s power waned,
Zhuān Xù received it;
Metal gives birth to Water,
hence he possessed the virtue of Water.
What Zhuān Xù established,
Dì Kù received it;
Water gives birth to Wood,
hence he possessed the virtue of Wood.
When Gāo Xīn Shì declined,
the world turned to Yáo;
Wood gives birth to Fire,
hence he possessed the virtue of Fire.
Yáo abdicated to Shùn;
Fire gives birth to Earth,
hence he possessed the virtue of Earth.
Shùn abdicated to Yǔ;
Earth gives birth to Metal,
hence he possessed the virtue of Metal.
Tāng attacked Jié and succeeded Yǔ;
Metal gives birth to Water,
hence he possessed the virtue of Water.
Zhōu attacked Shāng;
Water gives birth to Wood,
hence it possessed the virtue of Wood.
Hàn attacked Qín and succeeded Zhōu;
Wood gives birth to Fire,
hence it possessed the virtue of Fire.
Gòng Gōng and Qín were not in the correct cycle of the Five Phases' mutual generation,
hence they are called "surplus reigns."
The Three Kingdoms stood in a tripod formation.
The Jìn clan lost control of the reins of power,
and the Wǔ Hú caused widespread chaos.
From Sòng and Wèi onwards,
the South and North were divided,
each having its own national history,
mutually denouncing and rejecting each other.
The South called the North "Suǒ Lǔ" (Braided Barbarians),
and the North called
the South "Dǎo Yí" (Island Barbarians).
"Suǒ Lǔ" refers to
the Northerners' braided hair,
calling them "braided heads."
"Dǎo Yí" refers to
the Southeast bordering the sea,
with low-lying land,
calling it "among the islands."
When the four directions were torn apart,
and the Zhūxié entered Biàn,
comparing it to Qióng and Xīn,
Táng Zhuāng Zōng considered himself the successor to Táng,
comparing Zhū Liáng to Yǒu Qióng usurping Xià and the Xīn dynasty usurping Hàn.
All of these were cast aside and not counted.
These are all biased statements motivated by self-interest,
not objective and universally accepted arguments.
Your servant is truly insufficient to discern the legitimate and surplus reigns of past generations.
I humbly believe that if they could not unify the nine regions into one,
then all of them merely had the title of Son of Heaven without the substance.
Although the Huáxià
varied in benevolence or cruelty,
and in size and strength
at different times,
essentially they were no different from the ancient feudal states.
How could one exclusively honor and praise one state as the legitimate tradition,
while all others were considered usurpers and pretenders?
If one considers those who received the mandate from above as legitimate,
then from whom did the Chén clan receive it?
From whom did the Tuòbá clan receive it?
If one considers those who occupied the Central Plains as legitimate,
then the territories acquired by Liú, Shí, Mùróng, Fú, Yáo, and Hèlián
were all the old capitals of the Five Dì and Three Wáng.
If one considers those with moral virtue as legitimate,
then even in the smallest state there must be a good ruler,
and in the later periods of the Three Dynasties,
were there not also perverse kings?
Therefore, the debate over legitimate and surplus reigns,
from antiquity to the present,
has never had an explanation that could be universally understood
and firmly convince people beyond dispute.
What your servant now relates
merely seeks to chronicle the rise and fall of states,
and record the joys and sorrows of the people,
so that observers may choose for themselves good and evil, gain and loss,
as encouragement and warning.
It is not like the Chūnqiū, which established a system of praise and blame
to rectify chaotic times and restore them to proper order.
The question of legitimate and surplus reigns
is not something I dare to presume to know;
I only speak based on the actual accomplishments and deeds.
Zhōu, Qín, Hàn, Jìn, Suí, and Táng
all at one time unified the nine regions,
and transmitted their imperial lineage to later generations.
Even if their descendants were weak and scattered,
they still inherited the enterprises of their ancestors,
and held out hope of restoration.
Those who contended with them for supremacy from all directions
were all their former subjects.
Therefore, I have fully used the system of the Son of Heaven to describe them.
For the others, whose lands were similar and virtues equal—
"chǒu"
means "similar"; it means that the extent of their lands was similar.
—whose titles were not different,
and who were fundamentally not lord and subject,
I have treated them according to the system of feudal states,
considering them mutually equal,
neither suppressing nor elevating any,
so that it might not misrepresent the facts
and be closer to perfect impartiality.
However, during times when the world was fragmented,
one cannot be without years, seasons, months, and days to record the sequence of events.
Based on the fact that Hàn was transmitted to Wèi, and Jìn received it;
Jìn was transmitted to Sòng, and so on to Chén, and Suí took it;
Táng was transmitted to Liáng, and so on to Zhōu, and Dà Sòng inherited it,
therefore, I must use the reign titles of Wèi, Sòng, Qí, Liáng, Chén, Hòu Liáng, Hòu Táng, Hòu Jìn, Hòu Hàn, and Hòu Zhōu
to record the affairs of the various states.
After "Wèi,"
there should be
the character "Jìn."
This is to distinguish between legitimate and surplus reigns.
Although Zhāo Liè (Liú Bèi) was said to be a descendant of Zhōngshān Jìng Wáng,
his kinship was distant,
and he could not trace his generational lineage and status.
This is similar to Sòng Gāo Zǔ (Liú Yù) claiming descent from Chǔ Yuán Wáng.
Sòng Gāo Zǔ,
a native of Péngchéng,
claimed to be the twenty-first-generation descendant of Liú Jiāo, King Yuán of Chǔ, of the Hàn dynasty.
This was because Péngchéng was the capital of Chǔ,
so his descendants settled in this area.
Nán Táng initially wished to claim Prince Wú Kè as ancestor,
Someone requested [to have] Zǔ Zhèngwáng Yuán Yì (鄭王元懿) as an ancestor.
The Táng (唐) ruler ordered an examination of the descendants of the two kings.
As the grandson of Wúwáng (吳王), Yī (禕) had performed meritorious service,
and Yī's (禕) son Xiàn (峴) was chancellor,
Wúwáng (吳王) was then established as ancestor.
Therefore, they dared not compare themselves to Guāngwǔ (光武) or Jìn Yuándì (晉元帝),

5 Sūn Quán (孫權) moved his capital from Gōng'ān (公安) to È (鄂),

He married the daughter of the General of Chariots and Cavalry, Zhāng Fēi (張飛), to the Crown Prince.
7 When Tàizǔ (太祖) entered Yè (鄴),
he entered Yè (鄴) in the sixth-fourth卷, Hán (漢) Jiàn'ān (建安) tenth year.
He saw Yuán Xī's (袁熙) wife, the lady Zhēn (甄) from Zhōngshān (中山), who was beautiful, and he was pleased with her.

and she bore him a son, Ruì (叡).
When he ascended the imperial throne,
the Guō (郭) noble consort from Ānpíng (安平) was favored.
According to Chén Shòu's (陳壽) Records,
Consort Guō (郭)
was from Guǎngzōng (廣宗) in Ānpíng (安平).
The Hàn (漢) Guǎngzōng (廣宗) county belonged to the Jùlù (鉅鹿) commandery.

Pín (嬪),
read as 'pí bīn'.

8 The Emperor considered the ancestral temple to be in Yè (鄴).

"Calamities and anomalies occur

The 15th year, initially,

Liú Yè alone said:

Liú Yè's words

Zhōngguó refers to our court, or the Central Plains, meaning that our forces will take eight or nine tenths.
Wú and Shǔ each protect one province.
To put it simply,

If Wú perishes, then Shǔ will be isolated.
If we cut Wú in half and give it to Shǔ,

Yì (抑),

He led [his troops] back to Xiǎnměi (顯美).
Xiǎnměi (顯美) County

Yào (曜) then arrived,

Jì (既) rewarded and encouraged his officers and soldiers,

All the generals said:

Jì (既) said:
“Currently, the army has no visible provisions;

If the enemy sees our forces combined,

To pursue them would mean dangerous roads and extreme hunger;

In this situation,
the troops cannot be relieved.
This is what is called ‘letting an enemy go for a day
causes trouble for generations’.”
In the Zuǒ Zhuàn (左傳),
Xiān Zhěn (先軫) said:
“To let an enemy go for a day

In the eleventh month,
several thousand Hú (胡) cavalry,

All the officers and soldiers were terrified.
Jì (既) secretly hid three thousand elite soldiers at night for an ambush,
and ordered Military Supervisor Chénggōng Yīng (成公英) to lead over a thousand cavalry to challenge them.
The Xìng Pǔ (姓譜) says: Descendants of Wèi Chénggōng (衞成公) became the Chénggōng (成公) clan.
I dare not say this is reliable.
The Hú (胡) indeed rushed to pursue them.
Jì (既) then sprung the ambush to cut off their rear,

He routed them,

Later, Qū Guāng (麴光) of Xīpíng (西平) rebelled,

All the generals wanted to attack him.
Jì (既) said:
“Only Guāng (光) and his ilk are rebelling;
the people of the commandery are not necessarily all complicit.
If we immediately confront them with an army,
the officials, common people, Qiāng (羌), and Hú (胡) will surely believe that the state does not distinguish right from wrong,
which will make them all stand together.
This is like giving a tiger wings.
Guāng (光) and his ilk want to use the Qiāng (羌) and Hú (胡) as support.
We should first make the Qiāng (羌) and Hú (胡) attack them,
and heavily reward and recruit them.
Whatever they capture,
we will give it all to them.
This will frustrate their power externally and isolate their connections internally,
and they will surely be pacified without a fight.”
Thereupon, he issued a proclamation to all the Qiāng (羌),
pardoning those who had been misled by Guāng (光) and his ilk;
those who could behead the rebel leader and present his head would be granted titles and rewards.
Consequently, Guāng’s (光) faction beheaded Guāng (光) and sent his head,
and the rest all settled down as before.
In the 21st year, Xíng Zhēn (邢貞) arrived in Wú (吳).
The people of Wú (吳) thought it appropriate to address him as Supreme General
and Marquis of Jiǔzhōu (九州).
The Wáng Zhì (王制) mentions Jiǔzhōu (九州),
one of which is the Son of Heaven’s domain,
and the other eight have eight Marquises.
The King of Wú (吳) said:
“Marquis of Jiǔzhōu (九州) is [a title] unheard of in antiquity.

The event is found in Volume 9, Hàn Gāodì (漢高帝) Year 1.
What harm is there in that!”
So he accepted it.
The King of Wú (吳) went out to Dūtíng (都亭) to await Zhēn (貞).
When Zhēn (貞) entered the gate,
he did not dismount his carriage.
Zhāng Zhāo (張昭) said to Zhēn (貞):
“Courtesy knows no disrespect,
and law knows no non-observance.
Yet you dare to be so arrogant and self-important,
is it because you think Jiāngnán (江南) is weak
and lacks even a square inch of a blade?!”
Zhēn (貞) immediately dismounted his carriage in haste.
Colonel of the Gentlemen-of-the-Household Xú Shèng (徐盛) of Lángyá (琅邪) was furious,
and turning to his colleagues, said:
“We, Shèng (盛) and others, are unable to exert ourselves and risk our lives
to conquer Xǔ (許) and Luò (洛) for the state
and swallow Bā (巴) and Shǔ (蜀),
and instead, our lord has to make an alliance with Zhēn (貞).
Is this not a disgrace?!”
Thereupon, tears streamed down his face.
Zhēn (貞) heard of this
and said to his followers:
“The generals and ministers of Jiāngdōng (江東) are like this;
they will not be subordinate to others for long.”
Observing Zhēn’s (貞) words,
he was good at observing states.
When he returned,
did he ever report this to the Lord of Wèi (魏)?
However, seeing Zhēn (貞) dismount his carriage due to Zhāng Zhāo’s (張昭) words,
his spirit was already cowed.
The Lord of Wú (吳) sent Grandee Zhào Zī (趙咨) of Nányáng (南陽) to offer thanks.
The Emperor asked:
“What kind of ruler
is the Lord of Wú (吳)?”
He replied:
“He is an intelligent, benevolent, wise, and strategically ambitious ruler.”
The Emperor asked about his traits.
He replied:
“To accept Lǔ Sù (魯肅) from humble origins,
that is his intelligence;
to promote Lǚ Méng (呂蒙) from the ranks,
that is his insight;
to capture Yú Jìn (于禁) without harming him,
that is his benevolence;
to take Jīngzhōu (荊州) without shedding blood,
that is his wisdom;
to occupy three zhōu (州) and regard the world like a tiger,
The three zhōu (州) are Jīng (荊), Yáng (揚), and Jiāo (交).
and to humble himself before Your Majesty,
that is his strategy.”
The Emperor asked:
“Does the King of Wú (吳) know anything of learning?”
Zī (咨) replied:
“The King of Wú (吳) sails tens of thousands of ships on the river,
commands a million armored soldiers,
employs the worthy and uses the capable,
and is devoted to governance and strategy.
Though he has leisure,
he extensively reads books and chronicles,
studies historical records,
and gathers unusual anecdotes,
not merely copying scholars who search for phrases and excerpt sentences.”
The Emperor was fond of literary works,
hence Zhào Zī (趙咨) used these words to subtly mock him.
“Zhāi (摘)”
in the Shǔ (蜀) version is written as
“Can Wú (吳) be conquered?”
He replied:
“A great state has armies for conquest,
and a small state has defenses for protection.”
These two sentences are from Guǎn Zǐ (管子).
“Does Wú (吳) fear Wèi (魏)?”
He replied:
“With a million armored soldiers,
and the Jiāng (江) and Hàn (漢) rivers as moats,
what fear is there!”
The Emperor asked:
“How many men like you, Grandee, are there in Wú (吳)?”
He replied:
“Those who are intelligent and outstanding,
there are eighty or ninety;
as for those like your servant,
they can be counted by the carriage-load and measured by the dipper,
innumerable.”
The emperor sent envoys to Wú to seek spikenard, large cowries, luminous pearls, ivory, rhinoceros horns, tortoiseshell, peacocks, kingfishers, fighting ducks, and long-crowing chickens.
The Běncǎo identifies xiāngfùzǐ (Cyperus rotundus) as spikenard.
This item is found everywhere,
it is not a rarity,
perhaps it is a different thing.
Cowries
are white like jade,
with purple spots forming patterns,
all arranged in neat rows.
Luminous pearls
come from Hépǔ,
the large ones are an inch in diameter.
Elephants come from Jiāozhǐ,
the males have two long tusks,
over ten feet long.
Rhinoceroses also come from Jiāozhǐ,
only the tōngtiānxī (celestial rhinoceros) is the most valuable;
its horn has white lines like threads.
If rice is placed in a chicken coop,
and the chickens go to peck the rice,
upon seeing the rhinoceros horn, they are startled and retreat.
Southerners call it hàijīxī (chicken-frightening rhinoceros).
Tortoiseshell (dàimào) resembles a turtle,
with burnt spots on its plastron and carapace.
The large ones are like basins or platters.
The Zhūfān Zhì states: [AS-827B] "The dài resembles a turtle or softshell turtle,
with thirteen plates on its carapace,
black and white patterns interspersed,
and the edges notched like a saw.
It has no feet but four fins,
the front ones long and the rear ones short,
using its fins to paddle through water.
The fins and head have patterns like its shell.
Older ones have thick shells with clear black and white distinctions,
younger ones have thin shells with indistinct patterns.
The popular belief that beating it makes the spots is
false."

the male's tail is golden green,
shining beautifully.
The Píyǎ says: "The Bówù Zhì states: 'Peacocks' tails often change color,
sometimes red, sometimes yellow,
like clouds and mist,
their color is not fixed.
If one claps its tail, it will dance.
The tail has golden-green feathers,
which only fully develop after five years.
In the first three years of its life,
the golden-green feathers are still small.
They sprout in early spring
and wilt again after three or four months,
flourishing and fading with the calyx of flowers.
People collect its tail feathers to adorn fans and whisks.
If plucked alive, the golden-green color does not diminish.'
Southerners who take their tails
conceal themselves in dense bamboo groves with a knife,
waiting for one to pass by.
They swiftly cut off its tail;
if not severed immediately,
it turns its head for a glance,
and the golden-green feathers lose their luster.
Whenever it wants to rest,
it first chooses a place to rest its tail.
Therefore, to capture one alive,
one waits for heavy rain to seize it,
as its tail becomes wet and heavy,
preventing it from flying high.
Even if people approach,
it cherishes its tail
and will not fly away."
Kingfishers (fěicuì),
are the size of sparrows.
The male, red, is called fěi;
the female, blue-green, is called cuì.

Ducks are tame,

"Jīng and Yáng provinces

saying, "Today's joyous drinking

Cáo Zhēn ordered Zhāng Hé to defeat the Wú troops,
and consequently seize and occupy the central isle of Jiānglíng.
Last year, Wú general Sūn Shèng occupied the central isle.
郃 (hé),
pronounced gǔ hé,
also hé gé.
2. In the 2nd month,
Zhūgě Liàng arrived at Yǒng'ān.
Commentary to the Water Classic:
The Former Lord of Shǔ, defeated by Wú,
retreated and garrisoned at Báidì,
which was renamed Yǒng'ān,
the seat of Bādōng Commandery.
3. Cáo Rén (曹仁), with tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry, advanced towards Rúxū (濡須).
First, he spread rumors that he intended to attack Xiànxī (羨溪) to the east.
Xiànxī (羨溪) is to the east of Rúxū (濡須).
The original annotations for Shǔ (蜀) held it to be Shāxiàn (沙羡),
which is incorrect.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: Xiànxī (羨溪) is thirty *lǐ* (里) east of Rúxū (濡須).
The previous year, the King of Wú (吳王) appointed Zhū Huán (朱桓) as the Inspector of Rúxū (濡須督).
Rén (仁) advanced directly with his large army.
Huán (桓), hearing of it,
recalled the troops from Xiànxī (羨溪).
Before the troops arrived, Rén (仁) suddenly appeared.
At that time, Huán (桓) had only five thousand men under his command and belonging to his department.
The various generals were all nervous and fearful.
Kǒng Ānguó (孔安國) said: *Yèyè* (業業)
means an anxious and fearful state of mind.
"Whenever two armies confront each other,
victory or defeat lies with the general,
not with numbers.
Gentlemen, you have heard of Cáo Rén's (曹仁) military tactics and troop movements;
how do they compare with Huán's (桓)?
The Art of War states, 'The guest army is double, while the host army is half,'
meaning
that they are both on open plains without city walls or moats,
and also that the bravery and cowardice of the soldiers are equally matched.
Now, Rén (仁) is neither wise nor brave,
and his soldiers are extremely timid.
Moreover, they have marched a thousand *lǐ* (里) on foot,
and both men and horses are exhausted.
Huán (桓) and you gentlemen occupy a high city,
facing the great river to the south,
and backed by mountains and hills to the north.
We are well-rested awaiting the weary,
and are the host controlling the guest.
This is a situation for a hundred victories in a hundred battles.
Even if Cáo Pī (曹丕) himself came,
there would be no cause for worry,
let alone Rén (仁) and his like!"
Huán (桓) then furled his flags and silenced his drums,
externally showing weakness to lure Rén (仁).
Rén (仁) sent his son, Tà (泰), to attack the city of Rúxū (濡須),
and separately dispatched generals Cháng Diāo (常雕) and Wáng Shuāng (王雙) to attack Zhōngzhōu (中洲) by 'oil boats.'
'Oil boats'
were probably made of ox hide,
with oil applied externally to repel water.
This was where Huán's (桓) subordinates' families resided.
Jiǎng Jì (蔣濟) said:
"The enemy occupies the west bank,
arraying their ships upstream,
while their troops enter the *zhōu* (洲).
This is to enter hell from within."
*Nèi* (內)
is the same as *nà* (納).
Rén (仁) did not follow,
but personally led ten thousand men to stay at Tuógāo (橐皋).
Tuógāo (橐皋)
is in Jūcháo (居巢) County, Lújiāng (廬江);
during the Spring and Autumn period, Wú (吳) held a meeting at Tuógāo (橐皋),
which is this place.
Today it is called Zhègāo (柘皋),
north of Rúxū (濡須).
I, the annotator, observe from Bān Zhì (班志)
that Tuógāo (橐皋) County belonged to Jiǔjiāng (九江) Commandery.
Mèng Kāng (孟康) pronounced it *Tuò Gū* (拓姑).
Dù Yù (杜預) said: Tuógāo (橐皋) is southeast of Qūnjiù (逡遒) County in Huáinán (淮南).
Lù Démíng (陸德明) said: *Tuó* (橐)
is pronounced *zhāng yè* (章夜) reversed,
also *tuō* (託).
Huán (桓) sent a separate detachment to attack Diāo (雕) and his group, while he personally resisted Tà (泰).
Tà (泰) burned his camp and retreated.
Huán (桓) then beheaded Cháng Diāo (常雕) and captured Wáng Shuāng (王雙) alive,
killing or drowning over a thousand men in battle.
Originally,
Lǚ Méng (呂蒙) was critically ill.
The King of Wú (吳王) asked:
"If you do not recover, who can replace you?"
Méng (蒙) replied:
"Zhū Rán (朱然) has abundant courage and defensive capabilities;
I believe he can be entrusted with the responsibility."
Zhū Rán (朱然)
was the son of Zhū Zhì's (朱治) elder sister, Zhū Zhì (朱治) being the Administrator of Jiǔzhēn (九真).
His original surname was Shī (施);
Zhì (治) adopted him as his son.
At that time, he was the General Who Demonstrates Martial Might (Zhāowǔ Jiāngjūn).
The General Who Demonstrates Martial Might (Zhāowǔ Jiāngjūn)
was an office established by Wú (吳).
The King of Wú (吳王) granted Rán (然) the imperial insignia (jié)
and stationed him at Jiānglíng (江陵).
When Cáo Zhēn (曹真) and others besieged Jiānglíng (江陵),
and defeated Sūn Shèng (孫盛),
the King of Wú (吳王) dispatched Zhūgě Jǐn (諸葛瑾) and others with troops to relieve the siege.
Xiàhóu Shàng (夏侯尚) attacked and repelled them.
Communication with Jiānglíng (江陵) was cut off,
and many soldiers in the city suffered from swelling sickness.
Only about five thousand men were fit for battle.
Zhēn (真) and others erected earthen mounds,
dug tunnels,
and set up siege towers overlooking the city.
Arrows rained down like torrents,
causing all the generals and soldiers to lose color in their faces.
Rán (然), however, remained composed and showed no fear,
demonstrating what Lǚ Méng (呂蒙) called 'courage and defensive capabilities.'
Seizing an opportune moment,
he attacked and broke two Wèi (魏) encampments.
The Wèi (魏) army besieged Rán (然) for a total of six months.
Yáo Tà (姚泰), the Magistrate of Jiānglíng (江陵), led troops to guard the north gate of the city.
Seeing the strength of the enemy outside
and the scarcity of men in the city,
with provisions almost exhausted,
he feared they could not hold out
and plotted to become an inside informant.
Rán (然) discovered this and killed him.
At that time,
the waters of the Jiāng (江) were shallow and narrow.
*Xiá* (陿)
is the same as *xiá* (狹).
*Zhǔ* (渚)
means *zhōu* (洲),
which is the central isle of Jiānglíng (江陵).
Those debating the situation, who frequently traveled between north and south,
largely believed the city could certainly be captured.
Dǒng Zhāo (董昭) submitted a memorial, stating:
"Emperor Wǔ (武皇帝), whose wisdom and bravery surpassed all others,
was nonetheless cautious when deploying troops against an enemy,
and dared not take such an opponent lightly.
This means that when moving troops, one dared not tread dangerous paths.
This is a constant rule.
Even on flat ground without natural defenses,
operations are still difficult.
If one has to advance deeply,
the return path should ideally be easy,
but troops must advance and retreat,
and cannot always have things as desired.
Now, establishing a camp on the *zhǔ* (渚)
is extremely deep penetration;
crossing by pontoon bridge
is extremely dangerous;
and moving along a single route
is extremely narrow.
These three
are things feared by military strategists,
yet they are being done now.
If the enemy frequently attacks the bridge,
and there is any oversight or failure,
meaning the bridge might be cut off by the enemy,
then
the situation will transform into Wú's (吳) favor.
I am privately worried about this,
losing sleep and appetite.
*Qī* (慼)
means worry.
How can this not be baffling?
Moreover, the river water is about to rise;
if it suddenly surges,
how will we defend against it?
Even if we don't defeat the enemy,
we should at least preserve ourselves.
Why embrace danger
without fear?
I urge Your Majesty to consider this."
The Emperor immediately issued an edict to Shàng (尚) and others, urging them to withdraw quickly.
The Wú (吳) people pressed forward on both sides,
while the Wèi (魏) army withdrew along a single path,
unable to exit in time.
*Xiè* (泄)
means to leave.
The Wú (吳) general Pān Zhāng (潘璋) had already prepared rafts of reeds,
intending to burn the pontoon bridge,
but Shàng (尚) retreated and he stopped.
Ten days later,
the Jiāng (江) river greatly swelled.
The Emperor said to Dǒng Zhāo (董昭):
"How insightful your assessment of this matter was!"
At that time, a great plague broke out.
The Emperor then recalled all the armies.
In the third month,
on the *bǐng shēn* (丙申) day,
the imperial carriage returned to Luòyáng (洛陽).
At first,
the Emperor asked Jiǎ Xǔ, saying,
"I wish to conquer those who disobey in order to unite all under Heaven.
Which should I attack first, Wú or Shǔ?"
He replied,
"One who seeks to conquer should prioritize military power;
one who establishes a foundation should value virtuous transformation.
Your Majesty has accepted the mandate in due time and received the abdication,
governing all lands under Heaven.
If you pacify them with civil virtue and await their changes,
then subjugating them will not be difficult.
Wú and Shǔ, though tiny states,
rely on mountains and are blocked by water.
Liú Bèi has heroic talent;
Zhūgě Liàng is good at governing the state;
Sūn Quán discerns the real from the false;
Lù Yì sees military strategies.
Lù Yì
is Lù Xùn.
Xùn's biography says: Xùn's original name was Yì.
They navigate rivers and lakes;
all are difficult to attack swiftly.
'Relying on strategic points and guarding crucial passes' refers to Shǔ;
'navigating rivers and lakes' refers to Wú.
*Zú*
is pronounced *cù*.
One should win first and then fight,
assessing the enemy and discussing their generals,
so no strategy is ever overlooked.
Your humble servant secretly estimates that among your officials, none can contend with Bèi or Quán;
even if you descend upon them with celestial might,
a perfectly secure situation has not yet appeared.
In ancient times, Shùn brandished shields and battle-axes, and the Miáo submitted.
Shùn broadly spread civil virtue,
brandishing shields and feathers on the two staircases,
and after seventy days, the Miáo submitted.
The Emperor did not heed him,
and the army ultimately achieved no success.
4 On the *dīngwèi* day,
Chén Zhōnghóu Cáo Rén passed away.
5 Initially,
Huáng Yuán, disliked by Zhūgě Liàng,
heard that the Hàn ruler was gravely ill,
and fearing future trouble,
he raised a rebellion with his entire commandery,
burning the city of Línqióng.
Línqióng county
belonged to Shǔ Commandery under Hàn.
As Shǔ had later established Hànjiā Commandery,
it should at this time belong to Hànjiā.
Qióng
is pronounced *qúróng*.
Chéngdū being thinly defended,
Yuán became even more unrestrained.
Yìzhōu's Director of Merits, Yáng Hóng,
advised the Crown Prince to dispatch Generals Chén Hū and Zhèng Chuò to suppress Yuán.
The general consensus was that if Yuán could not besiege Chéngdū,
he would occupy Yuècuì and seize Nánzhōng.
Nánzhōng refers to the lands of the Hàn commanderies of Yìzhōu and Yǒngchāng.
"Yuán's nature is fierce and violent,
and he possesses no other kindness or trustworthiness.
How could he accomplish this!
He will merely take advantage of the water to go east,
hoping the Emperor is well,
and then with bound hands return to face death;
if something is amiss,
he will flee to Wú to seek survival.
Just instruct Hū and Chuò to ambush him at the Nán'ān峡kǒu,
and he will immediately be captured."
Yuán's army was defeated,
and he indeed went east down the river.
Hū and Chuò captured him alive
and executed him.
This refers to going east down the Qīngyī River of Shǔ.
The *Shuǐ Jīng Zhù* says: The Qīngyī River flows out from Mount Méng west of Qīngyī county,
goes east to Línqióng county in Shǔ Commandery where it joins the Mò River,
and then goes further east to Nán'ān county in Jiànwéi where it enters the Great River;
this is what is called Nán'ān Xiágkǒu.
6 The Hàn ruler's illness worsened,
and he ordered Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng to assist the Crown Prince,
with the Minister of the Secretariat Lǐ Yán as his deputy.
The Hàn ruler said to Liàng,
"Your talent is ten times that of Cáo Pī;
you will surely be able to pacify the state
and ultimately accomplish the great task.
If the successor can be assisted,
assist him;
if he is untalented,
you may take the throne yourself."
Among rulers entrusting their sons to guardians since ancient times, none has been as clear-sighted and enlightened as Zhāoliè.
"How dare your servant not exhaust the strength of his limbs,
dedicate his loyal and steadfast integrity,
and follow it with death!"
This uses the meaning of Xún Xī's reply to Duke Xiàn of Jìn.
"A person reaching fifty is not considered to have died young.
I am already over sixty,
so what more is there to regret?
I am only concerned about you and your brothers.
Strive,
strive!
Do not commit evil, no matter how small;
do not neglect good, no matter how small!
Only the virtuous and the moral
can command people's submission.
Your father's virtue is shallow,
not worth emulating."
Since the Hàn dynasty, among those who issued edicts to successor rulers,
could any have uttered such words?
"Serve him as you would a father."
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the *guǐsì* day,
the Hàn ruler passed away at Yǒng'ān,
aged sixty-three.
Posthumous title rules: 'Zhāo' means having illustrious virtue and merit;
'Liè' means having achievements and pacifying the people.
Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng escorted the funeral procession back to Chéngdū,
appointing Lǐ Yán as Protector of the Central Capital,
leaving him to guard Yǒng'ān.
In the fifth month,
Crown Prince Chán ascended the throne,
at the age of seventeen.
The Latter Ruler of Shǔ was named Chán, courtesy name Gōngsì.
A general amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed to Jiànxīng.
Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wǔxiāng,
and concurrently held the post of Governor of Yìzhōu.
All matters, great or small,
were decided by Liàng.
Liàng then regulated official positions
and revised laws and institutions.
It was due to the harmony between the Former Ruler and Kǒngmíng as ruler and minister,
that the regulation of official positions and revision of laws and institutions were carried out during the time of assisting the Latter Ruler.
This is the *Yì* [hexagram] warning against *Jùn* (difficulties) and *Héng* (perseverance).
"Indeed, those who participate in discussions
gather collective wisdom and broaden beneficial advice.
'Participate in discussions'
means for actions taken,
to compare their similarities and differences,
record them and carry them out.
If it is difficult to disagree or review,
then there will be omissions and losses.
*Wéi*
means different;
*fù*
means review.
If it is difficult to differ,
difficult to review,
then affairs will have omissions and losses.
*Yuǎn*
is pronounced *yúyuàn*.
It is like discarding worn sandals to gain pearls and jade.
However, people unfortunately cannot fully exhaust their efforts,
only Xú Yuánzhí remained unconfused by this.
Furthermore,
Dǒng Yòuzǎi participated in discussions for seven years;
Xú Shù,
courtesy name Yuánzhí.
Dǒng Hé,
courtesy name Yòuzǎi.
*Chù*
is pronounced *chānglǚ*.
He would appear ten times
to enlighten and admonish me.
This is what is called 'disagreeing and reviewing'.
Yòuzǎi's diligence
was loyal to the state,
so Liàng could have fewer faults."
He also said:
"Formerly, when I first befriended Zhōupíng,
I personally tilled the fields
and was good friends with Cuī Zhōupíng, Xú Shù, and others.
Zhōupíng
was Cuī Liè's son
and Jūn's younger brother.
Later I befriended Yuánzhí,
who diligently enlightened and taught me;
previously I worked under Yòuzǎi,
and he would always speak his mind;
later I worked under Wěidù,
who frequently advised me to stop.
Although my nature is humble and dim,
and I could not accept all of it,
yet maintaining good relations with these four individuals from beginning to end
is enough to show that I did not doubt frank criticism."
Wěidù
was Liàng's Chief Clerk, Hú Jì of Yáng.
Zhūgě Liàng 諸葛亮 once personally inspected the account books.
The chief clerk, Yáng Yǒng 楊顒, entered directly
and remonstrated, saying:
"Governance has its structure;
superiors and subordinates should not encroach upon each other's duties.
Allow me to illustrate this for you, my lord, with a household analogy:
Suppose there is a person
who assigns slaves to farming,
maids to cooking,
a rooster to announce the dawn,
and a dog to bark at thieves;
oxen bear heavy loads,
and horses travel long distances.
No private task is neglected,
all needs are met,
and the master rests at ease with a high pillow,
simply eating and drinking.
But suddenly, one day, he wants to personally undertake all these tasks,
no longer entrusting them to others.
He exhausts his physical strength
with these trivial matters,
becoming physically weary and mentally drained,
ultimately achieving nothing.
Is it because his wisdom is inferior to that of slaves, maids, roosters, and dogs?
No, it is a failure to observe the principles of a household master.
Therefore, the ancients said, 'To sit and discuss the Way
is called a king or a duke;
to act and implement it
is called a shidàfū 士大夫.'
This is from the 'Kǎogōngjì 考工記' of the Zhōu Guān 周官.
Bǐng Jí 丙吉, as Chancellor under Emperor Xuān of Han,
once went out and encountered a cleared road.
There were people fighting, dead or wounded lying across the road,
but Jí 丙吉 passed by without inquiring.
Further on, he met a man chasing an ox,
and the ox was panting with its tongue hanging out.
Jí 丙吉 ordered his cavalry officer to ask:
'How many li has this ox been chased?'
His clerks and scribes thought the Chancellor had been remiss in his inquiries, first and last.
Jí 丙吉 said:
'People fighting and killing each other—that is the responsibility of the Cháng'ān Lìng 長安令 and the Jīngzhàoyǐn 京兆尹.
It is now early spring, the Lesser Yang is ascendant,
and it should not yet be very hot.
I fear the ox has traveled a short distance
and is panting due to the heat.
If the season's qi is out of balance
and causes harm,
it is the duty of the Sāngōng 三公 to harmonize yin and yang,
and it is their concern.
That is why I asked about it.'
The clerks and scribes then submitted,
recognizing that Jí 丙吉 understood the larger principles.
The phrase 'There are those who have their own responsibilities'
is found in volume 13, under the first year of Emperor Wén of Han.
Now, my lord, in your governance,
you personally inspect the account books,
sweating all day long—
is this not exhausting?"
Zhūgě Liàng 諸葛亮 thanked him.
When Yáng Yǒng 楊顒 died,
Zhūgě Liàng 諸葛亮 wept for three days.
7. In the sixth month,
on the Jiǎxū 甲戌 day,
Rènchéng Wēiwáng Zhāng 任城威王彰 died.
The Shìfǎ 諡法 (rules for posthumous titles) states: "Fierce and resolutely strong is called Wēi 威;
Subduing rebels and establishing merit is called Wēi 威."
8. On the Jiǎshēn 甲申 day,
Wèi Shòusù Hóu Jiǎ Xǔ 魏壽肅侯賈詡 died.
Wèi Shòu 魏壽
is a pavilion name.
The Shìfǎ 諡法 states: "Righteous virtue that achieves completion is called Sù 肅;
Holding firm to one's heart and making resolute decisions is called Sù 肅."
9. Great floods occurred.
10. Wú Hè Qí 吳賀齊 attacked Qíchūn 蘄春,
capturing the Administrator Jìn Zōng 晉宗 and returning with him.
Qíchūn Xiàn 蘄春縣,
during the Han dynasty, belonged to Jiāngxià Jùn 江夏郡;
Wú 吳 later divided it to establish Qíchūn Jùn 蘄春郡,
which was also known as Qíyáng 蘄陽,
and was renamed during the Eastern Jìn dynasty to avoid a taboo name.
The Shuǐjīng 水經 states: "The Qíshuǐ 蘄水 flows from the northern mountains of Qíchūn Xiàn 蘄春縣, Jiāngxià 江夏."
The commentary says: "This is the Qí Shān 蘄山.
It flows southwest past Qí Shān 蘄山,
then south opposite Qíyáng 蘄陽,
meeting the Great River.
It is also called Qíhé Kǒu 蘄河口."
According to the Hè Qí Zhuàn 賀齊傳: Jìn Zōng 晉宗
was a Wú 吳 general who
rebelled and surrendered to Wèi 魏,
and was made Administrator of Qíchūn 蘄春.
Hè Qí 賀齊 attacked and captured him.
11. Initially,
the leader of Yìzhōu Jùn 益州郡, Yōng Kǎi 雍闓, killed the Administrator Zhèng Áng 正昂,
and through Shì Xiè 士燮, sought to align with Wú 吳.
He also seized the Administrator of Chéngdū 成都, Zhāng Yì 張裔, and handed him over to Wú 吳.
Wú 吳 then appointed Yōng Kǎi 雍闓 as Administrator of Yǒngchāng 永昌.
Yǒngchāng Gōngcáo Lǚ Kǎi 永昌功曹呂凱 and Fǔchéng Wáng Kàng 府丞王伉
led their officials and soldiers to close the borders and resist.
Yōng Kǎi 雍闓 could not advance,
so he sent Mèng Huò 孟獲, a man from the commandery, to incite the various Yi tribes.
All the Yi tribes followed him.
Zāngkē Tàishǒu Zhū Bāo 牂柯太守朱褒 and Yuèsuī Yíwáng Gāo Dìng 越巂夷王高定 all rebelled and sided with Yōng Kǎi 雍闓.
Zhūgě Liàng 諸葛亮, having recently suffered a great loss (of Liú Bèi 劉備),
appeased them all and did not immediately suppress the rebellion.
He focused on agriculture, cultivating grain,
closing the passes to allow the people to rest.
This refers to closing the Língguān 靈關 of Yuèsuī 越巂.
12. In autumn,
the eighth month,
on the Dīngmǎo 丁卯 day,
the Grand Master of Ceremonies, Zhōng Yáo 鍾繇, was appointed Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi 太尉),
and Gāo Ròu 高柔, who oversaw legal enforcement, replaced him as Grand Master of Ceremonies.
Emperor Xuān of Han once visited the Xuānshì 宣室,
dwelling there in purification to resolve matters,
and ordered two Palace Recorders to administer legal documents at his side.
Later, a separate office was established,
known as the Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ 治書侍御史.
When Wèi 魏 was established, it also created the office of Zhìshū Zhífǎ 治書執法,
which was in charge of impeachments and memorials,
while the Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ 治書侍御史 was in charge of laws and statutes.
Both offices were established concurrently.
However, under the Jìn 晉 dynasty, only four Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ 治書侍御史 were retained.
"Zhì 治" (in zhìshū 治書) is pronounced "zhí" (直之翻).
As Gāo Ròu 高柔 seldom participated in court politics,
he submitted a memorial, stating:
"The ministers of state,
all pillars of the nation, are looked up to by the people.
The Shī 詩 says: 'Illustrious are Shī Yǐn 師尹, the people all look up to you.'
Not allowing them to be aware of political affairs
is contrary to ancient practice, where the Sāngōng 三公 were called the 'Three Officials.'
The Shī 詩 says: 'The Three Officials and Great Officers.'
This refers to the Sāngōng 三公.
To 'rest at ease'
means to lie down and be self-content.
This is truly not in keeping with the court's principle of valuing and employing senior ministers,
nor does it embody the idea of ministers offering sound advice and rejecting the unsound.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn 左傳 states: Qí Yànzǐ 齊晏子 said, 'If the lord deems something acceptable but it has flaws,
the minister presents its flaws to perfect its acceptability.
If the lord deems something unacceptable but it has merits,
the minister presents its merits to remove its unacceptability.'
They would frequently discuss matters under the huái 槐 and jí 棘 trees.
The Zhōu Lǐ 周禮 states: The Court Officials managed the laws of the outer court.
Facing three huái 槐 trees,
the Sāngōng 三公 were positioned;
to the left, nine jí 棘 trees,
the gū qīng dàfū 孤卿大夫 were positioned.
Zhèng Xuán's 鄭玄 commentary states: 'Planting jí 棘 trees to mark positions
takes their red heart and outward thorns as an analogy for presenting one's innermost thoughts three times.'

Diān,
