Therefore, he entrusted me with the task of suppressing the rebels.
With the Late Emperor's sagacity
and his assessment of my talent,
he surely knew that when I attacked the rebels,
my talent would be weak and the enemy strong.
However, if the rebels were not attacked,
the royal enterprise would also perish.
Merely sitting and waiting for ruin,
how could that compare to attacking them?
This is why he entrusted me and did not doubt me.
From the day I received my commission,
I have not rested peacefully,
nor found food palatable.
I reflected that for the northern expedition,
it was advisable to first enter the south.
Thus, in the fifth month, I crossed the Lú River,
penetrating deep into the barren lands.
It was not that I did not value my own life,
but I considered that the royal enterprise could not be completely secured only in Shǔdū.
Therefore, I risked dangers and difficulties to fulfill the Late Emperor's dying wish,
yet those who debated considered it not a good plan.
Now the rebels are currently exhausted in the west
and busy in the east.
'Exhausted in the west'
refers to the armies at Méixiàn and Qíshān.
'Busy in the east'
refers to the armies at Jiānglíng, Dōngguān, and Shítíng.
This is the time to advance.
I humbly present the following matters: Gāodì's brilliance rivaled the sun and moon,
and his strategists were profound.
Yet he traversed dangers, suffered wounds,
and only after facing peril did he find peace.
Now, Your Majesty is not equal to Gāodì,
and your strategists are not as good as Liáng and Píng.
Yet you wish to achieve victory with a long-term strategy
and settle the world by sitting still.
This is the first thing I do not understand.
Liú Yáo and Wáng Lǎng each held their respective prefectures and commanderies.
They discussed peace and spoke of strategies,
constantly invoking the sages.
Full of doubts,
obstructed by numerous difficulties,
they did not fight this year
and did not campaign next year,
allowing Sūn Cè to grow powerful
and eventually annex Jiāngdōng.
This is the second thing I do not understand.
Cáo Cāo's wisdom and stratagems were extraordinary,
and his use of troops
resembled Sūn Wǔ and Wú Qǐ.
With Cāo's skill in using troops,
Liàng considered him resembling Sūn Wǔ and Wú Qǐ.
Sūn Wǔ and Wú Qǐ were indeed not easily rivaled talents.
He was in peril at Wūcháo,
in danger at Qílián,
pressed at Líyáng,
almost defeated by Bóshān,
and nearly died at Tóngguān.
Only then did he falsely secure temporary control.
'Trapped at Nányáng' refers to his defeat by Zhāng Xiù when attacking Ráng.
'In peril at Wūcháo' refers to the time when he attacked Chúnyú Qióng, Yuán Shào's general.
'Pressed at Líyáng' refers to the time when he attacked Yuán Tán and his brothers.
'Almost defeated by Bóshān' refers to the time when he fought the Wūhuán at Báilángshān.
'Nearly died at Tóngguān' refers to the time when he fought Mǎ Chāo.
'In danger at Qílián'
needs to be investigated;
some say it refers to when he besieged Yuán Shàng at Qíshān.
'Falsely secured'
means that although he achieved temporary success,
he had the intention of usurping Hàn,
hence it is called 'false.'
Jǐ,
pronounced jū xī.
Yet you wish to achieve stability without danger.
This is the third thing I do not understand.
Cáo Cāo attacked Chāng Bà five times without success,
crossed Cháohú four times without achievement.
He appointed Lǐ Fú, but Lǐ Fú plotted against him.
He entrusted Xiàhóu, but Xiàhóu was defeated and perished.
Chāng Bà
is Chāng Xī.
Cāo repeatedly attacked but could not take him, later ordering Yú Jìn to attack and kill him.
'Crossed Cháohú four times without achievement'
refers to attacking Sūn Quán.
Lǐ Fú
is probably Wáng Fú,
who plotted with Dǒng Chéng to assassinate Cāo and was executed.
Xiàhóu
refers to Xiàhóu Yuān, who guarded Hànzhōng and was defeated by the Former Lord.
Even he had such failures;
how can I, being inferior,
necessarily win?
This is the fourth thing I do not understand.
'Inferior'
is a self-deprecating metaphor using a horse,
like a slow, low-grade steed.
In merely a year,
we lost Zhào Yún, Yáng Qún, Mǎ Yù, Yán Zhī, Dīng Lì, Bái Shòu, Liú Hé, Dèng Tóng, and others, as well as over seventy quzhang and tunjiang,
and over a thousand tuzhang, wuqian,
Cóngsǒu, Qīngqiāng, sǎnqí, and wǔqí soldiers.
Shǔ soldiers called them sǒu.
Cóngsǒu
are soldiers from Bācóng.
Qīngqiāng
are also a type of Qiāng.
Sǎnqí and Wǔqí
were names for cavalry divisions at that time.
Cóng,
pronounced cáng zōng.
Qí,
pronounced qí jì.
We gathered elite forces from all directions,
not just what one province possesses.
If this continues for a few more years,
two-thirds will be lost.
How then can we plan against the enemy?
This is the fifth thing I do not understand.
It means that without fighting, the officers and soldiers have already been depleted to such an extent.
And affairs cannot cease.
'Affairs cannot cease'
means that whether we stay or go,
the toil and expense are exactly the same.
But it is not as good as taking advantage of their vulnerability.
Liàng means he wants to seize the opportunity while Wèi and Wú are still entangled in war,
to exploit their vulnerability.
This is the sixth thing I do not understand.
Zhī
means to hold;
zhǐ jiǔ
means to endure for a long time.
Previously, the Late Emperor's army was defeated at Chǔ.
At that time,
Cáo Cāo clapped his hands,
saying that the world was now settled.
But then the Late Emperor allied with Wú and Yuè in the east.
The event is seen in Volume 65, Jiàn'ān 13th year of Emperor Xiàn of Hàn.
'Clapped his hands' refers to the outward manifestation of delight.
The event is seen in Volume 67, Jiàn'ān 19th year.
Xiàhóu was beheaded.
The event is seen in Volume 68, Jiàn'ān 24th year.
Then Wú again broke the alliance,
and Guān Yǔ was defeated.
The event is seen in Volume 68, Jiàn'ān 24th year.
These two instances of 'then'
are transitional words,
differing in meaning from 'then' in other texts.
Cáo Pī proclaimed himself emperor.
The event is seen in Volume 69, Huángchū 1st and 3rd years.
Difficulties cannot be foreseen.
I shall exert myself to the utmost,
until death.
As for success or failure, advantage or disadvantage,
these are not things my sagacity can foresee."
After the defeat at Qíshān,
Liàng became more aware of the true nature of the Wèi people,
hence his words were thus.
In the twelfth month,
Zhūgě Liàng 引兵 came out of Sànguān,
besieging Chéncāng.
Chéncāng was already prepared,
so Zhūgě Liàng could not conquer it.
Cáo Zhēn had sent Hǎo Zhāo to guard it beforehand,
which is why Zhūgě Liàng could not conquer it.
This further explains the situation of Hǎo Zhāo defending and Zhūgě Liàng attacking,
a standoff between guest and host.
The writing style of the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn is often like this.
Hǎo Zhāo responded from atop the tower, saying:
"The laws and regulations of the Wèi house
are something you are familiar with.
Kē (科)
means 'regulations' (tiáo 條).
Liàn (練)
means 'practiced' (xí 習).
This is something you know.
I have received much grace from the state and my family is prominent.
There is nothing you can say to me,
only that you must certainly die.
You may return and report to Zhūgě Liàng,
then you can attack."
Xiáng reported Hǎo Zhāo’s words in detail to Zhūgě Liàng.
Zhūgě Liàng again sent Xiáng to persuade Hǎo Zhāo,
saying,
"Your men and my troops are not evenly matched.
You will
only destroy yourselves."
Hǎo Zhāo said to Xiáng:
"My previous words are already settled.
I know you,
but the arrows do not."
Xiáng then left.
Zhūgě Liàng considered that he had tens of thousands of troops,
while Hǎo Zhāo's troops numbered only a little over a thousand.
He also calculated that the eastern relief force would not arrive quickly.
The Wèi troops coming to relieve Chéncāng came from the east,
hence it is called 'eastern relief'.
Dù (度),
read 'tuó luò' (徒洛) (as in tuóluò fān 徒洛翻).
He erected cloud ladders and battering rams to approach the city.
Hǎo Zhāo then shot fire arrows at his ladders,
the ladders caught fire,
and all the people on the ladders were burned to death.
Hǎo Zhāo also used ropes to attach millstones and drop them on their battering rams,
breaking the battering rams.
Zhūgě Liàng then built new 'well-ladders' (jǐnglàn 井闌) a hundred feet high to shoot into the city.
They were constructed of wood, resembling a well-ladder.
He wanted to directly scale the city.
Hǎo Zhāo then built a heavy inner wall.
Zhūgě Liàng also made 'ground-tunnels' (dìtū 地突).
Dìtū (地突)
means 'tunnels' (dìdào 地道).
Hǎo Zhāo also dug tunnels within the city to intersect them horizontally.
They attacked and defended day and night for over twenty days.
Cáo Zhēn dispatched General Fèi Yào and others to relieve them.
The emperor summoned Zhāng Hé from Fāngchéng.
At that time, Zhāng Hé was leading troops to attack Wú,
stationed in Fāngchéng.
The Xù Hàn Zhì says: South of Yè Xiàn there is a long mountain called Fāngchéng.
What Qū Wán referred to as
"the State of Chǔ taking Fāngchéng as its wall"
is this very place.
The emperor personally went to Hénán Chéng,
set up a feast to send Zhāng Hé off.
Hénán Chéng was west of Luòyáng Chéng.
"If the general arrives late,
Zhūgě Liàng might have already taken Chéncāng!"
Zhāng Hé knew that Zhūgě Liàng had advanced deep without provisions,
and counting on his fingers, said:
"By the time your subject arrives,
Zhūgě Liàng will have already fled."
Zhāng Hé advanced day and night.
Before he arrived,
Zhūgě Liàng ran out of provisions
and withdrew.
General Wáng Shuāng pursued him,
but Zhūgě Liàng attacked and slew Wáng Shuāng.
An imperial edict bestowed Hǎo Zhāo the title of Guān nèi Hóu.
The attackers were insufficient,
the defenders had more than enough.
If we discuss their talents,
the talent of the one who saved the city and repelled the enemy
was not superior to that of the attacker.
The difference lay in the relative positions of guest and host.
Therefore it is said, in the art of war,
siege warfare is the lowest form.
12. Earlier,
Gōngsūn Kāng died.
His sons Huǎng, Yuān, and others were all young,
so his officials established his younger brother Gōng.
Gōng was weak and incompetent,
unable to govern the state.
Once Yuān grew up,
he coerced and seized Gōng's position,
then submitted a memorial explaining the situation.
Attendant Counselor Liú Yè said:
"The Gōngsūn clan was employed by the Hàn dynasty.
Gōngsūn Dù guarded Liáodōng,
see volume 59, the first year of Chūpíng of Emperor Xiàn.
In ancient times, titles were hereditary, but offices were not.
Jué (爵)
refers to duke, marquis, count, viscount, and baron;
guān (官) refers to ministers and high officials.
Now, what is called 'hereditary office'
is because the land occupied by the Gōngsūn clan,
the position of Administrator of Liáodōng under the Hàn,
was inherited by their descendants,
which is hereditary office.
By land, they are blocked by mountains;
externally, they are connected with the Hú and Yí;
they are far away and difficult to control,
and their power has been established for a long time.
If they are not punished now,
they will certainly cause trouble later.
If they harbor disloyalty and raise troops,
and only then are punished,
it will be difficult to accomplish.
It is better to take advantage of his recent establishment,
when there are factions and enemies.
He had factions, hence he could seize Gōng's position.
Those who are his enemies
are Gōng's faction.
Approach them with troops,
set up rewards and recruitment,
and it can be settled without tiring our forces."
The emperor did not follow this advice.
He appointed Yuān as General Yángliè and Administrator of Liáodōng.
This laid the groundwork for Gōngsūn Yuān's rebellion against Wèi.
13. The King of Wú appointed Lǚ Fàn, the Governor of Yángzhōu, as Grand Marshal,
but he died before the seal and sash were conferred.
Earlier,
Sūn Cè had tasked Lǚ Fàn with managing finances.
At that time, the King of Wú was young.
If his personal attendants had requests,
Lǚ Fàn would always report them and seek approval,
not daring to grant them on his own.
At the time, he was resented for this.
Wàng (望)
means 'to blame' (zéwàng 責望)
or 'to resent' (yuànwàng 怨望).
Yángxiàn county,
in the Former Hàn, belonged to Kuàijī Commandery;
in the Later Hàn, it belonged to Wú Commandery.
Xián says: The old city is in present-day Yìxīng County, Chángzhōu.
Zhǎng (長),
read 'zhī liǎng' (知兩) (as in zhīliǎng fān 知兩翻).
If Sūn Cè sometimes reviewed accounts,
the officer Zhōu Gǔ would immediately make false entries in the ledgers,
so that there would be no reprimands or inquiries.
The King was pleased with this at the time.
However, when he later took charge of affairs,
because Lǚ Fàn was loyal and sincere,
he placed great trust in him.
Because Zhōu Gǔ was capable of deceiving and altering ledgers,
he did not employ him.
The way Zhōu Shìzōng treated Zhōu Měi,
and how Tàizǔ of our dynasty valued Dòu Yí,
are similar cases.
Gēng (更),
read 'gōng héng' (工衡) (as in gōnghéng fān 工衡翻).
1 In spring,
Zhūgě Liàng of Hàn sent his general Chén Jiè to attack Wǔdū and Yīnpíng Commanderies.
The Yīnpíng Dao,
during the Former Hàn, belonged to Guǎnghàn Commandery;
during the Later Hàn, it belonged to the Commandant of the Guǎnghàn Protectorate;
Wèi divided it and established Yīnpíng Commandery;
in the Táng dynasty, it became Wénzhōu.
In the Yǔ Gòng, the Hēishuǐ and Xīhé formed Yōngzhōu.
Because it was a land of four mountains,
it was therefore named Yōng;
it is also said that it was the northwest position
which the yang could not reach,
where yin and yang were blocked and hindered.
The Zhōu capital was Fēng and Hào,
and Yōngzhōu was the royal domain;
when King Píng moved east,
Yōngzhōu became Qín territory.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn established thirteen zhōus;
he designated the western part of Yōngzhōu as Liángzhōu,
and the rest all belonged to Sīlì.
When Emperor Guāngwǔ made Luòyáng his capital,
Yōngzhōu was re-established in Guānzhōng,
but was soon abolished,
and Sīlì was again made to govern the Sānfǔ.
In the first year of Xīngpíng of Emperor Xiàn,
the region west of the river was cut off by river bandits,
so Yōngzhōu was established to govern the various commanderies west of the river.
By Wèi,
Liángzhōu was established in Hexi,
and Lǒngyòu was made Yōngzhōu.
And by Jìn,
Qínzhōu was established in Lǒngyòu,
while Yōngzhōu governed Jīngzhào, Féngyì, Fúfēng, Āndìng, Běidì, Xīnpíng, Wǔdū, and Yīnpíng.
Yōng,
read yú yòng.
Shuǐ Jīng Zhù: The Hàn River flows southwest past the south of Qíshān Military Command,
then flows west to merge with the Jiàn'ān Chuān River.
The Jiàn'ān River originates from the mountains northwest of Jiànwēi,
flows east past the south of Jiànwēi City,
then flows east again past the south of Xīxiàn and Lìchéng.
Zhù Mù said: Of the great rivers in the world,
there are two named Hàn;
Bān Gù called them the Eastern Hàn and Western Hàn,
and the Hàn River in Lízhōu which originates from Fēiyuè Lǐng is not included.
What Gù called the Eastern Hàn,
is the Yàng Hàn of the Yǔ Gòng,
whose source is in the Bōzhǒng Mountains of Xīxiàn in present-day Xīngyuán,
and which flows through Yáng, Jīn, Fáng, Jūn, Xiāng, Yǐng, and then reaches Hànyáng to enter the Jiāng, this is it.
As for the Western Hàn, it is what Sū Dài referred to as
"the troops from Hánzhōng,
in light boats departing from Bā,
sailing down the Xiàshuǐ to reach Wǔzhǔ in four days,"
its source is outside the border of Xīhézhōu,
it flows through Jiēmiǎn Chuān to meet the Jiālíng River,
commonly called the Western Hàn;
it then flows through Dà'ān Jūn, Lì, Jiàn, Làng, Guǒ, Hé to meet the Fú River,
reaching Yúzhōu to enter the Jiāng.
Liàng then captured the two commanderies and returned;
the Hàn lord again appointed Liàng as Chancellor.
2 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the day of bǐngshēn,
the King of Wú ascended the imperial throne,
granted a great amnesty,
and changed the era name to Huánglóng.
At this time, Xiàkǒu and Wǔchāng both reported seeing a yellow dragon,
so Quán accordingly changed the era name.
The Wú lord attributed the success to Zhōu Yú.
The General Who Pacifies Distant Lands, Zhāng Zhāo,
raised his tablet to praise his merits,
but before he could speak,
Shěn Yuē's note: Wèi established forty general titles,
Sūiyuǎn was the fourteenth.
"If it were according to Master Zhāng's plan,
we would now be begging for food."
Attributing the success to Zhōu Yú,
meaning his ability to resist Cáo Gōng and achieve the three-part division of the realm.
Begging for food,
refers to Zhāng Zhāo's desire to welcome Cáo Gōng.
The matter is found in Volume 65, Jiàn'ān Thirteenth Year of Emperor Xiàn of Hàn.
[Zhāng Zhāo] prostrated himself and sweat profusely.
The Wú lord posthumously honored his father Jiān as Emperor Wǔliè,
and his elder brother Cè as King Huán of Chángshā,
established his son Dēng as Crown Prince,
and enfeoffed Cè's son Shào as Marquis of Wú.
He appointed Zhūgě Kè as Crown Prince Left Assistant,
Zhāng Xiū as Right Protector,
Gù Tán as Correcting Assistant,
Chén Biǎo as Wing-Correcting Commandant,
Correcting Assistant and Wing-Correcting Commandant were both offices created by Wú itself.
This
is the ancient character for dào.
The Crown Prince ordered his Attendant Counselor Hú Zōng to compile a list of friends and associates.
Mù refers to
evaluating and classifying individuals based on their talent and character.
"Of outstanding talent,
surpassing peers,
it is Zhūgě Kè;
of keen insight into timely opportunities,
penetrating the obscure and delving into the minute,
it is Gù Tán;
of firm and broad eloquence,
whose words can resolve entanglements,
it is Xiè Jǐng;
Níng means
firm and steady.
Hóng means
vast and far-reaching.
Dá means
clear and penetrating.
Those who are fond of debate are often unable to maintain their stance,
therefore, it is said that he can maintain firm eloquence and his evidence is vast and far-reaching.
Those who are clear and penetrating can resolve difficult and confusing entanglements.
Of the same caliber as Yóu and Xià,
it is Fàn Shèn."
Jiū means
to thoroughly examine.
Zhēn means
to discern and distinguish.
Xià,
read hù yǎ.
[Hú Zōng also remarked:]
"Yuánsùn is talented but careless;
Zihēi is perceptive but ruthless;
Shūfā is eloquent but shallow;
Xiàojìng is profound but narrow-minded."
Zhūgě Kè,
courtesy name Yuánsùn;
Gù Tán,
courtesy name Zihēi;
Xiè Jǐng,
courtesy name Shūfā;
Fàn Shèn,
courtesy name Xiàojìng.
Hěn,
read hù kěn.
Xiá,
same as xiá.
Later, all four men met with failure,
just as [Hú Zōng] had said.
The King of Wú sent an envoy to Hán to inform them of the proposal to equally honor the two emperors.
The Hán people thought that such an alliance would be useless and that the proper designations were not in accord.
They believed it was appropriate to clearly state the correct principles
and sever the alliance.
Heaven has no two suns,
and earth has no two kings;
this is the righteous principle of all times.
Hǎo,
pronounced Hū-dào.
"Sūn Quán has long harbored intentions of usurpation and rebellion.
The reason the state has overlooked his hostile intentions
is to seek support for a pincer attack."
Xìn,
meaning a rift.
Qíng,
meaning desire.
The Zǔo Zhuàn states: Róngzǐ Jūzhī said to Fàn Xuānzǐ,
"Regarding the army at Xiáo,
Jìn held them from above,
and the Róng resisted them from below.
The Qín army did not return,
and we, the various Róng, indeed caused this.
It is like hunting a deer;
the Jìn people held its antlers,
and the various Róng held its legs,
and we brought it down with Jìn."
Dù Yù noted: "Jǐ its legs."
"His hatred for us will surely be deep. We should move our troops eastward to garrison,
engage in a struggle of strength with him,
and only after conquering his territory
should we discuss the Central Plains.
He still has many talented individuals,
and his generals and ministers are harmonious.
He cannot be subjugated in a single day.
To keep troops stationed, passively waiting to grow old,
is not the best strategy."
Xū,
meaning to wait.
"This is not the best of calculations.
The northern bandit,
referring to Wèi,
was generously allied with the former emperor to Wú."
Details are all seen before.
Yōu,
meaning ample or generous.
People today still call leniency "yōu ráo."
"This was a profound thought with long-term benefits,
not like the petty anger of common men."
It means the plan was grand.
"Unable to unite their strength,
and with his ambitions already satisfied,
he has no desire to 'go ashore',"
meaning Sūn Quán's ambition was to protect Jiāng,
and he could not "go ashore" and face north.
Shàng,
pronounced Shí-zhǎng.
"All these seem right but are not."
"Why?
His wisdom and strength are not equal to the task,
hence he limits himself to protecting the Jiāng.
Sūn Quán's inability to cross the Jiāng
is like the Wèi bandit's inability to cross the Hán.
This means Wèi cannot cross the Hán to conquer Jiānglíng.
This Hán
is what the Bān Zhì refers to as the Dōnghàn river.
And yet no advantage is taken.
If a large army were to launch a punitive expedition,
he would, at best, divide his territory as a future strategy;
at worst, he would plunder the people and expand his borders,
displaying military might internally.
He would not sit idly by."
It means if Shǔ defeats Wèi,
Wú will also share the spoils.
"If we campaign north,
without worries to the east,
the forces in Hénán cannot all move west.
This benefit
is already profound."
It means if Shǔ and Wú are at peace,
then even if the whole nation campaigns north,
there is no need to worry about the east to guard against Wú.
And Wèi's forces in Hénán,
wanting to remain to guard against Wú,
cannot all move west to resist the Shǔ army.
"It is not appropriate to make this clear yet."
Thereupon, Wèiwèi Chén Zhèn was sent as an envoy to Wú
to congratulate him on assuming the imperial title.
The King of Wú allied with the Hán people,
agreeing to divide the empire,
with Yù, Qīng, Xú, and Yōu belonging to Wú,
and Yǎn, Jì, Bīng, and Liáng belonging to Hán.
As for the territory of the Sī Zhōu,
Hángǔ Pass would serve as the boundary.
Emperor Wǔ of Hán established the Sīlì Xiàowèi,
whose jurisdiction included the Sānfǔ and Sānhé commanderies.
Its western boundary included the Jīngzhào, Fúfēng, and Féngyì commanderies of Yōng Zhōu;
its northern boundary included the Hédōng and Hénèi commanderies of Jì Zhōu;
and its eastern boundary included the Hénán and Hóngnóng commanderies of Yù Zhōu.
His position and prestige were superior to that of the Mù Bó,
with a silver seal and green ribbon,
above the thirteen regional inspectors.
Later, Hán abolished the Shuòfāng regional inspector and subordinated it to Bīng Zhōu,
counting Sīlì among the thirteen regional inspectors.
Wèi established Sī Zhōu with the Hédōng, Hénán, Hénèi, and Hóngnóng commanderies, and Píngyáng of Jì Zhōu,
totaling five commanderies,
and returned the Sānfǔ to Yōng Zhōu.
This statement that Sī Zhōu used Hángǔ Pass as its boundary
refers to dividing it according to what Hán's Sīlì used to govern.
Zhāng Zhāo, due to old age and illness, resigned his official positions and commands.
He was then re-appointed Fǔwú Jiāngjūn,
with rank second only to the Sān Sī,
and enfeoffed as Lóu Hóu.
Lóu
was an ancient county.
In the Former Hán, it belonged to Kuàijī Commandery;
in the Later Hán, it was assigned to Wú Commandery;
it is now the area of Kūnshān County in Sūzhōu.
Wú enfeoffed Zhāo there,
not meaning he was truly made king of Lóu and ruler of its people.
Whenever Zhāo had an audience,
his words and manner were strong and solemn,

Zhé,

Zhǔ,

Hàn Xuān succeeded after Zhāo Dì,

They successively followed this practice.
This refers to Hàn Ān Dì honoring his father, Qīng Hé Xiào Wáng, as Xiào Dé Huáng;

The Spring and Autumn Annals: Second year of Duke Wén,

Sacrifice

Huá
is pronounced 'hù huà fān'.
We must deeply take the actions of previous generations as a warning.

7th month,
9th month,

'Repelling the enemy thousands of miles away':

"From ancient times, those who have ruled states and possessed families

治 [zhì],
is pronounced 'zhí lì' (direct official) in transcription;
the same below.

A monarch, inheriting foundations from successive generations,
holding natural power,

操 [cāo],
is pronounced 'qiān gāo' (thousand high) in transcription.
(Since he) takes nothing from others,

1 In spring,
the ruler of Wú sent General Wèi Wēn and Zhūgé Zhí with ten thousand armored soldiers
to sail the sea in search of Yízhōu and Dànzhōu.
The "Records of the Eastern Barbarians" in the Hòuhànshū states: "Beyond Kuàijī there are Yízhōu and Dànzhōu.
Tradition says Qín Shǐhuáng sent Xú Fú with several thousand boys and girls into the sea
to seek the immortal land of Pénglái, but failed.
Xú Fú, fearing execution,
dared not return,
and thus settled on this island.
Generations succeeded one another,
with tens of thousands of families.
Their people sometimes came to trade in Kuàijī.
There were people from Kuàijī's Dōngyě county who sailed the seas,
encountered storms, and drifted to Dànzhōu.
Their location was extremely remote,
making travel impossible."
Shěn Yíng's Línhǎi Shuǐtǔ Zhì says: "Yízhōu is east of Línhǎi,
two thousand *lǐ* from the commandery.
The land has no frost or snow;
plants do not die.
All four sides are mountains and valleys.
The land has copper and iron.
They only use deer antlers as spears for fighting,
and sharpen bluestones to make bows and arrows.
They take raw fish and meat, store them mixed in large earthenware jars,
cure them with brine.
After more than a month,
they still eat them,
considering them a supreme delicacy.
Nowadays, people widely transmit that
the Wō people are from the land where Xú Fú settled and became king.
In their country, Xú Fú is still worshipped in temples to this day."
Lù Xùn and Quán Cóng both remonstrated,
saying:
"King Huán founded the base,
with not even one brigade of soldiers.
Now, the current forces in Jiāngdōng
are sufficient to accomplish matters.
One should not venture far into barren lands,
to attack people thousands of *lǐ* away.
The winds and waves are unpredictable.
Moreover, the people are susceptible to unfamiliar climates,
which will inevitably lead to illness and plague.
Wishing to gain will instead lead to loss;
wishing for benefit will instead result in harm.
Furthermore, these people are like wild beasts;
gaining them is not enough to help with affairs,
and lacking them is not enough to diminish our strength."
The ruler of Wú did not listen.
2 Shàngshū Lángyé Zhūgé Dàn, Zhōngshū Láng Nányáng Dèng Yáng and others—
*Zhōngshū Láng*
is *Tōngshì Láng*.

*Yáng*
is pronounced *yúzhāng*,
also *yúliàng*.

Xuán
was the son of Shàng.
Zhōngshū Jiān Liú Fàng's son Xī,
Zhōngshū Lìng Sūn Zī's son Mì,

*Bǐ*
means 'to rank equally'.

Acting Sītú Dǒng Zhāo
(One whose qualifications were too light to be appointed *gōng* was called 'acting' (*xíng*) *shì*.)
memorialized:
"All who possess the realm
value and esteem sincere, honest, and trustworthy gentlemen,
and deeply despise deceitful and insincere people,
because they corrupt teachings, disturb governance,
ruin customs, and harm transformation.

and Cáo Wěi was beheaded at the beginning of Huángchū.

The case of Cáo Wěi is found in volume 69, Huángchū 2nd year.)
(The emperor) deeply loathed the superficial and deceitful,
wishing to break up perverse factions,
often gnashing his teeth;
yet the officers of the law
all feared their power and influence,
unable to expose or correct them.
This ruined public morals,
and greed grew rampant.
I secretly observe that young people today no longer take learning as their foundation,
but instead specialize in social networking as their profession.
Gentlemen of the state no longer prioritize filial piety, fraternal duty, purity, and cultivation,
but rather consider chasing power and seeking gain as primary.
They form cliques and factions,
praising each other excessively.
They use disparagement and denigration as punishment and execution,
and factional praise as爵赏 (*juéshǎng*).
Those who attach themselves are praised with overflowing words.
(*Tàn* means to sigh in admiration and praise their beauty.
*Yíng* means overflowing.

overflowing in words and phrases,
is 'overflowing praise'.
A defect in jade is called *xiá*;
a crack in a vessel is called *xìn*.)
They only seek that people are not diligent in the human way,
and that they are not widely ensnared.
It means they widely spread party friends,
so they become each other's wings,
their bodies are safe and without trouble,
and they can pass through life.
'You only need to swallow them with medicine and soften them.'
This means that when praise and criticism are applied,
if they truly like praise and dislike criticism,
their hearts will become soft and compliant,
and they will not offend me,
like swallowing them with medicine.
They intrude and exit,
circulate in forbidden private areas,
exchange letters and documents,
making inquiries.
It means, for example, if one's position is *Shàngshū*,
entering and exiting the forbidden palace,
then there are *Lìshǐ*,
*Zhǔshū*,
*Cāngtóu*, and *Lú'ér* serving them.
Now, they allow their slaves and retainers to usurp their names,
and use their entry and exit to commit fraud.
All of these are not permitted by law,
and unforgivable by punishment.
Even the crimes of Wèi Fěng and Cáo Wěi
cannot surpass this!"
The Emperor approved his words.
In the second month,
on the *rénwǔ* day,
an edict stated:
"The simplicity and refinement of the world
change with teachings.
(It means Yīn favored simplicity,
Zhōu favored refinement,
each changing with their teachings.)

while younger generations strive for advancement
without following the canons and counsels.
Should those to be promoted not be distinguished by virtue?
Let the *Lánglì* who are thoroughly versed in one classic
and capable of governing the people
be examined and tested by the *Bóshì*.
Those who achieve high ranks
shall be promptly employed.
Those who are superficial and ostentatious, not dedicated to the fundamental principles of the Way,
shall be dismissed and removed!"
(*Lánglì*
refers to *Shàngshū Láng*.)

The Emperor agreed with this.
Mǎn Chǒng wanted to remove the defender of Xīnchéng
and bring the bandits to Shòuchūn.
The Emperor did not approve,
saying:
“In the past, Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn dispatched troops to occupy Luèyáng,
eventually defeating Wěi Xiāo.
This event is recorded in volume forty-two, Jiànwǔ eight years.
Defending Xiāngyáng in the south and
fortifying Qíshān in the west,
whenever bandits arrived, they were defeated beneath these three cities.
There are places that must be contested.
Héféi and Xiāngyáng are to guard against Wú,
and Qíshān is to guard against Shǔ.
You definitely cannot remove him.
Command all generals to hold firm.
I will personally go and campaign against them.
By the time I arrive,
I fear Sūn Quán will have fled.”
Then he sent the Protector of the Army for Suppressing Shǔ, Qín Lǎng, to command two myriad infantry and cavalry to assist Sīmǎ Yì in resisting Zhūgě Liàng,
instructing Yì:
“Just hold firm in your fortifications and defend to blunt their edge.
If they advance but do not achieve their aim,
and retreat with no one to fight,
if they halt for long, their provisions will run out,
and they will gain no spoils.
Then they will surely flee.
To pursue them when they flee
is the way to complete victory.”
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
the Emperor commanded his dragon boat to campaign eastward.
Mǎn Chǒng recruited brave warriors to burn the Wú siege equipment,
and shot and killed Tàishǐ Cí, the nephew of the Wú ruler.
Moreover, many of the Wú officers and soldiers fell ill.
Before the Emperor had arrived within several hundred *lǐ*,
his feinting forces arrived first.
The Wú ruler initially thought the Emperor would not be able to come out,
but hearing that the main army had arrived,
he fled.
Sūn Sháo also retreated.
Lù Xùn dispatched his close associate Hán Biǎn to carry a memorial to the Wú ruler,
but scouts captured him.
Zhūgě Jǐn, hearing of this, was greatly alarmed
and wrote to Xùn, saying:
“The imperial carriage has already returned.
The enemy has captured Hán Biǎn and knows our full situation, both wide and narrow.
Furthermore, the water is drying up.
It would be advisable to withdraw immediately.”
Xùn did not reply.
Instead, he was urging people to plant turnips and beans.
Turnips
are a type of vegetable,
also called *mànjīng*.
Beans
are a type of pulse.
Jǐn said:
“Bóyán has many strategies.”
Lù Xùn,
whose other name was Yì,
with the courtesy name Bóyán.
So Jǐn personally went to see Xùn.
Xùn said:
“The enemy knows that the imperial carriage has already returned
and has nothing more to worry about;
they can focus their strength on us.
Also, they have already taken control of strategic locations.
The soldiers' intentions are wavering,
thinking that since the enemy knows Sūn Quán has returned,
they calculate Xùn’s army should retreat,
and have already divided to hold strategic locations,
intending to intercept Xùn’s forces.
Since they no longer have the spirit to advance,
but are preoccupied with intercepting,
their morale will likely be shaken,
leading to either surrender or collapse.
*Fù*
is pronounced *fúyòufān*.
We must employ a ruse
and then withdraw.
If we show signs of retreat now,
the enemy will think we are afraid
and will come to press us,
which would be a certain defeat.”
So he secretly plotted with Jǐn,
ordering Jǐn to command the boats,
while Xùn led all his infantry and cavalry towards Xiāngyáng City.
The Wèi people had always feared Xùn’s reputation
and immediately returned to defend the city.
Jǐn then led the boats out,
and Xùn slowly arranged his formations,
making a show of force,
advancing on foot to the boats.
The Wèi people dared not approach.
When they reached Báiwéi—
It means they set up a fortified camp at the mouth of the Báihé river,
hence the name.
—he secretly sent generals Zhōu Jùn and Zhāng Liáng to attack Jiāngxià, Xīnshì, Ānlù, and Shíyáng.
Xīnshì and Ānlù counties
both belonged to Jiāngxià Commandery.
In the early Wèi period, Wén Pìn was made Administrator of Jiāngxià
and stationed at Shíyáng,
where boats and carriages converged,
making it quite prosperous.
Shěn Yuè said:
Jiāngxià Qǔlíng County was originally named Shíyáng.
In the first year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
it was renamed Qǔlíng.
In the sixth year of Tàishǐ of Emperor Míng of Sòng,
Qǔlíng was merged into Ānlù County.
His ministers thought that since Sīmǎ Yì and Zhūgě Liàng were still deadlocked,
the imperial carriage could proceed west to Cháng'ān.
The Emperor said:
“Sūn Quán has fled,
and Zhūgě Liàng’s courage is broken.
My great army is sufficient to control them.
I have no worries.”
So he advanced his army to Shòuchūn,
recorded the achievements of his generals,
and bestowed rewards accordingly.
8. In the eighth month,
on the *rénshēn* day,
Emperor Xiàoxiàn of Hàn was buried in Chánlíng.
The Records of Emperors and Kings state: Chánlíng is ten *lǐ* northwest of Zhuólù City.
Xián said: It is twenty-five *lǐ* north of today’s Huáizhōu Xiūwǔ County.
Liú Chéng’s geographical record states: Because Hàn abdicated to Wèi,
it was named thus.
9. On the *xīnsì* day,
the Emperor returned to Xǔchāng.
10. Sīmǎ Yì and Zhūgě Liàng maintained a standoff for over a hundred days.
Liàng repeatedly challenged him to battle,
but Yì did not come out.
Liàng then sent Yì women’s headwear and clothing.
Yì was enraged
and submitted a memorial requesting battle.
The Emperor sent the Grand Commandant Xīn Pí with a staff of authority as army advisor to restrain him.
The Protector of the Army Jiāng Wéi said to Liàng:
“Since Xīn Zuǒzhì has arrived with a staff of authority,
the enemy will no longer come out.”
Liàng said:
“He fundamentally has no intention to fight.
His insistent request for battle
is merely to display his martial prowess to his troops.
When a general is in the army,
there are some imperial commands he need not accept.
This is what Sūn Wǔzǐ and Sīmǎ Rángjū said.
*Jiàng*
is pronounced *jíliàngfān*.
How could one request battle from a thousand *lǐ* away!”
Liàng sent an envoy to Yì’s army.
Yì asked about his sleep, appetite, and the complexity of his duties,
but did not ask about military affairs.
Yì feared Liàng,
so he asked about his sleep, appetite, and the complexity of his duties
to gauge how long he might live.
Why ask about military affairs?
The envoy replied: “Lord Zhūgě rises early and sleeps late,
personally reviewing all punishments involving twenty or more strokes;
his daily food intake does not exceed a few *shēng*.”
Yì told others:
“Zhūgě Kǒngmíng eats little and has many duties;
how can he last long!”
Liàng became critically ill.
The Hàn
sent the Minister of the Court and Prefect of the Palace Writers, Lǐ Fú, to attend to him
and consult him on the major affairs of state.
When Fú arrived,
he spoke with Liàng,
then took his leave.
*Yǐ*
means "finished";
their conversation was finished and then he left.
Liàng said:
“I know your intention to return.
Though our recent conversation lasted all day,
some things were not fully discussed,
so you came back to seek a decision.
Regarding what you asked,
Jiǎng Wǎn is suitable.”
Fú apologized:
“Previously, I indeed failed to consult you.
Should you pass away,
who can be entrusted with important affairs?
That is why I returned.
May I ask again, after Jiǎng Wǎn,
who can be entrusted?”
Liàng said:
“Fèi Wěi can succeed him.”
When asked about the next in line,
Liàng did not reply.
Fèi Wěi,
whose courtesy name was Wénwěi.
Liàng not replying about the person to succeed Fèi Wěi
was not in the spirit of Emperor Gāo’s
“After this, it is not within my knowledge,”
but rather because he saw that there were no individuals in Shǔ capable of succeeding Fèi Wěi.
Alas!
In this month,
Zhūgě Liàng died in the army.
Chángshǐ Yáng Yí marshaled the army and withdrew.
The common people rushed to inform Sīmǎ Yì,
and Yì pursued them.
Jiāng Wéi ordered Yáng Yí to turn back the flags and beat the drums,
as if about to charge Sīmǎ Yì.
Yì gathered his troops and retreated,
not daring to press closer.
He still feared that Zhūgě Liàng was not yet dead.
Only after entering the valley was the mourning announced.
This refers to entering Xié Gǔ.
"The dead Zhūgě scares away the living Zhòngdá."
Sīmǎ Yì's
courtesy name was Zhòngdá.
Looking at the common saying of the people at that time,
what did the people of that time think of Kǒngmíng!
(Sīmǎ Yì) laughed and said:
"I can predict the living,
but not the dead."
Yì inspected the camp sites of Zhūgě Liàng
and sighed, saying:
"What a truly exceptional talent!"
When Zhūgě Liàng first set out,
Sīmǎ Yì thought that if he advanced west to Wǔzhàng Yuán,
the generals would have nothing to worry about.
When Zhūgě Liàng died and the army retreated,
Sīmǎ Yì inspected his camp sites
and concluded he was an exceptional talent.
From this,
one knows that Sīmǎ Yì had already anticipated Zhūgě Liàng's inevitable encampment at Wǔzhàng Yuán,
but was powerless to stop him,
so he merely said this to reassure his generals.
行 (háng),
read as "xià mèng" (孟).
Unable to catch up, he returned.
Initially,
the Han army's Qián Jūnshī Wèi Yán –
Shǔ had set up Zhōng Jūnshī, Qián Jūnshī, and Hòu Jūnshī.
– was skilled at caring for his soldiers.
Whenever he accompanied Zhūgě Liàng on campaigns,
he always wanted to request a force of ten thousand men,
to meet Zhūgě Liàng at Tóngguān by a different route,
following the precedent of Hán Xìn.
The precedent of Hán Xìn requesting troops
can be found in Volume 9, Han Gāodì Year 2.
Wèi Yán often considered Zhūgě Liàng to be timid,
and lamented that his own talents were not fully utilized.
Yáng Yí was efficient and keen;
whenever Zhūgě Liàng went on campaign,
Yáng Yí would always plan and divide tasks,
calculate and estimate provisions,
without needing to deliberate,
finishing it in a moment.
斯 (sī)
means "this";
須 (xū)
means "wait";
meaning that by this wait,
the work can be done.
分 (fēn),
read as "fú wèn" (扶問).
度 (dù),
read as "tú luò" (徒洛).
(Zhūgě Liàng) relied on Yáng Yí to get things done.
Wèi Yán was arrogant by nature;
everyone at the time avoided him and gave way,
but only Yáng Yí did not defer to Wèi Yán.
Wèi Yán found this utterly infuriating,
and their relationship was like fire and water.
Meaning they could not coexist.
(Zhūgě Liàng) could not bear to discard either one.
Fèi Yī was sent on an embassy to Wú.
The Lord of Wú, drunk,
asked Fèi Yī:
"Yáng Yí and Wèi Yán
are common men, like herdsmen,
though they have occasionally provided some barking and crowing benefit to current affairs.
However, having already appointed them,
it is impossible to dismiss them lightly.
If one day Zhūgě Liàng were gone,
they would surely cause trouble.
All of you, gentlemen, are muddled,
unaware of how to guard against this.
Is this what is meant by 'leaving plans for one's descendants'? "
Fèi Yī replied:
"The discord between Yáng Yí and Wèi Yán
arises merely from personal animosity,
and they do not have the treacherous hearts of Qíng Bù and Hán Xìn, who were difficult to control.
Qíng refers to Qíng Bù, Hán refers to Hán Xìn.
To unify all of China,
achievements are made by talent,
and enterprises are expanded by talent.
If we abandon these and do not employ them,
to guard against future trouble,
it would be like preparing for wind and waves by prematurely discarding the boat and oars.
That is not a wise long-term plan."
檝 (jí),
same as 楫 (jí).
When Zhūgě Liàng was critically ill,
he, along with Yáng Yí, Sīmǎ Fèi Yī, and others, drafted the retreat plans for after his death,
ordering Wèi Yán to cover the rear,
with Jiāng Wéi next;
if Wèi Yán did not obey,
the army was to withdraw on its own.
Zhūgě Liàng certainly knew Wèi Yán would not take orders from Yáng Yí.
Yáng Yí secretly did not announce the mourning,
and sent Fèi Yī to ascertain Wèi Yán's intentions.
Wèi Yán said:
"Although the Chancellor has passed away,
I am still here.
This is a boastful statement by Wèi Yán.
見 (jiàn),
read as "xián biàn" (賢遍).
One can simply bring the coffin back for burial.
The officials of the Chancellor's office
refers to those below the Chángshǐ.
Why should the affairs of the entire realm be abandoned because of one person's death?
Moreover, who is Wèi Yán,
that he should be commanded by Yáng Yí
and serve as the general covering the rear?"
He then, together with Fèi Yī, drafted a division of moving and staying,
and had Fèi Yī write it by hand with his own name affixed,
to announce to the generals.
At that time, Fèi Yī was Zhūgě Liàng's Sīmǎ.
Wèi Yán knew Yáng Yí would certainly not follow him,
so he seized the opportunity of Fèi Yī's arrival
to coerce him into jointly drafting the disposition for moving and staying.
行 (xíng)
refers to those who should return with Zhūgě Liàng's coffin;
留 (liú)
refers to those who should stay to resist the enemy.
Wèi Yán wanted Fèi Yī to handwrite these dispositional orders
and announce them to his subordinate generals.
"I should return for you and explain to Chángshǐ Yáng.
The Chángshǐ is a civil official,
rarely experienced in military matters,
so he will surely not disobey orders."
Fèi Yī left
and galloped away.
Wèi Yán soon regretted it,
but it was already too late.
尋 (xún)
means "following";
meaning he regretted it immediately after.
Wèi Yán sent someone to spy on Yáng Yí and the others.
He intended to follow Zhūgě Liàng's established rule that the various camps withdraw their armies in sequence.
Wèi Yán was furious,
thinking Yáng Yí had not yet departed,
so he led his forces directly south ahead of them,
burning and cutting off the plank roads as he went.
Wèi Yán and Yáng Yí each submitted memorials accusing the other of rebellion.
Within a single day,
urgent military dispatches arrived one after another.
The Han Lord consulted Shìzhōng Dǒng Yǔn and Liúfǔ Chángshǐ Jiǎng Wǎn.
Jiǎng Wǎn and Dǒng Yǔn both vouched for Yáng Yí and doubted Wèi Yán.
Yáng Yí and others ordered the mountains to be cleared and roads opened,
traveling day and night,
also following behind Wèi Yán.
Wèi Yán arrived first
and occupied the entrance to Nán Gǔ.
Nán Gǔ
is Bāo Gǔ.
The southern valley is called Bāo,
the northern valley is called Xié.
It is four hundred and seventy *lǐ* long,
forming a single valley.
Yáng Yí and others ordered General Hé Píng to block Wèi Yán in front.
Hé Píng
is Wáng Píng.
He was originally adopted into his maternal family, the Hé clan,
and later reverted to the surname Wáng.
This follows his initial surname.
(Hé Píng said to Wèi Yán's troops:) "The Duke is gone;
his body is not yet cold!
How dare you act like this!"
Wèi Yán's officers and men knew Wèi Yán was in the wrong,
and none were willing to fight for him;
they all dispersed.
Wèi Yán fled alone with a few of his sons,
escaping to Hànzhōng.
Yáng Yí sent General Mǎ Dài to pursue and behead him,
then exterminated Wèi Yán's three clans.
Jiǎng Wǎn led the palace guards and various camps northward to address the crisis.
After traveling several tens of *lǐ*,
news of Wèi Yán's death arrived,
so he returned.
The various armies returned to Chéngdū,
where a general amnesty was declared,
and Zhūgě Liàng was posthumously titled Zhōngwǔ Hóu.
Previously,
Liàng had reported to the Hàn Lord, saying:
"In Chéngdū there are eight hundred mulberry trees and
fifteen qǐng of poor land.
For my sons and brothers, there is
naturally more than enough food and clothing.
I have not sought other means of livelihood to increase my wealth by an inch.
If the day of my death comes,
there shall be no surplus silk within my home,
nor any excess wealth outside,
to betray Your Majesty."
It was exactly as he had said.
卒 (zú),
pronounced xù.
Zhāng Yì, the Chief Clerk to the Chancellor, often praised Liàng, saying:
"His rewards do not neglect the distant,
his punishments do not favor the close.
Ranks cannot be obtained without merit,
and penalties cannot be evaded by power and status.
This is why both the wise and the foolish equally forget their own interests!"
Chén Shòu comments: When Zhūgě Liàng served as Chancellor,
he soothed the common people,
established norms and rules.
儀 (yí)
means 'standard'.
軌 (guǐ)
means 'law'.
He acted according to circumstances,
opened his heart with sincerity,
and upheld public fairness.
Those who were loyal and beneficial to the times,
even if enemies, were certainly rewarded.
Those who violated laws and were negligent,
even if relatives, were certainly punished.
Those who confessed their crimes and submitted their feelings,
even if their offenses were serious, were certainly pardoned.
Those who used evasive words and clever deceptions,
even if their offenses were minor, were certainly executed.
No good deed, however small, went unrewarded;
no evil, however slight, went unpunished.
All matters were meticulously managed,
and the principles of things were rooted in their fundamentals.
This means that for all matters and things, he always acted upon their fundamental principles.
Falsehood and pretense were not tolerated.
Consequently, within the borders of the state,
all feared and loved him.
Although his penal administration was strict, there were no complaints,
because his intentions were impartial and his admonitions clear.
He could be called an excellent talent in governance,
comparable to Guǎn Zhòng and Xiāo Hé.
At first,
Liáo Lì, Commander of the Long River Guards,
considered his talent and reputation worthy of being Zhūgě Liàng's deputy.
Constantly dissatisfied with his wandering official position,
he incessantly complained and slandered.
Liàng dismissed Lì to commoner status
and exiled him to Wénshān.
According to the biography of Lì,
his dismissal and exile to Wénshān
occurred shortly after the Latter Lord ascended the throne.
Wénshān,
established as a commandery by Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
was merged into the Shǔ Commandery in the third year of Dìjié of Emperor Xuān.
Shǔ then
re-established Wénshān Commandery.
In the Táng dynasty, it was Wénshān County of Màozhōu.
汶 (wèn),
pronunciation [omitted].
Lì wept and said:
"I shall eventually be among the barbarians!"
Lǐ Píng heard of this
and also fell ill and died.
Píng's dismissal and exile
are mentioned above, in the fifth year of Tàihé.
To be able to restore himself
was something that later generations could not achieve.
Xí Zuòchǐ comments: In ancient times, Guǎn Zhòng took three hundred households from Bó Shì's Piányì,
and Bó Shì had no complaints until his death.
The sage considered this difficult.
See the Analects.
Zhèng Shì says: A lesser grandee of a small state
was granted a fief of one chéng,
which paid taxes from three hundred households.
Hence, three hundred households.
In fact, a lesser grandee of a large state also had three hundred households.
Therefore, the Analects say: Guǎn Zhòng took three hundred households from Bó Shì's Piányì.
The reason one chéng contained three hundred households is that
one chéng had nine hundred men.
After deducting for palaces, roads, mountains, and marshes,
one third was removed,
leaving six hundred men.
If each family received the land for two men,
this means three hundred households paid taxes.
Lǐ Yán was put to death,
how could he have had no complaints, let alone anything more!
Water is perfectly level, yet the crooked take it as a standard;
a mirror is perfectly clear, yet the ugly forget their anger.
The reason water and mirrors can fully reflect things without causing resentment
is their impartiality.
Water and mirrors are impartial,
yet they still avoid slander.
How much more so an upright gentleman who cherishes the joy of life
and embodies the virtue of generosity and clemency?
His laws are enforced where they cannot but be applied,
his punishments are imposed upon self-committed crimes.
He bestows titles without partiality,
and executes without anger.
How could anyone in the world not submit to him!
The people of Shǔ everywhere sought to build a temple for Zhūgě Liàng,
but the Hàn Lord would not permit it.
So the common people, following the seasons, privately offered sacrifices to him on the roadsides.
Xí Lóng, Commander of the Infantry, and others,
[Family Record]: Xí
was a state name,
later adopted as a surname.
Fēngsú Tōng: During the Hàn dynasty, there was Xí Xiǎng,
who was Chancellor of Chén.
built a single temple in Miǎnyáng
and put an end to the private sacrifices.
The Hàn Lord agreed.
The Hàn Lord appointed Wú Yì, Left General, as General of Chariots and Cavalry,
conferred upon him a ceremonial axe,
and made him Inspector of Hànzhōng,
replacing Wèi Yán.
He took overall charge of state affairs,
and soon after, Jiǎng Wǎn was appointed Acting Protector-General,
granted a ceremonial axe,
and served as Governor of Yìzhōu.
At that time, with the recent loss of the Marshal,
those near and far were anxious and fearful.
Jiǎng Wǎn stood out among the crowd,
類 (lèi)
means 'category'.
萃 (cuì)
means 'gather'.
showing neither sorrow
nor joy.
His demeanor and conduct
were as usual,
which gradually won the trust of the masses.
When the people of Wú heard that Zhūgě Liàng had died,
fearing that Wèi might take advantage of the decline to seize Shǔ,
they increased the garrison at Bāqiū by ten thousand men.
This Bāqiū is Bālíng.
Today, Bālíng County in Yuèzhōu has Tiānyuè Mountain,
facing the great river.
It is also called Mùfù.
In front of it are small hills,
called Bāshé Mound,
traditionally believed to be where Yì slew the Bāshé in Dòngtíng,
and its bones formed a mound,
hence it was called Bālíng.
They wanted to use this to divide affairs.
When the people of Hàn heard of this,
they also increased the garrison at Yǒng'ān to guard against emergencies.
The Hàn Lord sent Zōng Yù, Right Gentleman of the Household, as envoy to Wú.
The Wú Lord asked:
"The east and west,
are like one family,
yet I hear the west has further increased the garrison at Báidì.
Why is this?"
Yù replied:
"I believe that the east increasing the garrison at Bāqiū
and the west increasing the garrison at Báidì
are both appropriate responses to circumstances,
and neither should be questioned by the other."
The Wú Lord laughed heartily,
commending his resolute frankness.
This means his words were unyielding to Wú
and he concealed nothing.
After the Former Lord of Shǔ passed away,
Zhūgě Liàng took charge of the state,
and first sent Dèng Zhī as envoy to Wú.
13 Zhūgě Kè
of Wú
believed that Dānyáng's
mountains were perilous
and its people were numerous and robust.
Although troops had been dispatched there before,
they only managed to acquire commoners from the outer counties.
Lù Xùn
had previously organized the mountain Yuè
into soldiers.
This event can be found in Volume 68, during the 24th year of Jiàn'ān
of Emperor Xiàn
of Hàn.
No one had been able to completely subdue them.
Zhūgě Kè
repeatedly requested to be dispatched by the court to deal with them,
claiming that in three years he could raise 40,000 armored soldiers.
The general consensus was:
"Dānyáng's
terrain is perilous and rugged,
bordering the four commanderies of Wú Jùn, Kuàijī, Xīndū,
and Pányáng.
Its circumference spans several thousand *lǐ*,
with countless layers of mountains and valleys.
Its secluded inhabitants
have never entered cities
or confronted magistrates.
They all rely on weapons and live wild,
growing old in the forests and thickets.
Fugitives and hardened criminals
all escape and hide there together.
The mountains produce copper and iron,
from which they cast their own armor and weapons.
Their custom is to love martial arts and practice warfare,
valuing strength and prowess.
Their ascent of mountains and crossing of dangers,
crashing through thickets,
is like fish swimming in the depths or apes leaping through trees.
They watch for opportunities,
emerging as bandits and thieves.
Whenever troops are sent to campaign against them,
they seek out their hidden lairs.
When they fight, they appear;
when defeated, they scatter like birds.
Since previous generations,
no one has been able to restrain them."
Everyone considered it difficult.
Kè's
father, Jǐn,
heard of this
and also thought that the matter would ultimately not succeed.
*Dài*
means "to reach";
it means the number of mountain people Zhūgě Kè
claimed to raise could not reach 40,000.
"Kè
will either greatly uplift our family
or bring ruin upon our clan!"
Kè
vehemently argued for his inevitable victory.
Thereupon, the Ruler of Wú
appointed Kè
as Fǔyuè Jiāngjūn,
using the title of "pacifying and attracting the mountain Yuè"
as his general's designation.
He was sent to implement his strategy.
6 The emperor was fond of construction projects.
After the Xǔchāng Palace was built,
a record of this matter can be found in the previous volume, Tàihé year 6.
After Zhūgě Liàng's death,
the emperor then greatly expanded palaces and chambers.
This is what Jìn Shìxiè referred to as
"releasing Chǔ as an external threat".
Zhì,
pronounced like zhí.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: Emperor Míng modeled himself on Tàijí,
and built the Tàijí Hall in Luòyáng's southern palace,

Someone asked: "The governance of a ruler,

Zhì (質) said:
“Fánchéng (樊城) has low walls and few soldiers,
so we must advance our army to provide external aid.
Otherwise,
it will be perilous.”
Thereupon, he marched his troops to the siege,
and the people in the city were then reassured.
2 In the fifth month,
Wú Crown Prince Dēng (登) died.
3 Wú’s troops were still in Jīngzhōu.
Grand Tutor Yī (懿) said:
“One hundred thousand commoners and barbarians in Zābù
are separated on the south side of the water,
wandering without a leader.
Fánchéng (樊城) has been under attack
for months without being relieved.
This is a perilous situation,
I request to personally suppress it.”
In the sixth month,
Grand Tutor Yī (懿) commanded all armies to relieve Fán;
the Wú army, hearing this,
fled at night.
They were pursued to Sānzhōukǒu (三州口).
Sānzhōukǒu (三州口)
refers to the mouth of the three prefectures of Jīng (荊), Yù (豫), and Yáng (揚).
Wèi’s Jīngzhōu territory
extended east to Jiāngxià (江夏),
Yùzhōu’s territory
extended south to Yìyáng (弋陽),
Yángzhōu’s territory
extended west to Liù’ān (六安).
Sānzhōukǒu (三州口) should be within this area.
Also, according to Wáng Chǎng’s (王昶) biography: Chǎng (昶) supervised the military affairs of Jīng (荊) and Yù (豫) prefectures,
moved his garrison from Wǎn (宛) to Xīnyě (新野),
and trained naval forces at Sānzhōu (三州).
Thus, Sānzhōu (三州) is probably a place name.
Kǒu (口),
water mouth.
4 In the intercalary month,
Wú Grand General Zhūgě Jǐn (諸葛瑾) died.
Jǐn’s (瑾) eldest
son Kè (恪) had already been enfeoffed as a marquis.
Kè (恪) was the rightful heir to be the 世子 (shìzǐ);
to say "crown prince" (太子)
is an error.
Kè (恪) was enfeoffed as a marquis for his achievements in bringing out the mountain people.
This event is recorded in volume 62, the first year of Jǐngchū (景初).
He took over his father’s military profession.
Shè (攝),
to lead,
to inherit,
meaning to lead his father’s troops,
and inherit his father’s profession.
5 Hàn Grand Marshal Jiǎng Wǎn (蔣琬) noted that Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮) had repeatedly campaigned in Qínchuān (秦川),
the Guānzhōng (關中) area,
a fertile plain for a thousand *lǐ* (里),
the former territory of Qín (秦),
called Qínchuān (秦川).
Shù (數),
read *suǒ jiǎo*.
But had ultimately achieved no success.
So he built many boats and ships,
intending to descend eastward along the Hàn (漢) and Miǎn (沔) rivers,
to attack Wèixīng (魏興) and Shàngyōng (上庸).
The waters of Hàn (漢) and Miǎn (沔) flow eastward from Hànzhōng (漢中), passing through Wèixīng (魏興) and Shàngyōng (上庸), to reach Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
If one wishes to contend for天下 (tiānxià),
one should send troops to Qínchuān (秦川).
Wèixīng (魏興) and Shàngyōng (上庸)
are not the right places.
It was not yet time to act.
The Hàn people all believed that the venture would likely not succeed,
and the return route would be extremely difficult;
it was not a long-term strategy.
The Hàn ruler sent Imperial Secretary Fèi Yī (費禕)
and Central Army Supervisor Jiāng Wéi (姜維)
to explain his intentions.
Central Army Supervisor (中監軍)
is the same post as Central Army Protector (中護軍).
Shǔ (蜀) established Forward Army Supervisor, Rear Army Supervisor, and Central Army Supervisor,
ranking below the three army strategists.
“Now Wèi (魏) spans nine prefectures,
its roots and branches are widespread,
it is not easy to pacify and eliminate them.
If we combine our efforts from east and west,
attacking simultaneously from front and rear,
even if we cannot achieve our aspirations quickly,
we should at least divide and gradually consume them,
first destroying their factions.
However, Wú’s (吳) timing is uncertain,
and they have failed to achieve their objectives repeatedly.
Kè (克),
able;
Guǒ (果),
decisive;
meaning they are unable to advance their troops decisively.
Considering the strategic importance of Liángzhōu’s (涼州) Hu (胡) frontier,
with resources for both advance and retreat,
and the Qiāng (羌) and Hu (胡) barbarians longing for Hàn (漢) as if parched,
it is advisable to appoint Jiāng Wéi (姜維) as Governor of Liángzhōu (涼州).
Of Liángzhōu’s (涼州) territory,
Shǔ (蜀) only holds Wǔdū (武都) and Yīnpíng (陰平) commanderies.
I will manage the region west of the Hé (河),
and your servant will lead the army to serve as a reinforcing garrison for Wéi (維).
Now Fúshuǐ (涪水) has four land and water routes,
ready to respond to any urgent situation.
If there
is trouble in the east or west,
it will not be difficult to assist.
I request to move the garrison to Fú (涪).”
Fú (涪) County,
during the Hàn (漢) it belonged to Guǎnghàn (廣漢) Commandery,
during Shǔ (蜀) it belonged to Zǐtóng (梓潼) Commandery.
Fú (涪),
sound *fú*.
6 The court wished to expand agriculture and store grain between Yáng (揚) and Yù (豫) prefectures.
It dispatched Imperial Secretary Dèng Ài (鄧艾) of Rǔnán (汝南) to travel from Chén (陳) and Xiàng (項) eastward to Shòuchūn (壽春).
Chén (陳) County,
during the Hàn (漢) it belonged to Chén (陳) Kingdom.
Xiàng (項) County,
during the Hàn (漢) it belonged to Rǔnán (汝南) Commandery.
According to the *Jìn Zhì* (晉志),
both counties belonged to Liáng (梁) Kingdom.
Xíng (行),
read *xià mèng*.
“In the past, Grand Ancestor (Tàizǔ) defeated the Yellow Turbans,
and consequently established屯田 (túntián),
storing grain in Xǔdū (許都) to control the four directions.
This event is recorded in volume 62, the first year of Hàn Emperor Xiàn’s (漢獻帝) Jiàn’ān (建安) reign.
Military affairs are in Huáinán (淮南).
Whenever a large army goes on campaign,
transportation of troops consumes more than half [the resources],
and the expenses are enormous.
Between Chén (陳) and Cài (蔡),
the land is low and the fields are fertile.
We can save the various paddy fields around Xǔchāng (許昌),
and consolidate the water to move eastward.
The Rǔshuǐ (汝水), Yǐngshuǐ (潁水), Làngdàng Qúshuǐ (蒗蕩渠水), and Guōshuǐ (渦水) all pass through the area between Chén (陳) and Cài (蔡) and flow eastward into the Huái (淮) River.
Thirty thousand men in Huáinán (淮南),
two-tenths of whom are resting,
will constantly have forty thousand men simultaneously farming and guarding.
Fifty thousand men, with one tenth resting in rotation,
alternating garrison duties,
a cycle that repeats,
means there are always forty thousand men garrisoning and farming.
This opens up river transport.
Estimating after deducting all expenses,
we can annually complete five million *hú* (斛) to serve as military supplies.
In six or seven years,
we can accumulate twenty
million *hú* (斛) on the Huái (淮) River.
This is five years’ worth of food for a hundred thousand men.
With this, to attack Wú (吳),
there will be nothing that cannot be conquered.”
Grand Tutor Yī (懿) approved this.
This year,
the Grand Transport Canal (Cáoyùn) was first opened and expanded.
Whenever there were military affairs in the southeast,
large armies would be dispatched,
sailing down the canal,
reaching the Jiāng (江) and Huái (淮) rivers.
Provisions were abundant, and there were no water hazards.
The historian thoroughly discusses Dèng Ài’s (鄧艾) benefits of establishing *túntián* (屯田).
7 Guǎn Níng (管寧) died.
Níng's (寧) conduct was noble and pure.
People who gazed upon him
felt him to be distant and unattainable,
but when they approached, he was amiable and approachable.
He was able to guide people to goodness through their affairs,
and no one
failed to be influenced and submit.
When he died,
everyone in the world, whether they knew him or not,
sighed in lamentation.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
Jiāng Wéi (姜維) of Hàn (漢) led a detachment of troops from Hànzhōng (漢中) back to station at Fú (涪).
All Shǔ (蜀) armies at this time belonged to Jiǎng Wǎn (蔣琬);
Jiāng Wéi (姜維) merely commanded a detachment.
2 The ruler of Wú (吳) established his son Hé (和) as Crown Prince,
and issued a great amnesty.
3 In the third month,
Mǎn Chǒng (滿寵), the Marquis Jǐng (景) of Chāngyì (昌邑), died.
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
on the day Yǐyǒu (乙酉),
Jiǎng Jì (蔣濟), General of the Leading Army, was appointed Grand Commandant.
4 The ruler of Wú (吳) dispatched General Niè Yǒu (聶友) and Colonel Lù Kǎi (陸凱) with thirty thousand soldiers to attack Dān'ěr (儋耳) and Zhūyá (珠崖).
Dān'ěr (儋耳) and Zhūyá (珠崖)
were opened up as commanderies by Emperor Wǔ (武) of Hàn (漢),
belonging to Jiāozhǐ (交趾) Prefecture;
they were abandoned after Emperor Yuán (元).
Niè (聶),
pronounced Ní-zhé.
Dān (儋),
pronounced Dū-gān.
5 In the eighth month,
the ruler of Wú (吳) enfeoffed his son Bà (霸) as Prince of Lǔ (魯).
Bà (霸)
was the younger brother of Hé (和) by the same mother,
and was exceptionally favored and esteemed,
no different from Hé (和).
This laid the groundwork for the later deposition of Hé (和) and execution of Bà (霸) by Wú (吳).
[Someone] submitted a memorial, remonstrating:
"Your servant humbly believes that the Prince of Lǔ (魯) is endowed with outstanding virtues by Heaven,
possessing both civil and martial talents.
The present circumstances demand
that he should guard the four directions,
acting as a bulwark for the state,
propagating its virtues and excellences,
and widely manifesting its awe-inspiring might.
This is a sound plan for the state,
and what the people within the seas look forward to.
Moreover, there should be a distinction in rank between the two palaces,
to rectify the order of superior and inferior,
and clarify the foundation of moral education."
The memorial was submitted three or four times,
but the ruler of Wú (吳) did not listen.
1 In spring,
in the first month,
the Emperor came of age.
2 Zhūgé Kè (諸葛恪) of Wú (吳) attacked Liù'ān (六安).
The capital of Liù'ān (六安) Commandery of Hàn (漢) was Liù (六) County;
in Later Hàn (漢) it was the Marquisate of Liù'ān (六安),
belonging to Lújiāng (廬江) Commandery;
in Jìn (晉) it was Liù (六) County,
belonging to Lújiāng (廬江) Commandery.
3 In summer,
in the fourth month,
Empress Zhēn (甄) was established,
and a great amnesty was issued.
The Empress
was the granddaughter of Yǎn (儼), elder brother of Empress Wénzhāo (文昭).
4 In the fifth month,
on the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse,
which was total.
5 In winter,
in the tenth month,
Jiǎng Wǎn (蔣琬) of Hàn (漢) returned from Hànzhōng (漢中) to Fú (涪),
his illness worsening.
He appointed Wáng Píng (王平), the Administrator of Hànzhōng (漢中), as Front Supervising General and General Who Pacifies the North,
to command Hànzhōng (漢中).
6 In the eleventh month,
the ruler of Hàn (漢) appointed Fèi Yī (費禕), Minister of the Imperial Secretariat, as General-in-Chief and Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
7 Grand Chancellor Gù Yǒng (顧雍) of Wú (吳) died.
8 Zhūgé Kè (諸葛恪) of Wú (吳) sent spies far to observe and scout the strategic routes,
intending to attack Shòuchūn (壽春).
Grand Tutor Yī (懿) led troops into Shū (舒).
Shū (舒) County
belonged to Lújiāng (廬江) Commandery;
it was an ancient state during the Spring and Autumn period,
at that time on the border between Wú (吳) and Wèi (魏),
abandoned and uncultivated,
and very close to Wǎnkǒu (皖口).
The ruler of Wú (吳) moved Kè (恪) to garrison at Cháisāng (柴桑).
Cháisāng (柴桑) County
belonged to Yùzhāng (豫章) Commandery in Hàn (漢),
and to Wǔchāng (武昌) Commandery in Wú (吳);
it had Cháisāng (柴桑) Mountain;
it is in present-day Déhuà (德化), Jiāngzhōu (江州), ninety *li* west.
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: The South Chǔ (楚) City post station in Xúnyáng (尋陽) County, Jiāngzhōu (江州),
is the ancient Cháisāng (柴桑) County.
Sòng Bái (宋白) said: Ruìchāng (瑞昌) County, Jiāngzhōu (江zhōu),
is probably the old city of Cháisāng (柴桑).
9 Bù Zhì (步騭) and Zhū Rán (朱然) each submitted a memorial to the ruler of Wú (吳), saying:
"Those returning from Shǔ (蜀) all say that Shǔ (蜀) intends to break the alliance
and communicate with Wèi (魏),
building many boats
and repairing cities and fortifications.
Furthermore,
when Jiǎng Wǎn (蔣琬) was guarding Hànzhōng (漢中)
and heard that Sīmǎ Yī (司馬懿) was advancing south, he did not send troops
to take advantage of the emptiness and attack from two sides.
Instead, he abandoned Hànzhōng (漢中)
and returned closer to Chéngdū (成都).
The matter is already evident
and leaves no room for doubt;
preparations should be made."
The ruler of Wú (吳) replied:
"I have not treated Shǔ (蜀) poorly;
in terms of invitations, tributes, alliances, and oaths,
I owe them nothing.
How could they do this?
Sīmǎ Yī (司馬懿) previously advanced into Shū (舒),
but retreated within ten days.
Shǔ (蜀) is thousands of *li* away;
how could they know the urgency to send troops immediately?
In the past, when Wèi (魏) wanted to enter Hànchuān (漢川),
Cáo Zhēn (曹真) wanted to enter Hànzhōng (漢zhōng) –
the matter is mentioned in volume 71, in the fourth year of Tàihé (太和) of Emperor Míng (明) –
they did not yet take action,
meaning they massed troops but had not yet launched.
Could Shǔ (蜀) truly be suspicious because of this?
People's words are truly unreliable;
I will guarantee them to you at the cost of my family."
10 Wáng Chǎng (王昶), General Who Attacks the East and Area Commander of the armies of Yáng (揚) and Yù (豫),
stated in Wáng Chǎng's (王昶) biography:
Yáng (揚)
should be
Jīng (荊).
"The land has natural defenses,
but the defensive posture is not constant.
Now, garrisoned at Wǎn (宛), which is over three hundred *li* from Xiāngyáng (襄陽),
we cannot quickly respond in an emergency."
So he moved his garrison to Xīnyě (新野).
Xīnyě (新野) County
belonged to Nányáng (南陽) Commandery.
11. The Imperial Clansman Cáo Jiǒng.
Péi Sōngzhī said: Jiǒng
was a descendant of the elder brother of the Palace Attendant Chángshì, Shūxīng.
He was a distant ancestor of the young emperor.
"Ancient kings,
invariably established those of the same surname to illustrate family affection,
and invariably set up those of different surnames to illustrate valuing the worthy.
If the Way of family affection is exclusively applied,
then its gradual decline will be weak;
if the Way of valuing the worthy is unilaterally relied upon,
then its drawback will be usurpation and seizure.
This means that power and authority would oppress and coerce,
seizing the ruler and usurping the throne.
Therefore, by broadly seeking both relatives and strangers and employing them concurrently,
they were able to preserve their altars of soil and grain [the state],
and their reigns endured for a long time.
Jì
refers to an era or period.
When the Way of family affection is not fully implemented,
some are appointed but not given heavy responsibilities,
others are dismissed and not appointed at all.
Your servant privately considers this;
Wéi
means to ponder.
I have carefully compiled what I have heard,
and discuss its success and failure:
In ancient times, the Xià, Shāng, and Zhōu dynasties lasted for dozens of generations,
but Qín perished after two generations.
Why was this?
The rulers of the Three Dynasties shared their people with the realm,
thus the realm shared their worries.
Lǚ Yánjì said: 'Sharing their people with the realm' means establishing feudal lords and sharing governance with them,
sharing the benefits.
Therefore, when the realm faced difficulties,
the feudal lords shared the worries.
Thus, when they were in danger, no one came to their rescue.
Qín observed the failings of Zhōu,
believing that it became small and weak and was usurped.
Therefore, it abolished the five ranks of nobility
and established county officials.
Lǚ Xiàng said: Qín Shǐhuáng observed that the reason Zhōu declined
was because its power weakened and feudal lords usurped its state.
So he abolished the five ranks of nobility and established county officials.
The five ranks were
gōng (duke), hóu (marquis), bó (count), zǐ (viscount), and nán (baron).
Pí
also means to assist.
This is like pruning the limbs and legs,
and relying solely on the chest and abdomen.
Spectators were chilled to the heart by this,
but Shǐhuáng was complacent, believing it to be an enterprise for his descendants to be emperors for ten thousand generations.
How preposterous!
Therefore, the Han founder [Gāozǔ] brandished his three-foot sword,
led a disorderly rabble,
and within five years,
accomplished the imperial enterprise.
Why?
It is difficult to achieve success when cutting down deep roots,
but easy to exert force when destroying what is rotten and withered.
Such is the natural course of events.
This uses the meaning of Bān Gù's 'Biǎo of Han Imperial Clansmen and Feudal Kings.'
Yì
is pronounced like 'shǐ.'
They established and fostered their sons and younger brothers.
When the various Lǚs seized power
and plotted to endanger the Liú clan,
the reason why the realm was not shaken
was simply because the feudal lords were strong
and their solidarity was as firm as a rock.
However, Gāozǔ's enfeoffments
exceeded the ancient system,
so Jiǎ Yì believed that for the realm to be peaceful and stable,
nothing was better than widely establishing feudal lords and diminishing their power.
Jiǎ Yì's words in the 'Zhì'ān Cè'
are found in Volume 14, Emperor Wén's sixth year.
Shǎo
is pronounced like 'shàozǎo.'
Zhì
is pronounced like 'zhílì.'

猥用鼂錯之計，
削黜諸侯，
遂有七國之患。
事見十六卷漢景帝三年。
釁鍾文、景，
鍾，
聚也。
急之不漸故也。
所謂『末大必折，
尾大難掉』 ，
左傳田無宇之言。
折，
而設翻。
掉，
徒弔翻。
猶或不從，
況乎非體之尾，
其可掉哉！
武帝從主父之策，
下推恩之令，
事見十八卷漢武帝元朔二年。
遂以陵夷，
子孫微弱，
衣食租稅，
不預政事。
至于哀、平，
王氏秉權，
假周公之事而為田常之亂，
宗室諸侯，
或乃為之符命，
頌莽恩德，
事見三十六卷王莽初始元年。
由斯言之，
非宗子獨忠孝於惠、文之間而叛逆於哀、平之際也，
徒權輕勢弱，
不能有定耳。
賴光武皇帝挺不世之姿，
擒王莽於已成，
紹漢嗣於既絕，
斯豈非宗子之力也！
而曾不監秦之失策，
襲周之舊制，
至於桓、靈，
閹宦用事，
君孤立於上，
臣弄權於下；
由是天下鼎沸，
姦宄並爭，
宗廟焚為灰燼，
宮室變為榛藪。
謂董卓之亂也。
太祖皇帝龍飛鳳翔，
掃除凶逆。
大魏之興，
于今二十有四年矣；
自黃初受禪至是二十四年。
五代：夏、商、周、秦、漢。
子弟王空虛之地，
君有不使之民；
空虛，
謂有封國之名，
實不能有其地也。
君不使之民，
謂抗藩王之尊於國民之上，
不得而臣使也。
王，
于況翻。
不聞邦國之政；
權均匹夫，
勢齊凡庶。
內無深根不拔之固，
外無盤石宗盟之助，
呂延濟曰：盤石，
大石也，
以其堅重不可轉易也。
宗盟，
謂同姓諸侯盟會者也。
為萬世之業也。
且今之州牧、郡守，
古之方伯、諸侯，
皆跨有千里之土，
兼軍武之任，
或比國數人，
或兄弟並據；
而宗室子弟曾無一人間廁其間，
與相維制，
非所以強榦弱枝，
備萬一之虞也。
今之用賢，
或超為名都之主，
或為偏師之帥；
而宗室有文者必限小縣之宰，
有武者必置百人之上，
張銑曰：言宗室位卑也。
百人之上，
百夫長也。
語曰： 『百足之蟲，
至死不僵』 ，
馬蚿百足。
僵，
居良翻。
此言雖小，
可以譬大。
是以聖王安不忘危，
存不忘亡，
故天下有變而無傾危之患矣。 」

The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* states: 122 *lǐ* north of Xiǎochénggùchéng is Xīngshì Bǎn.
The *Huányǔ Jì* states: Xīngshì Shān is 43 *lǐ* north of Yángzhōu Xīngdào Xiàn,
where the current prefectural city lies.
Its shape is like a basin,
dangerous on the outside but with a large valley within.
It is a winding road for several *lǐ* upwards
before reaching the four gates,
hence the name Xīngshì.
Dōngpō's *Zhǐzhǎng Tú* places it in Xīngyuán,
which is probably incorrect.
Dù Yòu said: Xīngshì is Yángzhōu Xīngdào Xiàn.
The *Huányǔ Jì* is consistent with the *Tōngdiǎn*.
Sòng Bái said: Xīngshì Shān is 20 *lǐ* northwest of the present Xīngdào Xiàn.

Huángjīn Gǔ has Huángjīn Shù,
