4. The Hàn emperor issued a general amnesty.
Dà Sīnóng, Méng Guāng of Hénán,
(Méng) Guāng,
a native of Luòyáng, Hénán,
fled into Shǔ at the end of the Hàn dynasty. (He) said:
"Indeed, an amnesty
is like a 'one-sided blight' –
when one side of a tree flourishes while the other is withered and scorched,
it is called a 'one-sided blight.'
An amnesty
is to pardon the guilty.
If the guilty are pardoned,
then wicked and evil people escape the law and are exempted from punishment,
while good and virtuous people are suppressed and cannot have their grievances redressed.
Therefore, it is called a 'one-sided blight.'
Only when the state is in decline and in dire straits,
and there is no other option,
can it be expediently implemented.
Now, the Emperor is benevolent and wise,
and all officials are performing their duties.
How can there be an urgent crisis requiring repeated bestowal of extraordinary favors,
thereby benefiting treacherous villains!"
(Fèi) Yī merely looked at him, thanked him,
and bowed respectfully.
Previously,
during the time of Chéngxiàng Zhūgě Liàng,
someone said that the Duke was reluctant to issue amnesties.
Zhūgě Liàng replied:
"A state is governed by great virtue,
not by small favors.
Therefore, Kuāng Héng and Wú Hàn did not wish for amnesties.
Kuāng Héng's memorial is found in Volume 38, second year of Yuándì's Yǒngguāng era of Hàn.
Wú Hàn's words are found in Volume 43, twentieth year of Guāngwǔ's Jiànwǔ era.
Chén Jì,
courtesy name Yuánfāng.
Zhèng Xuán,
courtesy name Kāngchéng.
They never spoke of amnesties.
If one were like Liú Jǐngshēng, or Jìyù and his son,
(Liú) Cóng,
courtesy name Jìyù.
What benefit would they be to governance!"
Because of this, the people of Shǔ praised Zhūgě Liàng's sagacity,
and knew that Fèi Yī was not his equal.
The people of Shǔ esteemed Kǒngmíng and disparaged Fèi Yī,
not solely because of the matter of reluctance to issue amnesties.
Chén Shòu comments: In Zhūgě Liàng's governance,
military campaigns were often launched, but amnesties were not carelessly issued.
Was this not excellent!
5. The people of Wú found the large coins inconvenient,
so they abolished them.
In the fourth year of Qīnglóng,
Wú minted large coins,
each worth five hundred (small coins).
In the second year of Jǐngchū,
Wú again minted large coins,
each worth a thousand.
6. The Hàn Emperor appointed the governor of Liángzhōu, Jiāng Wéi, as Wèi Jiāngjūn,
and along with Dà Jiāngjūn Fèi Yī, they jointly oversaw the affairs of the Shàngshū.
The Yí people of Píngkāng, Wénshān, rebelled,
and Jiāng Wéi suppressed them.
In the second year of Yuánfēng of Hàn Wǔdì,
Wénshān Commandery was established from the northern part of Shǔ Commandery;
in the third year of Dìjié of Xuāndì,
it was merged into Shǔ Commandery;
Shǔ was again divided into Wénshān Commandery,
and Píngkāng county was established and belonged to it.
Dù Yòu says: Wénshān Commandery is now the territory of Tōnghuà Commandery in northwest Shǔ Commandery,
where the Rǎn Máng resided.
Sòng Bái says: Máozhōu Tōnghuà Commandery is
the ancient Wénshān Commandery.
Liú Xù says: Xuēchéng county of Wéizhōu
is where the Shǔ general Jiāng Wéi suppressed the rebellious Qiāng of Wénshān.
This is that place,
and the present city walls are Jiāng Wéi’s old fortress.
Wén
is pronounced Mín.
The Hàn Emperor frequently went out for sightseeing
and increased the scale of music and entertainment.
The Household Administrator of the Crown Prince, Qiáo Zhōu of Bāxī, submitted a memorial to remonstrate, saying:
"In the past, when Wáng Mǎng was defeated,
heroes rose in unison to contend for the imperial throne.
Talented and wise individuals sought someone to whom they could pledge allegiance,
not necessarily considering the extent of their power,
but rather the depth of their virtue.
At that time, Gēngshǐ, Gōngsūn Shù, and many others had already become powerful,
yet they all indulged their desires and inclinations,
neglecting to do good.
When Shìzǔ first entered Héběi,
Fēng Yì and others advised him: 'You should do what others cannot.'
So he dedicated himself to redressing wrongful cases,
promoted frugality,
and the northern provinces sang his praises,
his reputation spreading far and wide.
Thereupon, Dèng Yǔ pursued him from Nányáng,
(This event is found in Volume 39, first year of Hàn Gēngshǐ era.)
raising troops to assist him;
the rest, inspired by his reputation and admiring his virtue,
such as Pī Róng, Gěng Chún, and Liú Zhí,
even carried their sick and bore coffins,
carrying their infants on their backs, came to him,
their numbers uncountable.
(These events are all found in the second year of Gēngshǐ.)
Róng
is pronounced yú zhōng.
Shèng
is pronounced shēng.
When he was in Luòyáng,
he once wanted to go out for a short while,
but Tiáo Qī remonstrated,
and he immediately turned his carriage back.
Tiáo Qī's biography says: Guāngwǔ once went out with a close entourage of guards.
Tiáo Qī prostrated himself before the carriage, saying: 'Your subject has heard the ancient and modern warnings that changes arise unexpectedly.
I sincerely do not wish Your Majesty to frequently make incognito excursions.'
The Emperor turned his carriage back for him.
Tiáo
is pronounced yáo.
Kòu Xún requested Shìzǔ to personally go and confront the bandits,
and upon hearing the words, he immediately acted.
(This event is found in Volume 42, eighth year of Jiànwǔ.)
(When he) wished for a small excursion, he dared not;
when it came to urgent matters,
he would not indulge himself;
such was the desire for virtue in an emperor!
Therefore, the saying goes:
'The common people do not attach themselves idly,'
truly because virtue leads them.
Now, Hàn is facing a difficult fate,
and the empire is divided into three.
This is a time when heroic and wise individuals are looking for someone to follow,
meaning they hope for a wise ruler to unify the realm.
Moreover, serving the ancestral temple
is how one leads the people to respect superiors;
yet now, sometimes you do not attend the seasonal sacrifices,
but you often go out to visit ponds and gardens.
Your humble and obtuse subject
privately feels uneasy.
Indeed, those burdened with worry and responsibility
do not have time for full enjoyment.
The ambition of the late emperor
for the 'hall and framework' remains unfulfilled.
The Dà Gào says: 'If a father built a house,
and had already laid the foundation,
but his son was unwilling to raise the hall,
how much less would he be willing to erect the framework!'
I wish you would reduce the number of musicians and palace women,
and for all new constructions,
simply follow what the late emperor established,
thereby setting an example of frugality for your descendants."
The Hàn Emperor did not listen.
1. In spring,
first month,
Quán Cóng of Wú died.
2. In the second month,
there was a solar eclipse.
Shàngshū Hé Yàn and others sided with Cáo Shuǎng,
and were fond of changing laws and regulations.
Tàiwèi Jiǎng Jì submitted a memorial, saying:
"In the past, when Dà Shùn assisted in governance,
he warned against forming cliques;
when Shùn assisted Yáo,
he banished Huāndōu and Gònggōng because they mutually recommended each other,
and abhorred those who spoke ill and damaged conduct.
This was to warn against forming cliques.
Hǎo (好),
read Hū Dào fān.
Zhì (治),
read Zhí Lì fān;
same below.
Bǐ (比),
read Pí Zhì fān.
Be cautious about one's associates.
The 'Luò Gào' in the Shū (Book of Documents) states: Dàn (Duke of Zhōu) warned King Chéng, saying: 'Rúzǐ, form your associates,
Rúzǐ, form your associates,
and then proceed.'
Kǒng Ānguó commented: 'Young prince, be cautious about your cliques,
young prince, be cautious about your cliques,'
warning him from now on.
Only exceptionally talented individuals can establish their fundamental principles to be passed down to later generations.
How could middling or inferior officials be suitable for changing them?
In the end, it will bring no benefit to governance,
but merely harm the people.
It is proper to let civil and military officials
each guard their respective duties,
leading with integrity and fairness,
then harmonious energies and auspicious signs can be sensed and brought forth!"
The Lord of Wú (Sūn Quán) issued an edict to relocate timber and tiles from the Wǔchāng Palace to repair and build the Jiànyè Palace.
Officials reported:
"The Wǔchāng Palace is already twenty-eight years old.
Wú established its capital in Wǔchāng in the 24th year of Jiàn'ān during the reign of Emperor Xiàn of Hàn,
and by now it has been twenty-eight years.
It is fitting to issue an order to the local authorities
to generally fell more timber and transport it."
Fá zhì (伐致),
means to fell timber and transport it.
Tōng (通) here
means throughout the entire Wú territory.
"Dà Yǔ considered humble palaces beautiful.
Now military affairs are not yet concluded,
and levies are being imposed everywhere.
If we generally fell more timber,
it will hinder and damage agriculture and sericulture.
Relocating timber and tiles from Wǔchāng
can certainly be used."
So, he moved his residence to the Nángōng (Southern Palace).
In the third month,
the Tàichū Palace was rebuilt.
The Jìn Tàikāng Dì Jì states: "Wú had the Tàichū Palace,
measuring three hundred zhàng square."
For subordinates to serve superiors,
it is righteous to assist in building palaces.
Dàjiāngjūn Cáo Shuǎng, acting on the advice of Hé Yàn, Dèng Yáng, and Dīng Mì,
moved the Empress Dowager to the Yǒngníng Palace.
According to the fact that the Later Wèi built the Yǒngníng Temple west of the Tóngtuó Street,
it suggests the former site of the Earlier Wèi's Yǒngníng Hall.
Also, according to Chén Shòu's record,
the Empress Dowager referred to it as the Yǒngníng Palace,
not that she was moved.
It is likely that the Jìn officials wished to amplify Cáo Shuǎng's evil deeds,
by adding the character 'qiān' (遷, move).
The 'Wǔ Xíng Zhì' in the Jìn Shū states: "Shuǎng moved the Empress Dowager to the Yǒngníng Palace,
and the Empress Dowager and the Emperor wept as they parted."
This also likely follows what the Jìn officials recorded.
They extensively
established their partisans
and repeatedly changed institutions.
Tàifù Sīmǎ Yì could not restrain them
and had a rift with Shuǎng.
In the fifth month,
Sīmǎ Yì began to feign illness
and did not participate in political affairs.
This set the stage for Sīmǎ Yì's eventual execution of Cáo Shuǎng and others.
Yǔ (與),
read as Yù.
In Wú, Chéngxiàng Bù Zhì died.
The Emperor was fond of associating with
petty people and feasting in the imperial garden.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
Shàngshū Hé Yàn reported:
"From now on, when Your Majesty visits the Shìgān Hall
(Referencing records of Wèi and Jìn,
the Shìgān Hall should be in the Empress's palace.
Kūn represents the mother,
Qián represents the father,
implying that the Empress is the mother of the world,
taking Qián as her model,
following the righteousness of her husband.)
it is appropriate for all to consult with the high ministers,
seek their counsel on government affairs,
discuss the meaning of the classics,
and establish a law for ten thousand generations."
In winter,
the twelfth month,
Sànqí Chángshì and Jiànyì Dàfū Kǒng Yì reported:
(Qín established the Jiàn Dàfū,
responsible for discussion and deliberation;
Later Hàn added 'Yì' to make it Jiànyì Dàfū.)
"Now that the world is peaceful,
Your Majesty can close off the imperial garden,
practice riding horses.
When you go out, you should always ride in a royal carriage.
This would be a blessing for the world
and the wish of your subjects."
The Emperor did not listen to any of them.
The Lord of Wú (Sūn Quán) greatly mobilized troops and assembled them in Jiànyè,
announcing his intention to invade.
The Cìshǐ of Yángzhōu, Zhūgé Dàn, ordered the Tàishǒu of Ānfēng, Wáng Jī, to strategize against it.
(Ānfēng County
belonged to the Liù'ān Kingdom in the Hàn dynasty,
to Lújiāng Commandery in the Later Hàn,
and Wèi divided it to establish Ānfēng Commandery,
which belonged to Yùzhōu.)
Cè zhī (策之) means
to calculate it.
"Now Lù Xùn and others are dead,
Sūn Quán is old,
without worthy heirs internally,
and without wise strategists centrally.
If Quán comes out himself, he fears internal strife will suddenly arise,
like a festering carbuncle bursting.
If he sends generals, the old generals are all gone,
and the new generals are not yet trusted.
This is nothing more than wanting to mend and support his factions,
returning to protect himself."
Afterward, Wú indeed did not sally forth.
In this year,
the Qiāng and Hú peoples in Yōng and Liáng rebelled and surrendered to Hàn (Shǔ Hàn).
Jiāng Wéi of Hàn led troops out of Lǒngyòu to respond to them,
and fought with Guō Huái, the Cìshǐ of Yōngzhōu, and Xiàhóu Bà, the Tǎoshǔ Hùjūn, at Táoxī.
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhù states: "The Táo River and the Shǔ Bái River both originate from Mount Xīqīng.
The south side of the mountain is the source of the Bái River,
and the east side of the mountain is the source of the Táo River.
The Táo River flows eastward through Tǔyùhún,
then eastward through Líntáo, Āngù, Dídào,
then north to Páohǎn,
and enters the Hé (Yellow River)."
All these counties are east of the Táo River;
Táoxī, however, is where the Qiāng and other barbarians resided.
Táo (洮),
read Tǔ Dāo fān.
Jiāng Wéi moved them into Shǔ.
The Shǔ Zhì states: "They resided in Fán County."
According to the biography of Jiāng Wéi,
these were Báihǔwén and Zhìwúdài.
Also, in the Wèi Zhì,
Cáo Zhēn attacked and defeated the rebellious Hú Zhì Yuánduō,
so there was indeed a Zhì surname among the Hú.
All were pacified.
In spring,
the second month,
Zhōngshū Lìng Sūn Zī,
on Guǐsì day,
Zhōngshū Jiān Liú Fàng,
in the third month,
on Jiǎwǔ day,
and Sītú Wèi Zhēn each resigned their positions,
taking up residence as marquises,
with the title of Tèjìn.
The saying "chickens roosting in trees" was certainly fitting,
and "three horses eating from one trough" indeed came true.
In summer,
the fourth month,
Sīkōng Gāo Ròu was appointed Sītú,
and Guānglù Dàfū Xú Miǎo was appointed Sīkōng.
Xú Miǎo sighed, saying:
"The Sāngōng (Three Dukes) are officials who deliberate on the Dao.
If there is no suitable person, the position should remain vacant.
The Shū (Book of Documents) states: 'The Sāngōng deliberate on the Dao to govern the state,
regulating yin and yang.
The positions need not always be filled,
only by the right person.'
Tiǎn (忝),
means to disgrace."
In the fifth month,
Fèi Yī of Hàn (Shǔ Hàn) marched out to garrison in Hànzhōng.
From Jiǎng Wǎn to Fèi Yī,
although they resided in external regions,
matters of rewards, commendations, punishments, and authority
were all first consulted and decided from afar,
and only then carried out.
Fèi Yī was naturally humble and modest;
his achievements and reputation in governing the state
were roughly comparable to Jiǎng Wǎn's.
In autumn,
the ninth month,
Chēqí Jiāngjūn Wáng Líng was appointed Sīkōng.
5 The Yí of Fúlíng rebelled.
Fúlíng County
belonged to Bā Commandery in the Hàn dynasty.
Shǔ divided it and established Fúlíng Commandery.
It was Fú Zhōu in the Táng dynasty.
Sòng Bái said: Fú Zhōu, Fúlíng Commandery,
was the territory of Fúlíng County in the Hàn dynasty.
The Shǔ First Emperor, considering this land controlled the source of the river,
established Fúlíng Commandery here,
administering Hànpíng and Hànjiā two counties.
The Sìyí Xiàndào Jì says: The old city was south of the Shǔ River
and west of the Fú River.
The Fú River comes from Qíanzhōng to the south,
and flows west of the city, ascending the Shǔ River for fifteen *lǐ*.
There is Jīmíng Gorge,
above which is Zhǐ City,
which was Hàn Zhǐ County.
After Lǐ Xióng occupied Shǔ,
Zhǐ County fell into disuse.
When Huán Wēn pacified Shǔ,
a separate Zhǐ County was established ten *lǐ* northeast of the current commandery.
In the fourth year of Bǎodìng of Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu (564 CE),
Tián Sīhè, a leader of Fúlíng, submitted.
Fúlíng Garrison was established at the old Zhǐ City.
In the third year of Kāihuáng of the Suí dynasty (583 CE),
Hànpíng County was moved to the garrison city,
and Hànpíng was renamed Fúlíng County,
named after the garrison.
In the Táng dynasty it was Fú Zhōu.
In the third year of Yuánhé (808 CE),
because the territory of Fú Zhōu was close to Qíanzhōng,
an imperial edict ordered it to be subordinated to Qíanzhōng.
According to Huáyáng Guó Zhì: Fúlíng
was the southern border of Bā.
Entering from Zhǐ County
and ascending the Fú River,
Qín Sīmǎ Cuò used this route to take the Qíanzhōng territory of Chǔ.
After the rise of the Hàn dynasty, it was often administered by a Commandant.
With dangerous mountains and rapids,
the people were mostly Ráng and Dàn.
It only produced cinnabar, lacquer, honey, and *zhǐ* fruit.
The county was administered by Fú Zhōu.
In the Jiàn'ān era of the Hàn dynasty,
Xiè Běn of Fúlíng, considering Fúlíng to be vast,
proposed to the Provincial Governor Liú Zhāng to divide it and establish Dānxīng and Hànjiā two counties to form a commandery.
Zhāng then divided Fúlíng,
established Yǒngníng,
and, combining Dānxīng and Hànjiā,
a total of four counties, established a Dependent State Commandant,
who administered Fúlíng.
The Shǔ First Emperor changed it to a commandery,
renamed Yǒngníng as Wànníng,
and further established Hànfù County.
The Latter Emperor further established Hànpíng County.
The Jìn Tàikāng Dìzhì abolished Dānxīng County,
and the commandery administration moved to Hànfù.
It also said Wànníng was south of the commandery,
nine hundred *lǐ* by water.
That Wànníng is probably the present-day Fèi Zhōu.
In the Yánxī era of the Shǔ Latter Emperor,
Xú Jù, a powerful family head in Fúlíng, rebelled.
Dèng Zhī suppressed him.
Hàn Fúlíng was probably three hundred thirty *lǐ* southeast of present-day Fú Zhōu.
Qían Zhōu was its old administrative seat,
east of the river.
It also said: Hànfù County was ninety *lǐ* north of Fúlíng.
Its old administrative seat was probably Hóngdù County, now under Qían Zhōu.
It also said: Hànjiā was a hundred *lǐ* east of the commandery,
where the source of the Lǐ River emerged from its boundary.
This was probably the old Qían Zhōu city, ninety *lǐ* east of the present-day *zhōu*.
Dānxīng County was probably Qíanjiāng County, two hundred *lǐ* east of present-day Qían Zhōu.
Furthermore, Hànpíng County
was one hundred twenty *lǐ* east of present-day Fú Zhōu,
north of Luófú Mountain,
south of the Mín River,
near where the Bái River enters the river.
Furthermore, according to Shísān Zhōu Zhì,
Zhǐ was northeast of the commandery,
and Fúlíng was east of the commandery.
According to present knowledge, Qían Zhōu also bordered Bā Commandery to the southeast.
Based on what Xiè Běn argued
and what the Jìn Zhì said,
the five present-day *zhōu*s of Yí, Fèi, Sī, Bō, and Qíanfǔ
were all the old territory of Fúlíng.
Furthermore, the Suí Tújīng states that
Qíanzhōng was the territory of Yǒuyáng County of Wǔlíng Commandery.
However, Hàn Yǒuyáng was in the present-day Xī Zhōu Quǎnxīang County border,
about over a thousand *lǐ* from Qían Zhōu.
Another Yǒuyáng City, more than nine hundred *lǐ* northwest of present-day Sāntíng County,
was established by Liú Shǔ,
not the Hàn Yǒuyáng.
The Suí Tújīng and Zhēnguān Dìzhì both state that the Yǒuyáng established by Shǔ was Hàn Yǒuyáng,
which was probably a mistaken identification of the territory of Hàn Fúlíng.
After Yǒngjiā,
it was swallowed by the Yí and Láo.
Later records from the Yuán Wèi dynasty were not passed down.
When Tián Sīhè submitted in the Hòu Zhōu dynasty,
Fèng Zhōu was initially established in that territory,
then renamed Qían Zhōu.
During the Dàyè era,
it was again renamed Qían'ān Commandery.
Due to questions about the names of Suí *zhōu*s and commanderies,
it became difficult to distinguish it from the Qín and Hàn Qíanzhōng Commandery.
The administrative seat of Qín Qíanzhōng Commandery
was the old Qíanzhōng city, twenty *lǐ* west of present-day Chén Zhōu.
The Hàn dynasty renamed Qíanzhōng to Wǔlíng Commandery
and moved its administration to Yìlíng,
which is present-day Xùpǔ County of Chén Zhōu.
The Later Hàn dynasty moved its administration to Línyuán,
which is present-day Láng Zhōu.
Present-day Chén, Jǐn, Xù, Jiǎng, Xī, Lǐ, Láng, and Shī eight *zhōu*s
are the territory of Qín and Hàn Qíanzhōng Commandery,
separated from present-day Qían Zhōu and Yí, Fèi, Sī, Bō by steep ridges.
To the east, the Yuán River and various streams converge
and flow eastward into Dòngtíng Lake.
West of the ridges is the Bā River,
also named Fúlíng River,
which flows north from Zāngkē through Bō, Fèi, Sī, Qían, and other *zhōu*s,
and flows north into the Mín River.
Judging by mountains and rivers,
Fúlíng of Bā Commandery and the old territory of Qíanzhōng
are clearly distinct.
6 General-in-Chief Shuǎng
was arrogant and extravagant beyond measure.
His food and clothing
imitated that of the imperial chariot.
Rare treasures from the imperial workshops
filled his home.
He also privately took former emperors' concubines as entertainers.
He constructed a cave-chamber,
with intricately carved windows all around.
A cave-chamber
is a room dug into the ground.
Xián said: Qǐshū
means carved with brocade patterns.
His younger brother Xī was deeply worried by this
and repeatedly, with tears, advised him to stop,
but Shuǎng did not listen.
Shuǎng and his brothers often went out together on excursions.
Huán Fàn of Pèiguó, Minister of Agriculture, said to them:
"You manage all affairs of state
and command the imperial guards.
It is inappropriate for you all to go out together.
If someone were to close the city gates,
who would be able to re-enter?"
Shuǎng said:
"Who would dare to do that!"
Initially,
Qīnghé and Píngyuán disputed their boundary,
and for eight years it could not be resolved.
The Inspector of Jìzhōu, Sūn Lǐ, requested a map from the archives of the Tiānfǔ (Heavenly Treasury) that showed the boundaries when Lièzǔ enfeoffed Píngyuán, in order to resolve it.
Lièzǔ
was Míngdì,
who was enfeoffed as the King of Píngyuán.
The land division and establishment of states
had maps preserved in the Tiānfǔ.
The Zhōulǐ (Rites of Zhou) mentions the Tiānfǔ.
Zhèng Xuán's commentary states: "It manages the treasures of the ancestral temple";
also, "the writings of the virtuous and capable, as well as records of merits, were all stored in the Tiānfǔ."
Sūn Lǐ was told the maps could not be used.
He submitted a memorial to clarify his position,
his words being quite firm and sharp.
Cáo Shuǎng was greatly enraged,
and impeached Sūn Lǐ for harboring resentment,
sentencing him to five years of penal servitude.
"Sentencing him to five years of penal servitude"
means merely sentencing him to five years of penal labor without actually making him perform it.
"Hé"
is pronounced Hù-gài,
also Hù-dé.
Sūn Lǐ was again made Inspector of Bìngzhōu,
and went to see the Grand Tutor, Sīmǎ Yì.
He had an angry expression but said nothing.
Sīmǎ Yì said:
"Are you displeased with getting Bìngzhōu?
Are you angry about losing out in the boundary division?"
Wèi's Bìngzhōu governed Tàiyuán, Shàngdǎng, Xīhé, Yànmén, and Xīnxīng.
Jìzhōu was larger than other provinces.
Bìngzhōu bordered the desolate frontier,
so Sīmǎ Yì assumed Sūn Lǐ was resentful.
Sīmǎ Yì was full of stratagems,
and used these words to provoke Sūn Lǐ.
"Shǎo"
is pronounced Shī-zhǎo.
"Huì"
is pronounced Yú-bì.
"Fēn"
is pronounced Fú-wèn.
"How strange are your words, Illustrious Lord!
Although Lǐ is not virtuous,
how could he be concerned with official position or past events!
Originally, I thought you, Illustrious Lord, would emulate Yī and Lǚ,
assist the Wèi court,
repay Míngdì's trust above,
and establish merits for myriad generations below.
Now, the altars of soil and grain are in peril,
and the world is in turmoil.
This is why Lǐ is unhappy!"
Thereupon, tears streamed down his face.
Sīmǎ Yì said:
"Stop for now;
endure the unendurable!"
At this point,
Sūn Lǐ was already within Sīmǎ Yì's plans.
In winter,
Lǐ Shèng, the Mayor of Hénán, was sent out as Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
He went to bid farewell to the Grand Tutor, Sīmǎ Yì.
Sīmǎ Yì had two maids attend him.
When they held his clothes,
they fell off.
He pointed to his mouth and said he was thirsty.
When the maids offered porridge,
Sīmǎ Yì did not hold the cup but drank,
and all the porridge flowed out, wetting his chest.
Lǐ Shèng said:
"The general sentiment is that your old illness has recurred."
When Wèi Wǔ had summoned Sīmǎ Yì,
Sīmǎ Yì had declined, citing wind-stroke (fēngbì).
Therefore, Lǐ Shèng thought his old illness had recurred.
Sīmǎ Yì made his voice barely coherent,
feigning a frail and weakened state.
"Zhǔ"
is pronounced Zhī-yù.
"You are old and afflicted with illness;
death is imminent.
You will go to Bìngzhōu.
Bìngzhōu is close to the Hu;
prepare well for them!
I fear we will not meet again,
so I entrust my sons Shī and Zhāo to you."
Lǐ Shèng said:
"I will return to my native province."
Lǐ Shèng
was from Nányáng,
so he referred to Jīngzhōu as his native province.
Sīmǎ Yì then confused his words, saying:
"Are you going to Bìngzhōu?"
Lǐ Shèng replied again:
"I will be in Jīngzhōu."
Sīmǎ Yì said:
"I am old and my mind is confused;
I do not understand what you are saying.
Now, returning to your native province,
with your splendid virtue and heroic spirit,
build great achievements!"
Lǐ Shèng withdrew
and told Cáo Shuǎng:
"Duke Sīmǎ is a mere corpse with residual breath;
his body and spirit have already separated.
There is nothing to worry about."
He meant that his body and spirit had already separated,
and only his corpse remained with a lingering breath.
He also tearfully told Cáo Shuǎng and others:
Shedding tears without sound
is called chuíqì.
"The Grand Tutor's illness is beyond recovery;
it is truly saddening!"
Thus, Cáo Shuǎng and others no longer took precautions.
Hé Yàn heard that Guǎn Lù of Píngyuán was skilled in divination
and requested to meet him.
In the twelfth month,
on the day Bǐngxū,
Guǎn Lù went to see Hé Yàn.
Hé Yàn discussed the Yì with him.
At that time, Dèng Yáng was present
and said to Guǎn Lù:
"You claim to be skilled in the Yì,
but in your conversation you haven't mentioned the words and meanings of the Yì.
Why is that?"
Guǎn Lù said:
"Indeed, one who is skilled in the Yì does not speak of the Yì."
Hé Yàn smiled and praised him, saying:
"This can be called 'essential words without verbosity'!"
He then said to Guǎn Lù:
"Try to cast a hexagram for me.
Can you tell if my position will reach that of a Sāngōng (Three Dukes)?"
He also asked:
"I've repeatedly dreamt of dozens of green flies
gathering on my nose,
and I cannot drive them away.
What does this mean?"
Guǎn Lù said:
"In the past, Yuán and Kǎi assisted Shùn."
The Zuǒzhuàn states: "Gāoyáng Shì had eight talented sons:
Cāng Shū, Tuí Nài, Táoyǎn, Dà Lín, Lóng Jiàng, Tíng Jiān, Zhòng Róng, and Shú Dá.
They were all sagely and vast,
bright, sincere, and trustworthy.
The people of the world called them
'Bākǎi' (Eight Benevolent Ones).'
Gāoxīn Shì had eight talented sons:
Bó Fèn, Zhòng Kān, Shú Xiàn, Jì Zhòng, Bó Hǔ, Zhòng Xióng, Shú Bào, and Jì Lí.
They were loyal, solemn, respectful, and dignified,
proclaimed kindness and peace.
The people of the world called them
'Bāyuán' (Eight Primal Ones).'
All of them, through harmony, kindness, humility, and respect,
enjoyed abundant blessings;
this is not something divination can clarify.
Now, your lordly position is honored and your power is great,
yet those who cherish virtue are few,
while those who fear your might are many.
This is probably not the way of seeking blessings with a cautious heart.
Furthermore,
the nose is the 'mountain of the heavenly center'."
Physiognomy books consider the nose to be the heavenly center.
From the lips upward is the human center.
Péi Sōngzhī said: "Physiognomy books consider the location of the nose as the heavenly center.
The nose has the appearance of a mountain,
hence it is called the 'mountain of the heavenly center.'
This is where nobility resides permanently.
Now, foul-smelling green flies
gather on it.
Those in high positions fall,
and the frivolous and arrogant perish.
This must be deeply pondered!
I wish, my lord, that you would 'gather the many to aid the few' and 'not tread where propriety forbids.'
Then, the Sāngōng position can be reached,
and the green flies can be driven away."
Dèng Yáng said:
"This is an 'old scholar's common discourse'."
Guǎn Lù said:
"Indeed, the 'old scholar' sees what is not born;
the 'common discourse' speaks of what is not spoken of."
He meant that he would surely see their deaths.
"Tán"
is the same as "tán" (談).
In the residential quarter,
at Píngyuán's mansion,
Guǎn Lù's maternal uncle reproached him for speaking too sharply and directly.
Guǎn Lù said:
"Speaking to dead men,
what is there to fear!"
His uncle was greatly angered
and considered Guǎn Lù mad.
7 The Yí (barbarian) bandits of Wú's Jiāozhǐ and Jiǔzhēn attacked and captured cities and towns,
causing commotion in the Jiāo region.
The Ruler of Wú appointed Lù Yìn, the Supervising General of Hángyáng, as Inspector of Jiāozhōu and Commandant-Protector of Ānnán.
Lù Yìn entered the region,
explained the principles of benevolence and trust,
and over 50,000 households surrendered.
The provincial border was pacified again.
8 The Grand Tutor, Sīmǎ Yì, secretly conspired with his sons, Sīmǎ Shī, the Central Protector of the Army, and Sīmǎ Zhāo, the Palace Assistant Imperial Censor, to execute Cáo Shuǎng.
Although Sīmǎ Yì claimed illness,
he had already placed his two sons in crucial positions.
The first year of Jiāpíng
(Jǐsì, 249 CE).
The reign title was changed in the fourth month of this year.
In the 1st year of the Zhèngshǐ era [240 CE] of Emperor Shào of Wèi.
Spring, 1st month, on the day of
Jiǎwǔ,
the Emperor visited Gāopíng Líng.
Gāopíng Líng
is the tomb of Emperor Míng.
The commentary to the *Shuǐjīng* states: Dàshí Shān is south of Luòyáng.
In the valley of the mountain is Wèi Míngdì's Gāopíng Líng.
Sūn Shèng said: Gāopíng Líng is ninety *lǐ* from Luòchéng.
The Grand Tutor Sīmǎ Yì, acting on the order of the Empress Dowager,
closed all city gates,
mustered troops to occupy the arsenal,
and sent troops to garrison the floating bridge over the Luò Shuǐ.
The commentary to the *Shuǐjīng* states: The second gate from the west, opening south from Luòchéng, is called Xuānyángmén.
It was the Xiǎoyuànmén of Hàn.
Facing Chānghé,
it led directly south to the floating bridge over the Luò Shuǐ.
(He also) occupied Sòng Ruǎng's camp,
and the Grand Coachman Wáng Guān, acting as Superintendent of the Central Army,
occupied Sòng Xī's camp.
Thereupon, Sīmǎ Yì presented Suǎng's crimes to the Emperor, saying:
"When your servant returned from Liáodōng,
the late Emperor commanded Your Majesty, the Prince of Qín, and your servant to ascend the imperial couch.
He grasped your servant's arm,
deeply concerned about the future.
This event is recorded in the previous volume under Míngdì, Jǐngchū 3rd year.
He said: 'This (child) is what Your Majesty saw with his own eyes.
There is nothing to worry about.
Should anything unexpected occur,
your servant will serve the imperial decree even unto death.'
Now, the Grand General Sòng Ruǎng,
has betrayed the dying injunction,
and disrupted the national order.
Internally, he has usurped authority,
externally, he has monopolized power,
dismantled various camps,
seized all the imperial guards,
placed his confidants
in all important official positions,
replaced the palace guards
with his private retainers,
establishing a deeply entrenched network,
and growing ever more unrestrained.
Furthermore, he appointed the Yellow Gate Attendant Zhāng Dāng as Commander-in-chief,
to spy on Your Majesty,
sow discord between the two palaces,
and harm the imperial family.
The empire is in turmoil,
and people are filled with fear and apprehension.
Your Majesty has become a 'guest ruler'.
'Guest ruler'
means that although one holds the position of the Son of Heaven,
one is merely a temporary occupant.
This was not the original intention when the late Emperor commanded Your Majesty and your servant to ascend the imperial couch.
Although your servant is old and infirm,
'old and infirm'
means aged and debilitated,
with one's days already passed.
Grand Commandant Wáng Jì and others all believe that Suǎng harbors disloyal intentions,
and that he and his brothers should not command the imperial guards. This was reported to Yǒngnínggōng,
and the Empress Dowager issued an order to your servant to act as proposed.
Your servant immediately commanded the officials concerned and the Director of the Yellow Gates: 'Dismiss Suǎng, Xī, and Xùn's officers and soldiers,
and send them to their residences as marquises.
They are not to linger,
thereby delaying the imperial retinue.
Anyone who dares to delay
shall be dealt with according to military law!'
Your servant, despite his illness, is leading troops to garrison the floating bridge over the Luò Shuǐ,
to observe for any unusual developments."
*Zhé*
means 'to act on one's own authority'.
Although Sīmǎ Yì used the Empress Dowager's order to confront Suǎng,
he mentioned acting on his own initiative ("Your servant immediately commanded") twice in his memorial,
because the Emperor was with Suǎng.
Suǎng was unable to communicate (with his officials);
he was pressed and distressed, not knowing what to do.
He kept the imperial retinue overnight south of the Yī Shuǐ.
The commentary to the *Shuǐjīng* states: The Lái Rú zhī Shuǐ
originates from Bànshí zhī Shān,
flows southwest past Dàshí Shān,
then west to the east of Gāodū Chéng,
and enters the Yī Shuǐ from the west.
The Yī Shuǐ then flows northeast through Yīquè,
and further northeast to the south of Luòyáng Xiàn,
entering the Luò (Shuǐ) from the north.
He mobilized several thousand *túntián* soldiers as a guard.
When Wèi Wǔ founded the dynasty,
he ordered all provinces and commanderies to establish *túntián* officials.
Thus, Luòyáng also had *túntián* soldiers.
Sīmǎ Yì sent Palace Attendant Xǔ Yǔn of Gāoyáng and Minister Chén Tài to persuade Suǎng,
advising him to confess his crimes early.
He also sent the Palace Commandant Yǐn Dàmù, whom Suǎng trusted, to tell Suǎng
that he would only be dismissed from office.
According to the system of Wèi and Jìn,
there were Palace Generals, Central Regular Mounted Attendants, Commandants, and Sīmǎ.
When Yǐn Dàmù persuaded Suǎng,
Suǎng still did not suspect the Sīmǎ clan.
It was only when Yǐn Dàmù later spoke to Wén Qīn that he realized.
Chén Tài
was Chén Qún's son.
Earlier,
Suǎng regarded Huán Fàn as an old and respected elder from his hometown.
Huán Fàn
was from Pèiguó. Qíao and Pèi were neighboring commanderies.
*Lǎo*
means 'elderly'. *Sù*
means 'experienced'.
However, he was not very close to him.
When Sīmǎ Yì raised troops,
he summoned Huán Fàn by order of the Empress Dowager,
intending to make him acting Superintendent of the Central Army.
Huán Fàn intended to obey the order,
but his son stopped him, saying:
"The Emperor's retinue is outside.
It would be better to go south."
Huán Fàn then left.
When he reached Píngchāng Chéngmén,
the commentary to the *Shuǐjīng* states: Píngchāngmén
was formerly Píngmén,
the third gate from the west, opening south from Luòchéng.
The gatekeeper, Sī Fān,
was formerly an official recommended by Huán Fàn.
Sī
is a surname.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* mentions a Sī Chén of Zhèng.
Huán Fàn pretended, saying:
"There is an imperial edict summoning me.
Quickly open the gate!"
Sī Fān wanted to see the imperial edict.
From this, one can see
that at this time, bamboo or wooden tablets were still used for edicts.
By the Jìn dynasty, there were already edicts on green paper.
Huán Fàn said: "Are you not my former subordinate?
How dare you act like this?"
Sī Fān then opened it.
After Huán Fàn left the city,
he looked back at Sī Fān and said:
"The Grand Tutor is plotting rebellion!
You should come with me!"
Sī Fān, being on foot, could not catch up
and therefore avoided him by stepping aside.
He moved to the side of the road.
"The 'bag of wisdom' has gone!"
Wáng Jì said:
"Huán Fàn is indeed wise.
However, a clumsy horse clings to its fodder.
Suǎng will surely not make use of him."
Huán Fàn arrived,
urging the brothers Cáo Shuǎng to take the emperor to Xǔchāng,
and summon troops from all four directions to support themselves.
Cáo Shuǎng hesitated, undecided.
Huán Fàn said to Cáo Xī:
"This matter is so clear,
why do you bother with your studies!
Today, for people of your household,
can you even regain a life of poverty and low status!
Moreover, if an ordinary man pledges himself to one person,
he still hopes to survive;
this refers to the pledging of oneself in the chaos of the late Hàn dynasty.
'Zhì'
(pledge), pronounced 'zhì'.
If you issue an order to the world,
who would dare not respond!"
They both remained silent.
Huán Fàn again said to Cáo Xī:
"Your separate camp is close to the south of the palace gate.
The central army camp,
Sīmǎ Yì has already sent Wáng Guān to occupy it;
only your separate camp remains.
'Luòyáng diǎnnóng zhōnglángjiàng' and 'diǎnnóng dūwèi' are the offices it oversees.
Now, if we go to Xǔchāng,
it will take no more than a mid-night stop.
'Zhōngsù'
means a stop in the middle.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says: 'I command you three stops,
you will arrive at the mid-night stop.'
Lù Démíng says: 'Zhōng'
pronounced 'dìng zhòng fān'.
It would be enough for us to provision ourselves;
Xǔchāng has a separate armory storing weapons and armor.
Luòyáng has a military arsenal,
hence it is called a separate armory.
'Bèi jiǎ'
means to grant weapons.
'Bèi'
pronounced 'pí yì fān'.
And the seal of the 'Dàsīnóng' is with me."
Cáo Xī and his brothers were silent and did not comply.
From 'jiǎyè' to 'wǔgǔ',
'Jiǎyè'
is the beginning of the night.
The night has five watches: the first watch is 'jiǎyè',
the second watch is 'yǐyè',
the third watch is 'bǐngyè',
the fourth watch is 'dīngyè',
and the fifth watch is 'wǔyè'.
"I, too, won't fail to be a rich old man!"
Huán Fàn wept and said:
"Cáo Zǐdān was a fine man
to father you brothers,
you are mere piglets and calves!"
Cáo Zhēn,
courtesy name Zǐdān.
'Tún'
is the same as 'tún'.
A small pig is called 'tún',
a small calf is called 'dú'.
Cáo Shuǎng then sent Sīmǎ Yì's memorial,
petitioned the emperor to issue an edict dismissing him from office,
and escorted the emperor back to the palace.
Cáo Shuǎng and his brothers returned home,
and Sīmǎ Yì dispatched Lúoyáng officials and soldiers to surround and guard them.
Officials and soldiers under the authority of the Lúoyáng magistrate.
He ordered someone to observe the actions of Cáo Shuǎng and his brothers from upstairs.
When Cáo Shuǎng, holding a slingshot, went to the back garden,
someone upstairs immediately shouted:
"The former 'Dàjiàngjūn' is heading southeast!"
Cáo Shuǎng was troubled and did not know what to do.
On 'wùxū',
the relevant authorities reported:
"Huángmén Zhāng Dāng secretly gave chosen talented women to Cáo Shuǎng,
suspecting foul play."
Zhāng Dāng was arrested and handed over to the 'Tíngwèi' for examination and verification.
He confessed, saying:
"Cáo Shuǎng, together with 'Shàngshū' Hé Yàn, Dèng Yáng, Dīng Mì, 'Sīlì Xiàowèi' Bì Guǐ, and 'Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ' Lǐ Shèng, etc., conspired to rebel
and were due to act in the third month."
Thereupon, Cáo Shuǎng, Cáo Xī, Cáo Xùn, Hé Yàn, Dèng Yáng, Dīng Mì, Bì Guǐ, Lǐ Shèng, and Huán Fàn were all arrested and imprisoned.
They were impeached for grand treason and disloyalty,
and, along with Zhāng Dāng, their three clans were exterminated.
The 'Kǎoyì' states: The 'Wèi Shì Chūnqiū' says:
"Xuān Wáng made Hé Yàn supervise the case of Cáo Shuǎng and others.
Hé Yàn thoroughly investigated the partisans,
hoping to gain clemency thereby.
Xuān Wáng said: 'There are eight clans in total,'
Hé Yàn listed seven families, including Dīng and Dèng.
Xuān Wáng said: 'Not yet.'
Hé Yàn was at his wit's end and finally said: 'Could it be me, Hé Yàn?'
Xuān Wáng said: 'That's right.'
Then Hé Yàn was arrested."
According to this, when Xuān Wáng was prosecuting Cáo Shuǎng's faction,
how could he allow Hé Yàn to supervise their case!
Even if it were true,
how could Hé Yàn not know that he was closest to Cáo Shuǎng and yet hope to be the only one spared!
This is probably Sūn Shèng echoing the fabrication of storytellers.
Earlier,
when Cáo Shuǎng left,
'Sīmǎ' Lǔ Zhī remained in the residence.
Hearing of the disturbance,
he led cavalry from the camp to break through the 'jīnmén' to go to Cáo Shuǎng.
'Yíngqí'
means the knights of the 'Dàjiàngjūn's camp.
'Jīnmén'
is the first gate at the western end of the southern exit of Luòchéng;
it is also called 'Jiànchéngmén'.
'Qí'
pronounced 'qí jì fān'.
As he was about to leave,
'Zhǔbù' Yáng Zōng stopped him, saying:
"My lord holds the emperor and wields power,
abandoning this to go to the East Market?"
He meant that he would surely be executed in the market.
'Tàifù' Sīmǎ Yì said:
"They are each serving their master,
pardon them."
Soon after,
Lǔ Zhī was made 'Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng',
and Yáng Zōng was made 'Shàngshū Láng'.
When Lǔ Zhī was about to leave,
he called 'Cānjūn' Xīn Chǎng, wanting to go with him.
Xīn Chǎng
was the son of Xīn Pí.
His elder sister, Xīn Xiànyīng, was the wife of 'Tàicháng' Yáng Dān.
Xīn Chǎng consulted with her, saying:
"The emperor is outside,
the 'Tàifù' has closed the city gates.
People say it will be disadvantageous to the state;
is such a thing permissible?"
'Ěr'
means 'thus'.
"In my judgment,
the 'Tàifù's action
is merely to execute Cáo Shuǎng."
Xīn Chǎng said:
"Then the matter will succeed?"
Xīn Xiànyīng said:
"Will it not mostly succeed!
'Dài'
means 'close' or 'nearly'.
'Ǒu'
means 'pair'.
"Then can I, Xīn Chǎng, not go out?"
Xīn Xiànyīng said:
"How can you not go out!
Fulfilling one's duty
is a great principle of humanity.
When people are in distress,
they are still sometimes pitied;
to serve as someone's whip-bearer and abandon one's duty
is the greatest misfortune.
Moreover, to be appointed by someone,
to die for someone,
is the duty of intimacy and kinship.
Just follow the crowd."
Xīn Chǎng then went out.
After the matter was settled,
Xīn Chǎng sighed:
"If I had not consulted my sister,
I would have almost failed in my righteousness!"
Before this,
Cáo Shuǎng had summoned Wáng Shěn and Yáng Hù of Tàishān.
Wáng Shěn urged Yáng Hù to answer the summons.
Yáng Hù said:
"Pledging oneself to serve someone,
how could it be so easy!"
Wáng Shěn then went.
When Cáo Shuǎng was defeated,
Wáng Shěn was spared as a former subordinate.
He then said to Yáng Hù:
"I have not forgotten your earlier words."
Yáng Hù said:
"This was not something I foresaw at the beginning of my consideration!"
He meant that he also did not foresee Cáo Shuǎng's downfall,
and did not wish to be known as someone who had foresight.
Shuǎng's cousin's wife, Xiàhóu Lìngnǚ,
whose given name was Lìngnǚ.
Xià,
read as hù-yǎ.
Her father, Wénníng, wanted to marry her off;
Lìngnǚ cut off both her ears with a knife to pledge her resolve,
and always stayed with Shuǎng.
When Shuǎng was executed,
her family submitted a memorial to break off the marriage,
and forcibly brought her home.
They were again going to marry her off;
Lìngnǚ secretly entered her bedchamber,
drew a knife, and cut off her own nose.
Her family was shocked and grieved,
and said to her:
"Life in this world
is like light dust clinging to a frail blade of grass.
Why torment yourself to such an extent!
Moreover, your husband's family has been exterminated,
who are you preserving this for?"
Lìngnǚ said:
"I have heard that the benevolent do not change their principles due to prosperity or decline,
and the righteous do not alter their hearts due to existence or extinction.
When the Cáo clan was prosperous before,
I still wished to preserve my fidelity until the end.
How much more so now that they are in decline and ruined,
how could I bear to abandon them!
This is the
conduct of beasts,
how could I do such a thing!"
Sīmǎ Yì heard of this and esteemed her,
permitting her to adopt a child to raise as an heir for the Cáo clan.
Hé Yàn and others were then in power,
believing themselves to be the outstanding talents of their time,
unsurpassed by anyone.
Yàn once categorized famous scholars, saying:
" 'Only the profound can penetrate the will of all under Heaven' –
Xiàhóu Tàichū is such a one.
'Only the subtle can accomplish the affairs of all under Heaven' –
Sīmǎ Zǐyuán is such a one.
'Only the spirit, without hastening, is swift,
without moving, arrives' –
I have heard of this saying,
but have not seen such a person."
This was probably his intention to compare himself to the spirit.
Xiàhóu Xuán,
courtesy name Tàichū.
Sīmǎ Shī,
courtesy name Zǐyuán.
Yàn quoted from the commentary on the Great Commentary of the Yì Jīng to categorize them.
Jī,
read as jū-xī.
Liú Táo, the department head of the personnel selection office,
was Yè's son.
He was skilled in rhetoric in his youth,
and Dèng Yáng and his associates praised him as an Yī Yǐn or Lǚ Shàng.
Táo once said to Fù Xuán:
"Zhòngní (Confucius) was not a sage.
How do I know this?
A wise man dealing with the ignorant
is like playing with a ball in his palm;
yet he could not gain control of the world,
how then could he be a sage!"
Xuán did not refute him,
but simply said to him:
"The changes in the world are impermanent.
Now I see you in difficulty."
When Cáo Shuǎng was defeated,
Táo retired to his village home,
and then apologized for the error of his words.
Guǎn Lù's maternal uncle said to Lù:
"How did you know beforehand of Hé and Dèng's downfall?"
Lù said:
"Dèng's gait was such that
his sinews did not bind his bones,
and his veins did not control his flesh.
When he stood up, he swayed and tilted,
as if he had no hands or feet.
This indicates a demonic agitation.
As for Hé's appearance, his soul did not reside in its dwelling,
his blood did not give luster to his complexion,
his vital spirit floated like smoke,
and his countenance was like withered wood.
This indicates a demonic gloom.
Both are not symbols of lasting fortune."
When Guǎn Lù spoke with Hé and Dèng,
his articulation of principles was close to that of the ancients;
but when he answered his uncle about the reason for Hé and Dèng's downfall,
it was merely the talk of a physiognomist.
How contradictory are these two statements!
Hé Yàn was by nature self-satisfied;
he always kept white powder in his hand
to apply to his face.
He was particularly fond of the writings of Lǎozi and Zhuāngzi,
and with Xiàhóu Xuán, Xún Càn, and Wáng Bì of Shānyáng,
he engaged in "pure conversation,"
valuing emptiness and non-being,
and calling the Six Classics the dregs of the sages.
Because of this, the literati and officials of the realm vied to emulate him,
thus forming a trend
that could no longer be controlled.
The calamity of "pure conversation" began here.
He was Yù's son.
2 On the day of bǐngwǔ,
a general amnesty was declared.
3 On the day of dīngwèi,
Grand Tutor Yì was appointed Chancellor,
and granted the Nine Bestowals;
Yì steadfastly declined to accept.
4 Previously,
Right General Xiàhóu Bà was highly favored by Cáo Shuǎng.
Because his father Yuān had died in Shǔ,
(the event is found in volume sixty-eight, during Emperor Xiàn's Jiàn'ān twenty-fourth year).
he was made Protector of the Army for the Campaign against Shǔ,
stationed in Lǒngxī,
and under the command of the General Who Conquers the West.
He was under the jurisdiction of the General Who Conquers the West's headquarters.
Bà's cousin,
Xuán, was Shuǎng's maternal cousin.
The Cáo clan
was descended from the Xiàhóu clan.
Xuán's father Shàng also married into the Cáo clan,
hence Xuán was Shuǎng's maternal cousin.
Sīmǎ Yì summoned Xuán to the capital,
creating a pretext for Sīmǎ Shī to later kill Xuán.
Bà had always been at odds with Huái,
believing that disaster would surely befall him,
he was greatly afraid,
and so he fled to Hàn.
The ruler of Hàn said to him:
"Your father was merely killed in battle,
not by the hand of my ancestors."
He treated him very generously.
Jiāng Wéi asked Bà:
"Now that Sīmǎ Yì has control of their government,
will he still have ambitions for conquest?"
Bà said:
"He is currently focused on establishing his family,
and has no time for external affairs.
There is a Zhōng Shìjì;
though he is young,
if he comes to manage court affairs,
Wú and Shǔ will have worries."
Shìjì was
Zhōng Yáo's son, Shàngshū Láng Huì.
This laid the groundwork for Sīmǎ Zhāo to later use Huì to conquer Shǔ.
5 In the third month,
Zhū Rán, the Grand Marshal of the Left of Wú, died.
Rán was not even seven *chǐ* tall,
but his demeanor was distinct,
and his personal conduct was refined and pure.
All day he was reverent and serious,
as if
on the battlefield.
Máo Cháng said: Qīnqīn
means making people eager to advance.
His excellent qualities surpassed others.
Even when the world was peaceful,
every morning and evening, when the alarm drums sounded,
Yángǔ,
refers to beating drums rapidly,
nowadays called léigǔ (drum roll).
all would don their armor and assemble in formation.
By doing this, he toyed with the enemy,
making them unaware of what to prepare for,
hence his every sortie was successful.
Although he did not deploy troops,
he constantly maintained battle readiness.
Enemy scouts, accustomed to this,
would not know when to prepare for an actual attack.
The ruler of Wú reduced his meals by day
and lost sleep by night because of him,
and imperial envoys carrying medicine, food, and other provisions
were constantly seen on the road.
Whenever Rán sent an envoy to report on his illness,
the ruler of Wú would summon him,
personally inquire about his health,
and upon entering, would bestow wine and food,
and upon leaving, bestow cloth and silk.
When he died,
the ruler of Wú grieved intensely for him.
6 In summer,
fourth month,
on the day of yǐchǒu,
the era name was changed.
The era name was changed to Jiāpíng after Cáo Shuǎng was executed.
7 When Cáo Shuǎng was in Yīnán,
Jiǎng Jì, the Marquis Jǐng of Chānglíng, wrote to him,
(Posthumous titles: "Jǐng" means "accomplished through righteousness";
"Jǐng" also means "great in wisdom and foresight.")
saying that it would be no more than a dismissal from office.
After Shuǎng was executed,
Jì was promoted to Marquis of Dūxiāng.
He submitted a memorial firmly declining,
but it was not granted.
Jì was troubled by his erroneous statement,
considering his misstatement to Shuǎng as his own failing.
On the day of bǐngzǐ,
he died.
8 Autumn.
The Hàn general Wèi Jiāngjūn Jiāng Wéi 江維 attacked Yōngzhōu 雍州,
and built two cities near Qūshān 麴山.
Qūshān 麴山
was probably in Qiāng 羌 territory,
on the southwestern border of Wèi 魏's Yōngzhōu 雍州.
According to Guō Huái 郭淮's biography,
Qūshān 麴山 was on Chìshàng 翅上.
Chì 翅
refers to Chì 翅,
which was a strategic location.
Wèi 魏 stationed troops to defend it.
Jiāng Wéi 姜維 gathered Qiāng 胡 and Hú 胡 hostages,
and encroached upon various commanderies.
The Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn 征西將軍 Guō Huái 郭淮 and the Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ 雍州刺史 Chén Tài 陳泰 defended against him.
Chén Tài 陳泰 said:
"Although Qūchéng 麴城 is fortified,
it is dangerously far from Shǔ 蜀,
and will require constant grain transport.
The Qiāng 羌 and other barbarians are weary of Jiāng Wéi's 姜維's labor demands,
and will certainly be unwilling to submit.
If we besiege and take it now,
we can capture the city without shedding blood.
Even if they send reinforcements,
the mountain paths are rugged and dangerous,
not suitable for troop movement."
So Guō Huái 郭淮 ordered Chén Tài 陳泰 to lead the Tǎoshǔ Hùjūn 討蜀護軍 Xú Zhì 徐質 and the Nán'ān Tàishǒu 南安太守 Dèng Ài 鄧艾 to advance and besiege Qūchéng 麴城,
cutting off its supply routes and external water sources.
The commanders in Qūchéng 麴城 challenged them to battle,
but were refused.
The officers and soldiers were distressed,
sharing their rations and melting snow to survive.
Jiāng Wéi 姜維 led troops to relieve them,
emerging from Niútóushān 牛頭山.
Niútóushān 牛頭山 was probably south of the Táo Shuǐ 洮水,
named after its shape.
Wèi Shōu's 魏收 Dìxíng Zhì 地形志 records: In the fourth year of Zhēnjūn 真君 of the Later Wèi 魏,
Qiúchí Jùn 仇池郡 was established,
with its seat in Jiēlín Xiàn 階陵縣.
The county had Niútóushān 牛頭山.
The Wǔdài Zhì 五代志 states: Niútóushān 牛頭山 was in the territory of Shànglù Xiàn 上祿縣 of Chéngzhōu 成州.
Chén Tài 陳泰 said:
"The art of war values subduing the enemy without fighting.
Sūnzi 孫子 said: 'A hundred victories in a hundred battles is not the ultimate excellence;
subduing the enemy without fighting is the ultimate excellence.'
Jiāng Wéi 姜維 has no escape route;
he is our captive."
He ordered all armies to hold their strongholds and not engage in battle,
and sent an envoy to inform Guō Huái 郭淮,
asking Guō Huái 郭淮 to quickly proceed to Niútóu 牛頭 and cut off Jiāng Wéi's 姜維's return path.
Guō Huái 郭淮 followed his advice,
advancing to the Táo Shuǐ 洮水.
Jiāng Wéi 姜維 was alarmed and
fled.
The commanders in Qūchéng 麴城, isolated and desperate,
surrendered.
Guō Huái 郭淮 then moved west to attack the various Qiāng 羌 tribes.
Dèng Ài 鄧艾 said:
"The enemy has not gone far;
they might return.
It would be wise to divide our forces to guard against unforeseen events."
Thereupon, Dèng Ài 鄧艾 was left to garrison north of Báishuǐ 白水.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù 水經註 states: Báishuǐ 白水 originates from Xīqīngshān 西傾山 southwest of Líntáo Xiàn 臨洮縣 in Lǒngxī 隴西,
flows southeast past the south of Dèngzhì Chéng 鄧至城,
which is where Dèng Ài 鄧艾 was stationed.
Because Dèng Ài 鄧艾 arrived here,
the city was named after him.
Jiāng Wéi 姜維 sent his general Liáo Huà 廖化 to establish a camp facing Dèng Ài 鄧艾 south of Báishuǐ 白水.
Dèng Ài 鄧艾 said to his generals:
"Jiāng Wéi 姜維 is returning suddenly now.
Our army is small; by military law, he should cross the river here.
But he is not building a bridge.
This means Jiāng Wéi 姜維 is using Liáo Huà 廖化 to hold us here so he cannot return,
while Jiāng Wéi 姜維 himself must be attacking Táochéng 洮城 from the east."
Táochéng 洮城 was north of the river,
sixty *lǐ* from Dèng Ài's 鄧艾's camp.
Dèng Ài 鄧 Ài immediately advanced secretly that night and reached it.
Jiāng Wéi 姜維 indeed came to cross the river,
but Dèng Ài 鄧 Ài had already arrived and secured the city,
thus avoiding defeat.
The Hàn 漢 army then returned.
9 Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ 兗州刺史 Línghú Yú 令狐愚.
Xìngpǔ 姓譜: Gāo 高, son of King Wén 文 of Zhōu 周, was enfeoffed in Bì 畢.
His descendant was Bì Wàn 畢萬.
Bì Wàn's 畢萬's son, Chōu 犨, was enfeoffed in Wèi 魏,
becoming the Wèi 魏 clan.
Chōu's 犨's son, Kē 顆, was enfeoffed in Línghú 令狐,
becoming the Línghú 令狐 clan.
Lìng 令
is pronounced Lì Chéng翻.
Línghú Yú 令狐愚 was stationed at Píng'ā 平阿.
Shuǐjīng Zhù 水經註: The Huái Shuǐ 淮水 passes north of Dāngtú Xiàn 當塗縣,
and further north, the Shā Shuǐ 沙水 flows into it.
West of the Huái Shuǐ 淮水 is the old city of Píng'ā Xiàn 平阿縣.
Jìn Zhì 晉志: Píng'ā Xiàn 平阿縣 belonged to Huáinán Jùn 淮南郡
and had Túshān 塗山.
He held sole responsibility for Huáinán 淮南.
Wáng Líng 王淩 and Línghú Yú 令狐愚 secretly plotted,
believing the emperor to be weak and controlled by powerful ministers.
They heard that Chǔ Wáng Biāo 楚王彪 possessed wisdom and courage,
and wished to jointly establish him [as emperor],
welcoming him to the capital Xǔchāng 許昌.
In the ninth month,
Línghú Yú 令狐愚 sent his general Zhāng Shì 張式 to Báimǎ 白馬,
to communicate with Biāo 彪.
Chǔ Wáng Biāo 楚王彪,
a son of Emperor Wǔ 武帝,
was transferred to be King of Báimǎ 白馬 in the third year of Huángchū 黃初.
Báimǎ Xiàn 白馬縣 belonged to Dōng Jùn 東郡.
Láo Jīng 勞精
(Láo 勞 is the surname,
Jīng 精 is the given name).
Xìngpǔ 姓譜: Their ancestors lived on Láoshān 勞山 in Dōnghǎi 東海,
and thus took it as their clan name.
In the Later Hàn 後漢, there was Láo Bǐng 勞丙 of Lángyá 琅邪.
Láo Jīng 勞精 said:
"Whenever great undertakings are made,
they should align with human sentiment.
Cáo Shuǎng 曹爽 lost popular support through his arrogance and extravagance.
Hé Píngshú 何平叔 was outwardly showy and neglected governance.
(Hé Yàn 何晏,
courtesy name Píngshú 平叔).
Both were self-serving and competitive in the world.
Moreover, they altered court regulations
and frequently changed government decrees.
Although their intentions were lofty, their actions did not connect with the lower classes
(meaning, although their minds aspired to noble ideals, they were impractical and
did not connect with the lower classes).
No one followed them.
Therefore, though their power influenced all within the four seas
and their fame shook the world,
they were executed on the same day,
half the renowned scholars perished,
yet the common people remained at peace,
none grieving for them,
because they had lost popular support.
Now, Sīmǎ Yì 司馬懿's intentions, though hard to fathom,
have not yet been rebellious.
He promotes and employs worthy and capable individuals,
widely cultivating those superior to himself
(referring to Jiǎng Jì 蔣濟, Gāo Róu 高柔, Sūn Lǐ 孫禮, Chén Tài 陳泰, Guō Huái 郭淮, Dèng Ài 鄧艾, etc.).
He aligns with the desires of the populace.
All the evils that Cáo Shuǎng 曹爽 committed,
he will undoubtedly change
("bì" 必
should be "bì" 畢).
He prioritizes the welfare of the people.
His father, sons, and brothers all hold military power,
so he is not easily overthrown."
Wáng Líng 王淩 did not agree.
In winter,
the eleventh month,
Línghú Yú 令狐愚 again sent Zhāng Shì 張式 to the King of Chǔ 楚王.
Before Zhāng Shì 張式 returned,
Línghú Yú 令狐愚 fell ill and died.
10 In the twelfth month,
on the *Xīnmǎo* 辛卯 day,
Wáng Líng 王淩 was immediately appointed Tàiwèi 太尉.
("Immediately appointed" means he was appointed Tàiwèi 太尉 in Shòuchūn 壽春 itself.)
On the *Gēngzǐ* 庚子 day,
the Sīlì Xiàowèi 司隸校尉 Sūn Lǐ 孫禮 was appointed Sīkōng 司空.
11. Gūnglù Dàfū Xú Miǎo died.
Xú Miǎo was famous for his integrity and purity.
Lú Qīn once wrote a book in which he praised Xú Miǎo, saying:
“Lord Xú’s aspirations are lofty, and his conduct is pure.
He is broadly talented and fierce in spirit.
In his application,
he is lofty but not narrow-minded;
pure but not unapproachable;
broad but still adheres to restraint;
fierce but capable of leniency.
Saints consider purity difficult,
but for Lord Xú, it is easy!”
Someone asked Lú Qīn:
“When Lord Xú was in the era of Wǔ Dì,
people considered him accommodating.
But ever since he became the Cìshǐ of Liángzhōu—
in Míng Dì’s Tàiwǔ era,
Xú Miǎo was the Cìshǐ of Liángzhōu—
people considered him unapproachable.
Why is this?”
Lú Qīn replied:
“In the past, Máo Xiàoxiān and Cuī Jìguī were in power,
valuing men of purity and simplicity.
At that time, everyone changed their carriages and attire to seek high renown.
The matter is found in Volume 65, Jiàn'ān Thirteenth Year of Hàn Xiàn Dì.
Máo Jiè,
courtesy name Xiàoxiān.
Cuī Yǎn,
courtesy name Jìguī.
Thus, people considered him accommodating.
Recently, the world has become extravagant and wasteful,
mutually imitating one another.
Yet Lord Xú maintained his elegant principles as before,
not conforming to popular customs.
Therefore, what was accommodating in former days
is unapproachable today.
This shows the inconstancy of worldly people, and the constancy of Lord Xú.”
Lú Qīn
was the son of Lú Yù.
1. In the summer,
fifth month,
Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn Guō Huái was appointed Chēqí Jiāngjūn.
2. Initially,
Lady Pān of Kuàijī was favored by the Lord of Wú.
She bore a young son, Liàng.
Shǎo (young).
Shī, zhào fān.
The Lord of Wú loved him.
As Princess Quán already had a rift with Crown Prince Hé—
the matter is found in the previous volume, Zhèngshǐ Sixth Year—
she frequently praised Liàng’s virtues,
and married her husband’s nephew’s daughter to him.
This laid the groundwork for Sūn Chěn to later kill Sūn Shàng, depose Liàng, and banish Princess Quán.
Shù (frequently).
Suǒ, jiǎo fān.
Qī (to marry a daughter to).
Qī, xì fān.
The Lord of Wú also disliked him in his heart,
and said to Shìzhōng Sūn Jùn:
“If the sons and brothers are not harmonious,
and the ministers are divided into factions—
Fēnbù (divided into factions)
means each forming their own factions,
like the Northern and Southern divisions of Gānlíng in Hàn.
The matter is found in Volume 64, Jiàn'ān Seventh Year.
If only one person is established,
how can there not be chaos!”
Thus, he had the intention of deposing Hé and establishing Liàng,
but he still hesitated for years.
Chényínzhě (hesitated)
means having the intention to decide but not yet having decided.
This expression is still used by people today.
Chén (to hesitate).
Chí, lín fān.
He was the great-grandson of Sūn Jìng.
Sūn Jìng
was Sūn Jiān’s youngest brother,
seen in Volume 62, Jiàn'ān First Year.
In autumn,
the Lord of Wú thereupon imprisoned Crown Prince Hé.
Piàojí Jiāngjūn Zhū Jù remonstrated, saying:
“The Crown Prince is the very root of the state;
moreover, he has a naturally benevolent and filial character,
and the empire is devoted to him.
In the past, Jìn Xiàn Dì used Lí Jī, and Shēn Shēng did not survive.
The note has already been seen before.
The matter is found in Volume 22, Zhēnghé Second Year of Hàn Wǔ Dì.
Even if a palace of longing for the son was established,
nothing could be restored!”
The Lord of Wú did not listen.
Zhū Jù, along with Shàngshū Púyè Qū Cháo,
led all the generals and officials to tie themselves up with mud on their heads,
and for several days went to the palace gate to plead for Hé.
The Lord of Wú ascended Bái Jué Guān
and saw them.
He was greatly displeased.
Bái Jué Guān was in the Jiànyè Palace.
Guān (a tower/platform).
Gǔ, wán fān.
“Do not be so hasty!”
Cōngcōng (hasty)
means hurried and not attentive to details.
The Lord of Wú placed left and right Wúnán Camp soldiers,
and also established five camp soldiers,
each with their own commanders.
The Lord of Wú was furious,
and exterminated the families of Zhèng and Xiàng.
He had Zhū Jù and Qū Cháo dragged into the hall.
Zhū Jù and Qū Cháo still remonstrated verbally,
kowtowing until their heads bled,
their words and demeanor unyielding.
The Lord of Wú beat each of them with one hundred strokes of the rod.
He demoted Zhū Jù to Xīndū Jùnchéng
and dismissed Qū Cháo to return to his fields.
More than ten other officials who were sitting because of their remonstrations were executed or banished.
He then deposed Crown Prince Hé to a commoner,
and exiled him to Gùzhāng.
Gùzhāng County belonged to Dānyáng Commandery.
Xián said: It was the seat of Qín’s Zhāng Commandery,
in the present-day Ānjí County area of Húzhōu.
Shīgǔ said: Zhāng,
Shīgǔ said: Zhāng,
pronounced zhāng.
He killed Yáng Zhú
and floated his corpse down the river.
He also executed Quán Jì, Wú Ān, and Sūn Qí,
all because they were partisans who slandered Hé.
The matter of partisan slander against Hé
is found in the previous volume, Zhèngshǐ Sixth Year.
Yáng Zhú gained a reputation in his youth,
but Lù Xùn predicted his eventual downfall,
and urged Zhú’s brother, Mù, to separate himself from their family.
When Zhú fell,
Mù was spared death due to his numerous remonstrances and warnings to Zhú.
Shù (numerous).
Suǒ, jiǎo fān.
Zhōngshū Lìng Sūn Hóng was ordered to grant him death.
3. In winter,
tenth month,
Lújiāng Tàishǒu Wén Qīn
feigned rebellion
to lure Wú Piānjiāngjūn Zhū Yì,
wanting Yì to personally lead troops to welcome him.
Zhū Yì knew it was a ruse,
and memorialized the Lord of Wú,
believing that Qīn should not be welcomed.
The Lord of Wú said:
“Currently, the northern lands are not unified.
Wén Qīn wishes to surrender;
it is fitting to welcome him for now.
If we suspect his trickery,
we should simply set up a trap to ensnare him
and deploy heavy troops to defend against him.”
So he dispatched Piānjiāngjūn Lǚ Jù to supervise two myriad men to join forces with Zhū Yì and proceed to the northern border.
Běijiè (northern border)
refers to the borderland between Wèi and Wú,
south of Wèi’s Lújiāng Commandery,
which was north for Wú.
Zhū Yì
was the son of Zhū Huán;
Lǚ Jù
was the son of Lǚ Fàn.
4. In the eleventh month,
Dàlì Jǐnghóu Sūn Lǐ died.
According to Sūn Lǐ’s biography,
Sūn Lǐ was enfeoffed as Dàlì Tínghóu.
5. The Lord of Wú established his son Liàng as the Crown Prince.
6. The Lord of Wú dispatched an army of one hundred thousand to construct Tángyì and Tú Táng
to flood the northern road.
Tángyì County,
in former Hàn it belonged to Línhuái Commandery,
in later Hàn it belonged to Guǎnglíng Commandery.
Wèi and Wú regarded it as abandoned land between their two borders.
Xián said: Tángyì
is today’s Lùhé County of Yángzhōu.
Dù Yòu said: Lùhé County of Yángzhōu
was Tángyì of Chǔ in the Spring and Autumn period,
and became Tángyì in Hàn.
Flooding the northern road was to cut off Wèi’s soldiers from spying on Jiànyè.
The Lord of Wú was old,
and many good generals had died;
this was merely a defensive measure for self-preservation.
“Tú”
should be
“Tú”;
read as Chú.
7. In the twelfth month,
on the day of Jiǎchén,
Dōnghǎi Dìngwáng Lín died.
According to the rules for posthumous names: “Pure conduct without fault” is Dìng;
“Bringing peace to the people and following ancient laws” is Dìng.
8 General Who Attacks the South, Wáng Chǎng, submitted a memorial, saying:
"Sūn Quán has banished his loyal ministers;
'Loyal ministers'
refers to Zhū Jù and others.
Chǎng
is pronounced with the initials 'ch' and 'l' in different readings.
We can seize this opportunity to attack Wú."
The imperial court followed his advice,
and dispatched Zhōu Tài of Nányáng, the Administrator of Xīnchéng, to attack Wū and Zǐguī.
Zhōu
is the surname;
Tài
is the given name.
The Jìn dynasty had a Zhōu Chuò.
The Fēngsú Tōng says: Their ancestors took their fief at Zhōu,
and so adopted it as their clan name.
The Inspector of Jīngzhōu for Wèi was originally stationed at Wǎn alongside the General Who Attacks the South's headquarters;
by this time, he had already moved his troops to Xīnyě.
Wáng Chǎng constructed a bridge using bamboo cables,
crossed the water, and attacked them.
The great general of Wú, Shī Jì,
fled into Jiānglíng during the night.
Jì
was the son of Zhū Rán.
Rán was originally of the Shī clan;
Zhū Zhì adopted him as a son,
and the Wèi people referred to him by his original surname.
Wáng Chǎng first sent five armies to return along the main road,
allowing the Wú to see them and rejoice.
He also paraded the captured armor, horses, and heads around the city to provoke them,
and set up an ambush to await them.
Shī Jì indeed came in pursuit.
Wáng Chǎng engaged him in battle,
utterly defeating him,
and beheading his generals Zhōnglí Mào and Xǔ Mín.
9 Jiāng Wéi of Hàn again raided Xīpíng,
but failed.
1 In spring,
the first month,
Wáng Jī and Zhōu Tài attacked the Wú forces,
defeating them all,
and thousands surrendered.
2 In the second
month,
Sīmǎ Fú, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, was made Sīkōng.
3 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the day Jiǎshēn,
Wáng Chǎng was appointed Grand General Who Attacks the South.
This was a promotion for defeating the Wú forces.
4 On the day Rénchén,
a general amnesty was granted.
5 Grand Commandant Wáng Líng heard that the Wú people had blocked the Túshuǐ river,
which was the Dángyì and Tútáng he had previously constructed.
Yáng Zhènghéng said: Tú
is pronounced "Chú."
Based on the current Chúhé river,
it flows from Chúzhōu to Zhēnzhōu.
Sè
is pronounced 'sì' and 'zé'.
He sternly arrayed his armies
and submitted a memorial requesting to attack the rebels;
the imperial edict replied, refusing his request.
Wáng Líng sent General Yáng Hóng to inform Huáng Huá, the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu, of the matter concerning the deposition and enthronement.
Huáng Huá and Yáng Hóng jointly signed a report to Sīmǎ Yì.
Sīmǎ Yì led his central army by waterway to attack Wáng Líng.
He first issued an amnesty pardoning Wáng Líng's crimes,
and also wrote a letter to admonish Wáng Líng,
after which his main army unexpectedly arrived at Bǎichǐ.
The commentary to the Shuǐ Jīng says: The Shāshuǐ river flows southeast past Chénxiàn,
then southeast into the Yǐng,
where it is called Jiāokǒu.
By the water there is a great weir,
which is the ancient Bǎichǐ Weir;
