an edict appointed Sīmǎ Zhāo as Dàjiāngjūn and Lù Shàngshū Shì.
From then on, Huì often showed signs of self-importance.
Gǔ warned him, saying:
"Your ambition surpasses your capacity,
and achieving great deeds is difficult. How can you not be cautious?"
This laid the groundwork for Zhōng Huì's later rebellion.
Sūn Jùn of Wú, hearing that Zhūgě Dàn had occupied Shòuchūn,
thereupon withdrew his troops.
He appointed Wén Qīn as Dūhù, Zhèn Běi Dàjiāngjūn, and Yōuzhōu Mù.
The Hàn established Dūhù in the Western Regions,
where they were called Dūhù Jiāngjūn, but this was never considered a general's title.
It was not until Guāngwǔ that the office of Dūhù Jiāngjūn existed.
During the Three Kingdoms, its rank was equivalent to a Duke;
under the Jìn system, it was below Fǔjūn and above Zhènjūn.
Wú established Zǔo Yòu Dūhù,
but these were not considered general's titles either.
Now, appointing Qīn as Dūhù
was probably even above the Zǔo Yòu Dūhù.
In the third month, Empress Biàn Shì was installed,
and a general amnesty was declared.
The Empress
was the great-granddaughter of Bǐng, the younger brother of Empress Wǔxuān.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
Wú generals Sūn Yí, Zhāng Yí, and Lín Xún conspired to assassinate Sūn Jùn,
but failed,
and dozens of people died.
Quán Gōngzhǔ slandered Zhū Gōngzhǔ to Jùn,
saying, "She conspired with Yí."
Jùn then killed Zhū Gōngzhǔ.
Zhū Gōngzhǔ
was the daughter of Wú Lord Quán,
who was married to Zhū Jù.
Jùn ordered Wèiwèi Féng Cháo to fortify Guǎnglíng.
The Wèi's Guǎnglíng Commandery seat was at Huáinán;
the old city of Hàn's Guǎnglíng had been abandoned and not administered.
No one in the court dared to speak,
only Téng Yìn advised against it.
Jùn did not listen,
and the project ultimately failed.
Jiāng Wéi of Hàn again proposed to launch an army.
Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn Zhāng Yì strongly argued against it,
believing: "The state is small and the people are weary; it is not advisable to engage in excessive warfare."
Wéi did not listen,
and led Chēqíjīangjūn Xiàhóu Bà and Yì to advance together.
In the eighth month,
Wéi led tens of thousands of men to Fúhǎn.
Fúhǎn County
belonged to Jīnchéng Commandery in the Former Hàn,
to Lǒngxī Commandery in the Later Hàn,
and was abolished by Wèi.
Fú
is pronounced fū.
Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn Chén Tài ordered Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Jīng to advance and garrison Dídào,
waiting for Tài's army to arrive, and only then, with forces combined, to advance.
Tài's army was at Chéncāng.
The armies under Jīng's command fought the Hàn people at Gùguān and suffered a disadvantage.
Gùguān
refers to the old border pass from the Hàn era,
west of the Táo River.
Tài, believing that Jīng would not firmly hold Dídào
and that there would certainly be other complications,
led his various armies to reinforce him.
Jīng had already fought Wéi west of Táo,
suffering a great defeat.
He returned with over ten thousand men to secure Dídào City,
while the rest fled and scattered.
Tens of thousands died.
Zhāng Yì pleaded with Wéi, saying:
"We can stop now.
It is not advisable to advance further,
lest we ruin this great achievement
and 'draw legs on a snake'."
The Zhànguó Cè says: "Zhāo Yáng, on behalf of Chǔ, attacked Wèi,
destroying their army and killing their general. He then moved his forces to attack Qí.
Chén Zhěn, acting as an envoy for the King of Qí,
met Zhāo Yáng and said: 'In Chǔ, there was a sacrificer who gave a cup of wine to his retainers.
The retainers said to each other:
"It's not enough for several people to drink,
but it's too much for one person.
Let's each draw a snake on the ground,
and whoever finishes first will drink the wine."
One person finished first,
took the wine and drank it.
He then held the cup with his left hand,
and with his right hand drew a snake, saying:
"I can draw its legs."
Before he finished drawing the legs,
another person's snake was completed later.
He snatched the cup, saying:
"Snakes naturally have no legs!
How can you draw legs for it!"
And then drank the wine.
Now, your lord has already won against Wèi,
but you again move your forces
to attack Qí.
This is like 'drawing legs on a snake'."
Zhāo Yáng understood,
and withdrew his army.
[Wéi] then advanced and besieged Dídào.
On the Xīnwèi day,
an edict appointed Dèng Ái (鄧艾), the Commander of Chángshuǐ (長水), as Acting General Who Guards the West (Ānxī Jiāngjūn),
to join forces with Chén Tài (陳泰) to resist Wéi (維).
The Jìnzhì (晉志) states: The four 'An' (安) generals emerged in the early Wèi (魏) dynasty.
They were below the four 'Zhen' (鎮) generals.
On the Wùchén day,
Tàiwèi Fú (太尉孚) was again appointed as the successor.
Tài (泰) advanced his army to Lǒngxī (隴西).
All the generals said:
"Wáng Jīng (王經) has just been defeated,
the enemy forces are greatly invigorated,
and for a general with a rabble of troops
to follow on the heels of a defeated army,
against the momentum of a victorious enemy,
it will most certainly be impossible.
As the ancients said: 'If a viper bites one's hand,
a brave man severs his wrist.'
The Hánshū Tián Róng Zhuàn (漢書田榮傳) states: 'If a viper bites the hand, cut off the hand;
if it bites the foot, cut off the foot.'
Yìng Shào (應劭) said: 'Fù (蝮),
also known as huǐ (虺),
if it bites a person's hand or foot,
then cut away the flesh;
otherwise, death will ensue.'
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: 'The Éryǎ (爾雅) and Shuōwén (說文) both consider fù (蝮) and huǐ (虺) to be the same.
It is three cùn (寸) wide,
with a head as large as a thumb.
However, Guō Pú (郭璞) says they are different kinds of snakes.
The fùshé (蝮蛇) has a slender neck, a large head, and a burnt tail,
its color resembles ribbon patterns,
with hair-like fur between the patterns,
like a mane.
It has a needle on its nose.
Large ones are seven or eight chǐ (尺) long.
It is also called fǎnbí (反鼻),
and is not of the huǐ (虺) kind.'
Now, judging by common names,
Guō's (郭) statement is correct.
Huǐ (虺) are earth-colored,
and found everywhere.
Fùshé (蝮蛇) only appear in the south.
Fù (蝮),
pronounced fāng lìu.
Shì (螫),
pronounced shì yì.
Wàn (腕),
pronounced wū guàn.
Lù Diàn Bīyǎ (陸佃埤雅) says: 'When a fùshé (蝮蛇) is angry,
its venom is in its head and tail.
If it bites a hand, the hand is lost;
if it bites a foot, the foot is lost.
It is the most venomous and fierce of snakes.'
'There are places that should not be held.'
This means that a small loss can preserve a greater whole.
It is better to rely on natural barriers for self-preservation,
observe their weaknesses and await their exhaustion,
and then advance to rescue.
This is the wisest course of action."
Tài (泰) said:
"Jiāng Wéi (姜維) with his light troops has penetrated deep,
precisely desiring to contend with us on the open plains,
seeking the advantage of a decisive battle.
Wáng Jīng (王經) should have built high walls and deep fortresses,
to blunt their sharp edge.
Now, by engaging in battle,
he has allowed the bandits to succeed in their plan.
Since Jīng (經) has been defeated and fled,
if Wéi (維), with the momentum of a victorious battle,
advances his army eastward,
and occupies the stores of grain at Lìyáng (櫟陽)—
Lìyáng Xiàn (櫟陽縣) belonged to Zuǒ Fēngyì (左馮翊) in the Former Hàn (漢);
it was abolished in the Later Hàn (漢) and Wèi (魏).
I say Lìyáng (櫟陽) is northeast of Cháng'ān (長安).
Wéi's (維) troops are currently at Dí Dào (狄道).
How could they easily occupy Lìyáng (櫟陽) to the east?
Tài (泰) must have meant Lüèyáng (略陽).
Lì (櫟) is pronounced 'yào' (藥).
'Yào' (藥) and 'lüè' (略) sound similar,
and thus a mispronunciation led to a miswritten character.
—and recruits the Qiāng (羌) and Hú (胡),
he will contend for Guānzhōng (關中) and Lǒngyòu (隴右) to the east,
sending proclamations to the four commanderies.
The four commanderies
refer to Lǒngxī (隴西), Nán'ān (南安), Tiānshuǐ (天水), and Lüèyáng (略陽).
Lüèyáng (略陽) was known as Guǎngwèi Jùn (廣魏郡) at the time,
and was renamed Lüèyáng (略陽) in the Jìn (晉) dynasty.
—and yet, if with his victorious troops,
he assaults a formidable city,
the sharp-edged soldiers
will exert their strength and risk their lives.
The dynamics of offense and defense are different,
and the positions of guest and host are not the same.
The art of war says: 'Constructing great wheeled siege engines and mantlets
takes three months to complete,
and raising earthworks to assault a city takes three months to finish.'
These are the words of Sūnzǐ (孫子).
Sūnzǐ's (孫子) view
is that attacking a city should be a last resort.
Wèi Wǔ's (魏武) commentary says: 'Xiū (脩) means to repair or prepare.
Lǔ (櫓) is a large shield.
Fénwēn (轒轀) refers to a fénchuáng (轒牀),
a four-wheeled bed-like vehicle
pushed from within to the base of the city wall.'
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: 'A siege weapon,
a four-wheeled cart,
with a rope frame on top,
covered with raw ox-hide.
It can hide ten men underneath.
It is pushed across the moat,
directly to the base of the city wall,
and can be used for assault and digging.
It cannot be damaged by metal, fire, wood, or stone,
and is called a fénwēnchē (轒轀車).'
The commentary also says: 'Jùyīn (距堙) means to raise earth gradually higher and forward to approach the city.'
Dù Yòu (杜佑) said: 'An earth mound,
which is what Sūnzǐ (孫子) called jùzhēn (距闉).'
Yìng Shào (應劭) said: 'Fénwēn (轒轀) is a Xiōngnú (匈奴) cart,'
which is incorrect.
'It is simply a siege cart.'
Shī Gǔ (師古) said: 'Fén (轒) is pronounced fú yún.
Wēn (轀) is pronounced yú yún.'
Now Wéi (維) is an isolated army far from home,
with no continuing grain supply.
This is the time for us to advance swiftly and defeat the bandits.
As the saying goes, 'A swift clap of thunder leaves no time to cover the ears.'
These are the words of Wénzǐ (文子),
and Huáinánzǐ (淮南子) also has this saying.
The Táo Shuǐ (洮水) flows on their outer flank,
and Wéi (維) and his men are within it.
Now, by occupying the high ground and advantageous position,
overlooking their necks and collars,
they will surely flee without a fight.
Bandits must not be allowed to escape,
and a siege must not be prolonged.
Why do you all speak in such a way?"
Thereupon, he advanced his army and crossed Gāochénglǐng (高城嶺).
The Shuǐjīngzhù (水經註) says: 'In Shǒuyáng Xiàn (首陽縣) of Lǒngxī (隴西) there is Gāochénglǐng (高城嶺),
and on the ridge there is a city called Wèiyuán Chéng (渭源城).'
That night, they reached the high mountains southeast of Dí Dào (狄道),
raised many signal fires,
and beat drums and blew horns.
The officers and soldiers inside Dí Dào (狄道) city, seeing the rescue arrive,
were all enraged and leapt up.
Wéi (維) had not expected the rescue troops to arrive so suddenly.
He quickly came down the mountain to attack them.
Tài (泰) engaged in battle with him,
and Wéi (維) retreated.
Tài (泰) led his troops and spread rumors that he intended to cut off their return route.
Wéi (維) was frightened.
In the ninth month,
on the Jiǎchén day,
Wéi (維) fled,
and the officers and soldiers in the city were then able to come out.
Wáng Jīng (王經) sighed, saying:
"The grain would not have lasted ten days.
If the rescue troops had not arrived swiftly,
the entire city would have been slaughtered and torn apart,
and a whole province would have been lost!"
Lǒngxī (隴西), Lüèyáng (略陽), Tiānshuǐ (天水), Nán'ān (南安) were Qínzhōu (秦州).
Sàng (喪),
pronounced sī làng.
He sent back the previously dispatched troops,
and selected other troops to guard.
Chā (差),
means to select.
The officers and soldiers formerly under Wáng Jīng (王經) were sent back,
and other troops were selected to guard Dí Dào (狄道).
Láo (勞),
pronounced lì dào.
Chā (差),
pronounced chū jiā.
He returned and garrisoned at Shàngguī (上邽).
Whenever there was trouble in one region,
Tài (泰) would often use false rumors to stir up the entire land.
Therefore, he rarely submitted detailed reports,
and his urgent dispatches never traveled more than six hundred lǐ (里).
Dí Dào (狄道) is over two thousand two hundred lǐ (里) east of Luòyáng (洛陽).
And the urgent dispatches were no more than six hundred lǐ (里).
This means they were transmitted to nearby commanderies and counties,
and then sent to Luòyáng (洛陽) via normal postal services.
"Chén (陳), the General Who Conquers the West (Zhēngxī), is profoundly brave and decisive,
bearing the heavy responsibility of a regional commander.
He rescued a city on the verge of falling,
yet did not request additional troops,
and also rarely submitted detailed reports.
He will surely be able to deal with the bandits.
Should not a Grand Commander (Dūdū Dàjiāng) be like this!"
Jiāng Wéi (姜維) retreated and stationed at Zhōngtí (鍾提).
Zhōngtí (鍾提) must be in Qiāngzhōng (羌中),
which is in the territory of Shǔ's (蜀) Liángzhōu (涼州).
9 At first,
Wú Dàdì did not establish an imperial ancestral temple,
because Wǔliè had once been the Administrator of Chángshā,
so a temple was erected for him in Línxiāng.
Wú Dàdì posthumously named his father, Jiān, Wǔliè Huángdì.
The commandery seat of Chángshā was Línxiāng County.
In winter,
the tenth
month,
an imperial ancestral temple was finally constructed in Jiànyè,
and Dàdì was honored as Tàizǔ.
The Kǎo Yì states: The Wú Lì says:
"In the first month of Tàipíng元年 (first year),
the temple of Tàizǔ was established."
Shěn Yuè's Sòng Shū says:
"When Sūn Liàng ascended the throne,
in the first month of the following year,
Quán's temple was established."
We now follow the Wú Zhì.

Under Gāo Guì Xiāng Gōng
Gānlù 元年 (first year) (Bǐngzǐ, 256) In the sixth month of this year,
the era name was changed.
1 In spring,
the first month,
Jiāng Wéi of Hàn was promoted to Grand General.
2 In the second month,
on the day Bǐngchén,
the Emperor hosted a banquet for his officials in the East Hall of Tàijí,
and discussed with the various scholars the relative merits of Xià Shàokāng and Hàn Gāozǔ,
considering Shàokāng superior.
The Emperor said that Shàokāng was born after the kingdom's destruction,
reduced to a servant of a vassal state,
yet was able to spread his virtue and initiate his plans,
eventually destroying Guò and Gē,
restoring Yǔ's achievements,
sacrificing to Xià and matching Heaven,
not losing his ancient heritage.
Without supreme virtue and immense benevolence,
how could he have accomplished such merit!
Hàn Zǔ, taking advantage of a disintegrating situation,
wielded temporary power,
relying solely on his intellect and strength to achieve his endeavors,
but his actions and conduct often violated sacred precepts.
As a son, he frequently endangered his parents;
as a ruler, he imprisoned virtuous ministers;
as a father, he could not protect his son.
After his death,
the altars of soil and grain nearly collapsed.
If he had been in Shàokāng's position in a different era,
he might not have been able to restore Dà Yǔ's achievements.
Alas!
The Emperor certainly had a high regard for Shàokāng,
yet could not annihilate Jiāo and Yì and died at the hands of others,
because he could not spread his virtue and initiate his plans.
I observe that the Emperor's discussion of the merits of these two rulers
was merely a scholar's talk,
unable to match the powerful and incisive rhetoric of Shí Lè.
Xià,
pronounced Hùyǎ (hùyǎ) in reverse.
Shào,
pronounced Shīzhào (shīzhào) in reverse.
3 In summer,
the fourth month,
Grand General Zhāo was bestowed with the ceremonial robes of a gǔnmiǎn,
and a pair of red slippers.
This was a gradual step towards the Nǐn Xī (Nine Bestowals).
4 On the day Bǐngchén,
the Emperor visited the Imperial Academy,
and discussed the Shū, Yì, and Lǐ with the various scholars.
None of the scholars could surpass him.
At that time, the Emperor debated the Yì with Academician Chúnyú Jùn,
the Shū with Yǔ Jùn,
and the Lǐ Jì with Mǎ Zhào.
Examining their difficult questions and answers,
it was nothing more than probing the meanings of the classics and the differences between Wáng and Zhèng,
not the learning suitable for a ruler.
Furthermore, when they wrote essays,
he showed them special courtesy,
calling Xiù "Elder of the Ruist Forest" and Shěn "Master of Literary Records."
The Emperor was impatient;
when he summoned someone, he wanted them to come quickly.
As Wàng Zhí was serving outside the capital,
he was specially provided with a zhuīfēngchē (chaser carriage) and five hǔbēn (tiger guards).
Wàng was the Central Protector of the Army,
but his post was outside the capital.
Fù Zǐ says: The zhuīfēngchē
had an all-covering canopy.
When in haste, one would ride it,
with five hǔbēn carrying it.
The Jìn Zhì says: The zhuīfēngchē removed the small flat canopy
and added an all-covering canopy,
like a yáochē (light carriage),
drawn by two horses.
The name zhuīfēng
derived from its speed.
Used between military formations,
it was a chuánchéng (relay carriage).
Bēn,
pronounced bēn.
They would gallop to arrive.
Xiù
was the son of Qián.
Péi Qián served Wǔ Dì
and became renowned for defending Dàijùn.
5 In the sixth month,
on the day Bǐngwǔ,
the era name was changed.
This was presumably because sweet dew (gānlù) had fallen.
6 Jiāng Wéi was at Zhōngtí.
Many commentators believed that Wéi's strength was exhausted
and he could not launch another expedition.
General of the Pacified West, Dèng Ài, said:

see the previous year in the preceding卷.

Now, in terms of strategy:
they have the advantage of victory,

Their superiors and subordinates are accustomed to each other,

Xī (犀),

Our weaponry has not been restored;

I (meaning our side) am (using) land forces,

in the seventh month,

In the ninth month,
Minister over the Masses Gāo Róu (高柔) was made Grand Commandant.
Wén Qīn (文欽) persuaded the Wú (吳) people of the advantages of attacking Wèi (魏).
Sūn Jùn (孫峻) sent Qīn (欽), along with General of Cavalry Lǚ Jù (呂據),
General of Chariots Liú Zuǎn (劉纂), General Who Guards the South Zhū Yì (朱異), and Front General Táng Zī (唐咨), to enter the Huái (淮) and Sì (泗) rivers from Jiāngdū (江都).
Jiāngdū Xiàn (江都縣) belonged to Guǎnglíng Jùn (廣陵郡).
This means entering the Huái (淮) from Hángōu (邗溝),
and then entering the Sì (泗) from the Huái (淮).
Wèi's (魏) Qīng Zhōu (青州) administered Qí (齊), Jìnán (濟南), Lè'ān (樂安), Chéngyáng (城陽), and Dōnglái (東萊).
Xú Zhōu (徐州) administered Xiàpī (下邳), Péngchéng (彭城), Dōnghǎi (東海), Lángyá (琅邪), Dōngguǎn (東莞), Dōng'ān (東安), Guǎnglíng (廣陵), and Línhuái (臨淮).
The Jìn Zhì (晉志) states: The Zhōu Lǐ (周禮) says: "Due east is Qīng Zhōu (青州),"
probably taking the idea that scholars reside in Shàoyáng (少陽),
and its color is blue (青).
Xú Zhōu (徐州) takes the meaning of relaxation and ease.
Or it is said
it was named after Xú Qiū (徐丘).
Jùn (峻) encountered a sudden illness.
He entrusted his affairs to his paternal cousin's younger brother, Partial General Lín (綝).
On the day Dīnghài (丁亥),
Jùn (峻) died.
The Wú (吳) people appointed Lín (綝) as Imperial Household Grandee, General of the Martial Guard, and Supervisor of All Military Affairs, inside and outside the capital,
and recalled Lǚ Jù (呂據) and others.
On the day Jǐchǒu (己丑),
Wú's (吳) Grand Marshal Lǚ Dài (呂岱) died,
aged ninety-six.
Initially,
Dài (岱) was close to Xú Yuán (徐原) of Wú Jùn (吳郡),
who was generous and ambitious.
Dài (岱) knew he could achieve greatness,
and bestowed upon him a headcloth and a single robe.
The Shì Míng (釋名) states: Jīn (巾) [headcloth]
means "careful" (謹).
Upon reaching twenty, a man comes of age:
scholars wear a cap (冠), commoners wear a headcloth (巾),
meaning one should be careful and cultivate oneself in the four teachings.
Duō (褠) [single robe]
is a single garment.
Since the Hàn (漢) and Wèi (魏) dynasties,
it has been used by scholars and commoners as ceremonial attire.
Duō (褠)
is pronounced gǔ hóu.
Later, Dài (岱) recommended and promoted him,
and he reached the position of Palace Censor.
Yuán (原) was loyal and robust by nature,
and fond of speaking plainly.
Whenever Dài (岱) made mistakes,
Yuán (原) would immediately remonstrate
and also publicly discuss them.
He publicly discussed his successes and failures among the multitude.
Dài (岱) sighed and said,
"This is why I value Déyuān (德淵)!"
Xú Yuán's (徐原) courtesy name was Déyuān (德淵).
Dài (岱) wept for him with great sorrow,
saying,
"Xú Déyuān (徐德淵)
was Lǚ Dài's (呂岱) beneficial friend.
The Lúnyǔ (論語) states: Confucius said, 'There are three kinds of beneficial friends: a straight friend,
a sincere friend,
and a widely informed friend.'
The Lúnyǔ (論語) states: 'Unfortunately, he died young.'
Those who discuss it praise him.
Lǚ Jù (呂據) heard that Sūn Lín (孫綝) had replaced Sūn Jùn (孫峻) in assisting the government
and was furious.
He and the various chief generals jointly memorialized, recommending Téng Yìn (滕胤) as Chancellor.
Lín (綝) instead appointed Yìn (胤) as Grand Marshal,
to replace Lǚ Dài (呂岱) and be stationed at Wǔchāng (武昌).
Jù (據) led his troops back
and sent someone to inform Yìn (胤),
intending to depose Lín (綝) together.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
Lín (綝)
sent his paternal cousin, Xiàn (憲), to lead troops to intercept Jù (據) at Jiāngdū (江都).
He sent imperial envoys to order Wén Qīn (文欽), Liú Zuǎn (劉纂), Táng Zī (唐咨), and others to attack and seize Jù (據).
He also sent Imperial Household Grandee and Left General Huá Róng (華融) and Palace Writer Dīng Yàn (丁晏).
Under the Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉) systems,
there was no Palace Writer (中書丞);
this was an office established by Wú (吳).
Huá (華)
is pronounced hù huà.
He told them they should quickly go to Wǔchāng (武昌);
otherwise, there would be punishment.
Meanwhile, he detained Róng (融) and Yàn (晏) to command troops to protect himself.
He summoned Army Commandant Yáng Chóng (楊崇) and General Sūn Zī (孫咨).
Yáng Chóng (楊崇)
was probably an army commandant under Yìn (胤).
He forced Róng (融) and others to
write a letter refuting Lín (綝).
The character yǒu (有) is the opposite of wú (無).
Here, its meaning is not clear in the context.
Since the Tōngjiàn (通鑑) follows the old text of the Sānguó Zhì (三國志),
I do not wish to lightly alter it now.
Nán (難)
is pronounced nǎi dàn.
They submitted a memorial stating that Yìn (胤) was rebelling.
He promised General Liú Chéng (劉丞) a noble title
and ordered him to lead cavalry to attack and besiege Yìn (胤).
Yìn (胤) also coerced Róng (融) and others to falsely issue an edict to mobilize troops.
Róng (融) and others refused
and were all killed.
Someone advised Yìn (胤) to lead his troops to Cānglóng Mén (蒼龍門).
Cānglóng Mén (蒼龍門)
was the eastern gate of Wú's (吳) Jiànyè (建業) palace.
He must abandon Lín (綝) and side with the public.
Wěi (委)
means to abandon.
Yìn (胤) relied on his appointment with Jù (據)
and also found it difficult to raise troops against the palace.
So he gave orders to his subordinate troops.
Yuē (約)
means to control and command.
Thus, they all fought to the death for Yìn (胤),
and none dispersed.
Yìn's (胤) expression did not change,
and he talked and laughed as usual.
At that time, there was a great wind.
By dawn,
Jù (據) had not arrived.
Lín's (綝) forces had gathered in great numbers,
and so they killed Yìn (胤) and dozens of his officers and soldiers,
and exterminated Yìn's (胤) three clans.
On the day Jǐyǒu (己酉),
a general amnesty was proclaimed,
and the reign era was changed to Tàipíng (太平).
Someone advised Lǚ Jù (呂據) to defect to Wèi (魏),
but Jù (據) said,
"I am ashamed to be a traitor."
Then he committed suicide.
Jù's (據) father, Fàn (範),
assisted Sūn Cè (孫策) in founding Wú (吳).
Therefore, he was ashamed to be a traitor,
and committed suicide to demonstrate his integrity.
In the 11th month, Sīkōng Zhèng Chōng was appointed Sītú,
and Zuǒ Púshè Lú Yù was appointed Sīkōng.
The Jìn Zhì states: The Shàngshū Púshè
was originally a single post in the Hàn dynasty.
In the 4th year of Jiàn'ān during Emperor Xiàn of Hàn's reign,
Róng Hé, the Zhí Jīn Wú, was appointed Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè,
and the division of the Púshè into left and right positions began from this point.
Through the Wèi to the Jìn dynasties,
and down to the Jiāngzuǒ period,
the abolishment and establishment [of the posts] were inconsistent.
When two were established, they were called Zuǒ Yòu Púshè;
sometimes only one was established,
simply called Shàngshū Púshè.
If the decree was lacking, the left would be the head of the department.
If both left and right were lacking,
then a Shàngshū Púshè would be appointed to manage the affairs of the department.
Yù,
pronounced Yú Liù.
The imperial edict did not permit it.
Wáng Xiáng's nature was utterly filial.
His stepmother, Lady Zhū, treated him atrociously,
yet Xiáng became even more respectful and diligent.
Lady Zhū's son, Lǎn,
was several years old.
Whenever he saw Xiáng being beaten and flogged,
Chǔ refers to a thorn;
Tà refers to a beating.
Bèi is pronounced Pí Yì.
and his mother unreasonably forced Xiáng to work,
Lǎn would always go along with Xiáng.
When he grew up
and married,
his mother cruelly oppressed Xiáng's wife.
Lǎn's wife also quickly joined her,
which troubled his mother,
and she somewhat ceased her actions.
Xiáng gradually gained a good reputation,
but his mother deeply resented him,
and secretly tried to poison Xiáng.
Lǎn learned of this,
immediately stood up and took the wine.
Xiáng struggled with him and would not give it to him.
His mother quickly snatched it back.
In the Hàn Shū, Qí Dàohuì Wáng Biography: "He snatched back Emperor Xiàohuì's wine cup."
Shī Gǔ says: Fǎn
is pronounced Fān.
When his mother offered Xiáng food,
Lǎn would always taste it first.
His mother feared that Lǎn would die from it,
and so she stopped.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, he encountered chaos,
and Xiáng lived in seclusion for over thirty years,
not responding to invitations from provinces and commanderies.
When his mother died,
he was so grief-stricken and emaciated
that he could only rise with the aid of a staff.
Lǚ Qián, the Cìshǐ of Xúzhōu, summoned him as Biejà,
entrusting him with provincial affairs.
The provincial borders became peaceful,
and good governance was widely implemented.
People at the time sang:
"The peace of Hǎiyí,
truly relies on Wáng Xiáng;
The land of Xúzhōu,
reaches the sea to the east,
and borders the Sì and Yí rivers to the northwest,
hence called Hǎiyí.
The merit of the Biejà!"
In the 12th month,
Sūn Lín of Wú was promoted to Dà Jiàngjūn.
Lín, presuming on his high position, was arrogant
and frequently behaved disrespectfully.
Jùn's cousin, Xiàn, had once participated in executing Zhūgě Kè.
Jùn treated him generously,
and his official post reached Yòu Jiàngjūn and Wúnán Dū,
overseeing the affairs of the Nine Officials.
The Nine Officials are the Nine Ministers.
In the 2nd year of Tàihé during Emperor Míng of Wèi's reign,
the ruler of Wú returned to Jiànyè,
leaving the Shàngshū and Nine Officials in Wǔchāng.
Xiàn was angry,
and conspired with General Wáng Dūn to assassinate Lín.
The plot was leaked,
Lín killed Dūn,
and Xiàn died by taking poison.
In the 1st month, spring,
the 3rd month, Lú Yù, the Dàliáng Chéng Hóu, died.
In the 2nd month, summer,
the 4th month, the ruler of Wú ascended the main hall,
granted a general amnesty,
and began personally attending to state affairs.
Sūn Lín's memorials
were often met with difficult questions.
He also conscripted over three thousand sons of soldiers, aged eighteen and below, but fifteen and above.
Kē means to measure;
to measure their height, size, and stature.
Some say:
"Kē"
should be
"liáo,"
pronounced liáo,
meaning to estimate or measure.
He made them generals,
and they drilled daily in the imperial park.
He said:
"I established this army,
wishing to grow old with them."
He also frequently went out from the Zhongshū department to review old records from the time of the Great Emperor,
and asked his attendants:
"The late emperor often made special decrees –
special decrees refer to orders specially issued by the emperor,
promulgated by handwritten edict.
Shù is pronounced Suǒ Jué.
'Asking about affairs' is similar to 'presenting memorials';
not saying 'presenting' shows a humble attitude.
To 'write 'kě'' means
to 'draw 'kě'.'
He sent a huángmén to the Zhōngcáng to fetch honey.
The Zhōngcáng was the Central Treasury,
in charge of silk, gold, silver, and various goods.
Mì is bee sugar.
Cáng is pronounced Cú Làng;
the same below.
He summoned and questioned the treasury official.
The official kowtowed.
The ruler of Wú said:
"Did the huángmén ask you for honey?"
The official said:
"He asked just now," meaning he had asked for honey a moment ago.
The huángmén did not admit it.
The ruler of Wú ordered a rat dropping to be broken open.
The inside of the dropping was dry,
so he laughed loudly and said to his attendants:
"If the dropping had been in the honey earlier,
both the inside and outside would be wet;
but now the outside is wet and the inside is dry,
this must be the doing of the huángmén."
When interrogated,
he indeed confessed;
none of the attendants were not astonished and terrified.
3 Zhūgě Dàn, General Who Conquers the East, had always been good friends with Xiàhóu Xuán, Dèng Yáng, and others.
When Xuán and the others died,
Xuán's death is recorded in the previous volume, Zhèngyuán 1st year.
Yáng's death is recorded in volume 75, Shàolíng Lìgōng Jiāpíng 1st year.
Yáng,
pronounced Yú Zhāng.
Also pronounced Yú Liàng.
Wáng Líng's death is recorded in volume 75, Jiāpíng 3rd year.
Guànqiū Jiǎn's death is recorded in the previous volume, Zhèngyuán 2nd year.
He then emptied the treasury to distribute gifts and grants,
and selectively pardoned criminals to win popular support.
He also raised several thousand young knights and adventurers in Yángzhōu as his elite personal guards.
Taking advantage of the Wú people's desire to advance towards Xú'è,
Xú'è,
is Xútáng,
east of Dōngguān.
È,
pronounced Wū Gè.
He also requested to build a city in Línchuái to guard against Wú raids.
When Sīmǎ Zhāo first took charge of the government,
his Chief Clerk, Jiǎ Chōng, requested to send aides to comfort and inspect the Four Generals Who Conquer.
Wèi established the General Who Conquers the East stationed in Huáinán to guard against Wú;
the General Who Conquers the South stationed in Xiāng and Miǎn to guard against Wú;
the General Who Conquers the West stationed in Guān and Lǒng to guard against Shǔ;
the General Who Conquers the North stationed in Yōu and Bīng to guard against the Xiānbēi;
all were entrusted with heavy troops.
Since Sīmǎ Zhāo was just taking charge of the state,
Chōng therefore requested to comfort and inspect them to observe their aspirations.
Láo,
pronounced Lì Dào.
Zhāo sent Chōng to Huáinán.
When Chōng met Dàn,
he discussed current affairs,
and then said:
"The worthies in Luòzhong [Luòyáng]
all wish for the abdication of the throne.
What do you think of this?"
Dàn sternly replied:
"Are you not the son of Jiǎ Yùzhōu?
Chōng's father, Kuí,
had previously served as Yùzhōu and died,
hence the designation.
How can one wish to hand over the altars of soil and grain [the state] to others!
If there is trouble in Luòzhong,
I shall die for it."
Chōng remained silent;
upon returning,
he reported to Zhāo, saying:
"Zhūgě Dàn has served twice in Yángzhōu.
Dàn first supervised Yángzhōu.
After the defeat at Dōngguān,
he was reassigned to supervise Yùzhōu.
After Guànqiū Jiǎn's death,
he again supervised Yángzhōu.
If we summon him now,
he will surely not come,
but his rebellion will be swift and the disaster small;
if we do not summon him,
then his rebellion will be delayed and the disaster great.
It is better to summon him."
Zhāo followed his advice.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
an imperial edict appointed Dàn as Sīkōng,
and summoned him to the capital.
Upon receiving the edict, Dàn
became even more afraid,
suspecting Lè Lín, the Inspector of Yángzhōu, of spying on him.
He then killed Lín.
The General Who Conquers the East and the Inspector of Yángzhōu governed Shòuchūn together.
The appointments of Wèi's Four Generals Who Conquer
usually had the Inspector of their respective province as the reserve commander,
hence Dàn suspected Lín of spying on him.
Jiān,
pronounced Gǔ Xiàn.
Wèi's commanderies and counties all established garrison farms (túntián).
All inhabitants of the túntián were government soldiers.
He amassed enough grain for one year's food,
planning to close the gates and defend himself.
He sent his Chief Clerk Wú Gāng with his younger son Jìng to Wú,
Jiāng,
pronounced as written.
Shǎo,
pronounced Shī Zhào.
Jìng,
pronounced Jí Yǐng,
also pronounced Jí Zhèng.
and also requested to send the sons and younger brothers of his yámén officers as hostages.
Yámén,
refers to the sons and younger brothers of various generals.
Zhì,
pronounced Yīn Zhì.
4 The wives of Wú's Téng Yìn and Lǚ Jù
were both sisters of Sūn Yī, the Commander of Xiàkǒu.
Yī,
was the illegitimate son of Sūn Huàn.
Xià,
pronounced Hù Yǎ.
Sūn Chěn sent Zhū Yì, General Who Guards the South, to lead troops from Hǔlín to attack Yī.
When Yì reached Wǔchāng,
Yī led his troops to defect.
On the day Yǐsì,
an imperial edict appointed Yī as General of Chariots and Cavalry, Governor of Jiāozhōu,
ennobled him as Marquis of Wú,
granted him the right to establish a bureaucracy and make appointments,
bestowed upon him the ceremonial status of a Grandee Remonstrant,
and awarded him a ceremonial robe and red slippers,
treating him with great generosity.
Sūn Yī was greatly honored
to attract those with wavering loyalties.
5 Sīmǎ Zhāo escorted the Emperor and Empress Dowager to attack Zhūgě Dàn.
If Zhāo were to go himself,
he feared that someone might seize the two imperial personages to create a rebellion later,
hence he escorted them to attack Dàn.
Wú Gāng arrived in Wú.
The Wú people were overjoyed and sent Generals Quán Yì, Quán Duān, Táng Zī, and Wáng Zuò to lead thirty thousand troops,
together with Wén Qīn, to rescue Dàn;
they appointed Dàn as Left Protector-in-chief,
granted him an imperial credential, Grand Minister of Education, General of Agile Cavalry, Governor of Qīngzhōu,
and ennobled him as Marquis of Shòuchūn.
Yì,
was the son of Cóng;
Duān,
was his cousin.
In the sixth month,
on the day Jiǎzǐ,
the imperial carriage arrived at Xiàng.
Sīmǎ Zhāo supervised the twenty-six myriad troops and advanced to station at Qiūtóu.
In this campaign,
Sīmǎ Zhāo renamed Qiūtóu to Wǔqiū
to commemorate the military achievements.
Wǔqiū,
became Shěnqiū County during the Táng dynasty.
He and Chén Qiān, General Who Guards the East, besieged Shòuchūn.
When Jī first arrived,
the siege had not yet been fully closed.
Wén Qīn, Quán Yì, and others, from the northeast of the city,
taking advantage of the mountains and difficult terrain,
managed to lead their troops and break into the city.
Outside Shòuchūn city, there are no other mountains,
only Bāgōng Shān to the north of the city.
Jī repeatedly requested to advance and attack.
At this time, Wú's Zhū Yì led thirty thousand men and advanced to station at Ānfēng,
as an external force for Wén Qīn.
Ānfēng County,
belonged to Lújiāng Commandery during the Hàn dynasty,
Wèi divided it to belong to Ānfēng Commandery.
Today, Ānfēng County is eighty lǐ south of Shòuchūn.
Jī said to his generals:
"Now the siege works are becoming increasingly solid,
and troops are gathering.
We should just focus on strengthening our defenses and wait for them to attempt a breakthrough,
but instead, we are shifting troops to guard strategic points,
allowing them to act freely.
Even a wise man would not be able to manage the consequences well!"
He then acted according to circumstances,
and submitted a memorial saying:
"Now we are confronting the enemy,
and should be as still as a mountain.
If we move and rely on strategic points,
people's hearts will waver,
which will greatly harm our position.
All our armies are holding deep trenches and high ramparts,
and the hearts of the multitude are settled and cannot be shaken.
This is the essence of military control."
After the memorial was submitted,
permission was granted.
Jī was granted permission to implement his strategy.
At that time, the Emperor was in the army,
so all military dispositions were subject to imperial edicts,
but Sīmǎ Zhāo was actually the one who decided their feasibility.
There were two layers of inner and outer defenses,
and the trenches and ramparts were extremely formidable.
Wén Qīn and others repeatedly sallied out to assault the siege,
but were counterattacked
and driven back.
Sīmǎ Zhāo also sent Shí Bāo, General Who Displays Military Prowess and Supervisor of all Qīngzhōu military affairs,
to supervise Zhōu Tài, Inspector of Yǎuzhōu, and Hú Zhì, Inspector of Xúzhōu, with elite troops to form a mobile force,
to guard against external enemies.
Tài defeated Zhū Yì at Yángyuān.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: The Jué River flows out from the north of Yúlóu County in Lújiāng,
passes east of Ānfēng County,
and then flows north again,
where it meets the Yángquán River on the right.
West of the river is the old city of Yángquán County,
which was the former Yángquán Township.
Emperor Líng of Hàn enfeoffed Huáng Wǎn as a marquisate here.
The Jué River then flows north into the Huái River.
Tài pursued them,
killing and wounding two thousand people.
Autumn,
seventh month.
Wú Grand General Zhū Yì (朱異) led a large army out to garrison Huòlǐ (鑊里).
Later, the Wú King blamed Sūn Lín (孫綝) for keeping to the lake and not going ashore even one step.
Thus, Huòlǐ (鑊里) must have been in the territory of Cháo Xiàn (巢縣).
Yì (異) left his baggage train at Dūlù (都陸).
The commentary to the Shuǐ Jīng (水經註) states: Bóxiāng Xiàn (博鄉縣),
Wáng Mǎng (王莽) renamed it Yánglù (楊陸).
The Xiè Shuǐ (泄水) flows out from there,
passing north over the Sháopí (芍陂),
then northwest into the Huái (淮).
Perhaps Dūlù (都陸) is Yánglù (楊陸)?
According to the Jìn Jì (晉紀),
Dūlù (都陸) was south of Lípū (黎漿).
Zhòng (重),
pronounced like zhí yòng.
The commentary to the Shuǐ Jīng (水經註) states: The canal of Sháopí (芍陂) flows east into the Lípū Shuǐ (黎漿水),
this water flows east past the south of Lípū Tíng (黎漿亭),
then east into the Féishuǐ (肥水).
This is called the mouth of Lípū Shuǐ (黎漿水口).
Tàishān (太山) Administrator Hú Liè (胡烈) led five thousand elite troops to raid Dūlù (都陸),
burning all of Yì's (異) provisions.
Yì (異) led the remaining soldiers to eat kudzu leaves
and fled back to Sūn Lín (孫綝).
Sūn Lín (孫綝) ordered Yì (異) to fight to the death again,
but Yì (異), citing the soldiers' lack of food,
did not obey Lín's (綝) command.
Lín (綝) was enraged.
Ninth month,
jǐsì day,
Lín (綝) beheaded Yì (異) at Huòlǐ (鑊里).
Xīnwèi day,
he led his troops back to Jiànyè (建業).
The siege of Shòuchūn (壽春) was already secure;
even if Zhōu Yú (周瑜), Lǚ Méng (呂蒙), and Lù Xùn (陸遜) were to be reborn,
they could not have relieved it.
If Sūn Lín (孫綝) had been able to lead the forces of Jīng (荊) and Yáng (揚) out of Xiāngyáng (襄陽) towards Wǎn (宛) and Luò (洛),
the troops at Shòuchūn (壽春) city would surely have divided and returned to save themselves.
If Zhūgě Dàn (諸葛誕) and Wén Qīn (文欽) had at this time broken the siege and fought with all their might,
there might still have been a chance.
But to lose soldiers and commoners
and kill a famous general
was why the Wú people all resented him.
This laid the groundwork for the later Wú regime to execute Sūn Lín (孫綝).
Sīmǎ Zhāo (司馬昭) said:
"Yì (異) did not reach Shòuchūn (壽春),
and the Wú people killed him.
This was not his crime;
they wanted to apologize to Shòuchūn (壽春) and strengthen Dàn's (誕) resolve,
making him still hope for rescue.
Now we should solidify the siege,
prepare for their escape,
and mislead them in many ways."
Thereupon, he released double agents,

"Someone asked: In ancient times, those who were able to overcome the strong with the weak,

those in a great position without worries are often arrogant,
while those in a small position with anxieties often contemplate good.
Arrogance leads to chaos,
and contemplating good leads to governance;
this is a constant principle.
Therefore, King Wén (文王) of Zhōu (周) nurtured his people
to gain much from little,
and Gōu Jiàn (句踐) cared for his people
to defeat the strong with the weak.
This was their method.
King Wén (文王) governed Qí (岐),
starting from a hundred square *lǐ* (里),
and gained two-thirds of the world,
which is what is meant by gaining much from little.
Gōu Jiàn (句踐) returned to Yuè (越),
mourned the dead and inquired about the sick,

and trained his people for ten years,
thereby using weak Yuè (越) to defeat strong Wú (吳).
Xiàng (項) was strong and Hàn (漢) was weak;
they fought against each other.
Xiàng Yǔ (項羽) and Hàn (漢) agreed to divide the land at Hónggōu (鴻溝),

Zhāng Liáng (張良) believed that the people's will was already settled,

He said: At the juncture of Shāng (商) and Zhōu (周),

The people were accustomed to what was monopolized;

hence they were devoted to supporting their superiors.
Those firmly established are difficult to dislodge.
At this time,
even Emperor Gāo (高) of Hàn (漢), how could he have taken the world by brandishing a sword and whipping a horse?
After Qín (秦) abolished the enfeoffment of nobles and established commanderies and prefectures,
this refers to abolishing the feudal lords of the various states and establishing thirty-six commanderies,
with a governor (守) for each commandery.
The world crumbled,

Like startled birds and frightened beasts,

Those who acted swiftly gained much,

If the people are weary and exhausted,

If superiors are arrogant and inferiors violent,

The proverb says: 'Repeatedly shooting at random and missing

*Diē* (跌)
means to miss.
If one repeatedly misses the target,

Do not carelessly change your steps,

*Wèi* (為),

in the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Guǎnghàn Commandery,
and was part of Jiāmáng County.
The First Ruler of Shǔ appointed Huò Jùn as Administrator of Zǐtóng,
and there was Jiàngé County.
Fú Qín sent Xú Chéng to invade Shǔ,
attacking the two Jiàn.
He conquered them,
and only then did the name "two Jiàn" emerge.
4. Gāo Róu, the Marquis of Ānguó, died.
5. In winter,
the tenth month,
the Hàn people sent an urgent plea to Wú.
On the day of Jiǎshēn,
the Ruler of Wú sent the Grand General Dīng Fèng to lead various armies towards Shòuchūn.
General Liú Píng joined Shī Jì in Nánjùn
to discuss the direction of military action.
Generals Dīng Fēng and Sūn Yì went to Miǎnzhōng to relieve Hàn.
Miǎnzhōng
was at that time Wèi territory,
so Wú's troops could not reach it.
This merely indicates their intended direction.
Wú's Wū, Zǐguī, and other counties
are all north of the Yangtze River,
bordering Wèi's Xīnchéng.
Marching troops from here
could also lead to Miǎnzhōng,
but it would be like drawing water from the Western River to save fish in a dry rut.
6. An imperial edict stated that since reports of victories from the generals campaigning in Shǔ were arriving one after another,
the Grand General Zhāo was again ordered to advance in rank.
His titles and rewards were as in the previous edict.
Zhāo then accepted the command.
He now accepted the appointments of Chancellor, Duke of Jìn, and the Nine Bestowals.
Zhāo appointed Wèi Shū of Rènchéng as Chancellor's Chief Clerk.
Initially,
Shū was slow-witted in his youth
and not highly regarded by his relatives in the community.
"Xiānglǐ" refers to relatives.
"Shào"
is read as "shī zhào".
Those famous in his time
also did not know him,
and made him guard a water mill.
"Shuǐduī" is next to the water,
with a wheel placed behind the mill.
A horizontal timber passes through the wheel.
At both ends of the horizontal timber,
another piece of wood, about two *chǐ* long,
is crossed and passes through it,
directly at the tail of the millstone.
The water strikes the wood and rotates the wheel.
When the wheel turns, the crossed woods strike the tail wood of the millstone,
causing it to grind by itself
without human effort.
This is called a water mill.
"Duī"
is read as "dū nèi".
"Shū is only fit to be a head of a few hundred households,"
meaning a head of a small district.
"Zhǎng"
is read as "zhī liǎng".
Shū also did not take it to heart,
nor did he engage in ostentatious or risky deeds.
"Jiǎo" means
seeking to make oneself conspicuously clear to the world.
"Lì"
means dangerous conduct.
"You will eventually become a chief minister."
He often helped him with his wants and needs,
and Shū accepted without declining.
At over forty years old,
the commandery nominated him as Supervisor of Accounts
and he was investigated as an "exemplary filial and incorruptible" (xiàolián) candidate.
His clan members, considering Shū to lack academic achievements,
advised him not to accept the position,
as it would be considered noble.
Shū said:
"If I try and do not succeed,
the fault lies with me.
How can I falsely steal the nobility of non-acceptance to glorify myself!"
Thereupon, he self-studied,
mastering one classic in a hundred days.
Consequently, he responded to the examination and ascended to a higher rank,
gradually rising to become Chief Clerk to General of the Rear, Zhōng Yù.
Yù often practiced archery with his staff and subordinates.
"Cānsá" refers to the Chief Clerk and various junior officials.
"Yù"
is read as "yú liù".
Drawing lots for archery
is like casting tallies in *tóuhú*.
"Wéi"
is read as "yú wěi";
the "wéi" below is the same.
With Shū making up the number,
archery was practiced in pairs.
Archery with pairs
is like the ancient archery ritual having "óu" (pairs).
The Rites of Zhōu state: The King shoots three targets with six pairs;
feudal lords shoot two targets with four pairs;
ministers and grand masters shoot one target with three pairs;
and士 (scholars) shoot the *yànhóu* target with three pairs.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn records: Duke Xiāng of Lǔ hosted Fàn Xiànzǐ,
and there were three pairs of archers.
The Duke's servants were insufficient,
so he took from his household retainers.
Dù Yù's commentary says: Two people form a pair.
Shū's shots never missed.
The entire assembly was astonished,
and no one could rival him.
Yù sighed and apologized, saying:
"My inability to fully utilize your talent
is evident in this archery,
and it is surely not the only instance!"
When he became Chancellor's Chief Clerk,
in the trivial matters of the chancellor's office and court,
he never showed partiality.
"Fǔcháo" is synonymous with "fǔtíng".
"Cháo"
is read as "zhí yáo".
"Jiàn"
is read as "xián biàn".
When no one else could make a decision,
Shū slowly devised a plan,
often going beyond the general opinion.
Zhāo deeply valued and esteemed him.
7. On the day of Guǐmǎo,
Empress Biàn was instated.
She was the granddaughter of the General Who Manifests Awe, Bǐng.
8 Dèng Ái 鄧艾 advanced to Yīnpíng 陰平.
He selected his elite troops,
intending to proceed with Zhūgě Xù 諸葛緒 from Jiāngyóu 江油 to Chéngdū 成都.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* 水經註 states: The Fúshuǐ 涪水 emerges from outside the *jiàowài* 徼外 (frontier) of Gāngdī Dào 剛氐道 in the commandery of Guǎnghàn 廣漢.
It flows southeast,
passing north of Mínzhú Xiàn 緜竹縣,
and then southeast, passing north of Jiāngyóu Shù 江油戍.
Dèng Ái 鄧艾 himself from Yīnpíng 陰平, by the Jǐnggǔ 景谷 foot-path, with suspended troops and bound horses, entered Shǔ 蜀,
passing through Jiāngyóu 江油 and Guǎnghàn 廣漢.
Sòng Bái 宋白 said: From Lóngzhōu 龍州, Jiāngyóu Jùn 江油郡, it is three hundred and thirty *lǐ* 里 over the mountains north to Wénzhōu 文州.
Wénzhōu 文州
was the land of Hàn Yīnpíng 漢陰平.
Dèng Ái 鄧艾 traversed seven hundred *lǐ* 里 of uninhabited land from Yīnpíng 陰平 to Jiāngyóu 江油.
This is it.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* 九域志 states: From Lóngzhōu 龍州 north to Wénzhōu 文州 is four hundred and thirty *lǐ* 里.
The *Yuánfēng Jiǔyù Zhì* 元豐九域志 states: Lóngzhōu 龍州 governed Jiāngyóu Xiàn 江油縣,
and it was over two hundred *lǐ* 里 south to Miánzhōu 綿州.
Xù 緒's westward march was not according to the original imperial edict,
so he led his army towards Báishuǐ 白水.
This is Báishuǐ Guān 白水關.
Xián 賢 said: It is now west of Jīnniú Xiàn 金牛縣 in Liángzhōu 梁州,
and one hundred and eighty *lǐ* 里 northeast to the pass city.
Huì 會, wanting to take sole command of the army,
secretly reported that Xù 緒 was timid and did not advance.
He was brought back in a cage cart,
and his army was entirely handed over to Huì 會.
Jiāng Wéi 姜維 set up camps to guard the perilous defenses.
Huì 會 attacked them but could not overcome them.
The supply route was perilous and distant,
and the army ran short of provisions.
He intended to withdraw.
Dèng Ái 鄧艾 submitted a memorial:
"The enemy is already shattered.
It is fitting to press on.
If we go from Yīnpíng 陰平 by a side path through Hàn Déyáng Tíng 漢德陽亭—
Note: In the Former Hàn there was no Déyáng Xiàn 德陽縣.
The Later Hàn Gazetteer states: Guǎnghàn Jùn 廣漢郡 first had Déyáng Xiàn 德陽縣.
It was probably established as a county based on an old Hàn pavilion.
After Shǔ 蜀 divided Guǎnghàn 廣漢 to establish Zǐtóng Jùn 梓潼郡,
Jiàngé Xiàn 劍閣縣 belonged to Zǐtóng 梓潼,
and Déyáng Xiàn 德陽縣 belonged to Guǎnghàn 廣漢.
The *Xù Hàn Zhì* 續漢志 considered that Déyáng Xiàn 德陽縣 had Jiàngé 劍閣.
Now Jiāng Wéi 姜維 is defending Jiàngé 劍閣 against Zhōng Huì 鍾會,
while Dèng Ái 鄧艾 intends to proceed from Déyáng Tíng 德陽亭 to Fú 涪.
Thus, it is clear that at this time it was divided into two counties.
However, Déyáng Tíng 德陽亭 was also not the seat of Déyáng Xiàn 德陽縣 at this time.
It was probably the old site of Déyáng Tíng 德陽亭 from the Former Hàn.
This path is what is called the Yīnpíng 陰平, Jǐnggǔ 景谷 Road.
It exits one hundred *lǐ* 里 west of Jiàngé 劍閣,
and is over three hundred *lǐ* 里 from Chéngdū 成都.
If we send a surprise force to strike their vital center,
catching them off guard,
the defenders of Jiàngé 劍閣 will certainly return to Fú 涪.
Then Huì 會 can advance unobstructed.
If the Jiàngé 劍閣 army does not return,
then the troops responding to Fú 涪 will be few."
Thereupon, he himself traversed over seven hundred *lǐ* 里 of uninhabited land from Yīnpíng 陰平,
cutting mountains to open up a path,
and constructing bridge-towers.
Today, sixty *lǐ* 里 north of Yīnpíng Xiàn 陰平縣 in Lóngqìng Fǔ 隆慶府, there is Mǎgé Shān 馬閣山.
It is steep and rugged,
extremely arduous and dangerous.
When Dèng Ái's 鄧艾 army reached this point,
the path was impassable.
So they suspended their carts and bound their horses,
constructing栈阁 *zhàn gé* (plank roads)
to finally reach Jiāngyóu 江油.
Hence it was named Mǎgé 馬閣.
Also, from Qīngtáng Lǐng 青塘嶺 in Wénzhōu 文州 to Lóngzhōu 龍州 is one hundred and fifty *lǐ* 里.
For those traveling from north to south,
their right shoulder could not easily change its burden,
so it was called Zuǒdàn Lù 左擔路 (Left-Carry Road).
This was also Ái's 艾 path for attacking Shǔ 蜀.
According to Zhōng Huì's 鍾會 biography,
Ái 艾 entered Jiāngyóu 江油 by the Zuǒdàn Dào 左擔道 from Hàn Déyáng Tíng 漢德陽亭.
Thus, Déyáng Tíng 德陽亭 was probably on the path of Mǎgé Shān 馬閣山.
It was extremely arduous and dangerous,
and their food supply was almost exhausted,
on the verge of peril.
Ái 艾 wrapped himself in felt
and rolled down.
The officers and soldiers all clung to trees and climbed cliffs,
advancing in a single file.
The mountain cliffs were dangerous and narrow,
allowing only single-file advance, one after another,
like strung fish.
Jiāngyóu 江油 is now the area of Jiāngyóu Xiàn 江油縣 in Lóngzhōu 龍州.
It is over two hundred *lǐ* 里 south to Miánzhōu 綿州.
Miánzhōu 綿州
was the ancient Fúchéng 涪城.
Zhūgě Zhān 諸葛瞻 led his armies to resist Ái 艾.
Upon reaching Fú 涪,
he stopped and did not advance.
Chén Shòu 陳壽 said: Fú 涪 is three hundred and sixty *lǐ* 里 from Chéngdū 成都.
He was the son of Quán 權.
Huáng Quán 黃權 was employed by Liú Zhāng 劉璋.
The Former Lord (Liú Bèi 劉備) attacked Wú 吳 and was defeated,
and Quán 權 was cut off north of the river,
so he surrendered to Wèi 魏.
He advised not to allow the enemy to enter the open plain.
Zhān 瞻 hesitated and did not accept.
Chóng 崇 spoke to him repeatedly,
to the point of tears,
but Zhān 瞻 could not follow.
Ái 艾 then advanced unimpeded,
defeating Zhān's 瞻前 vanguard.
Zhān 瞻 retreated and settled in Mínzhú 緜竹.
Mínzhú Xiàn 緜竹縣
belonged to Guǎnghàn Jùn 廣漢郡.
Now, Mínzhú Xiàn 綿竹縣 is over one hundred *lǐ* 里 northeast to Miánzhōu 綿州.
"If you surrender,
I will certainly memorialize for you to be appointed King of Lángyá 琅邪."
The Zhūgě 諸葛 clan
was originally from Lángyá 琅邪,
hence this was used to entice him.
Yòu 誘 is pronounced *yǒu*.
He (Zhān 瞻) executed Ái's 艾 envoy
and arrayed his forces to await Ái 艾.
Ái 艾 sent his son Huìtáng Tínghóu Zhōng 惠唐亭侯忠 to lead the right flank,
and Sīmǎ Shī Zuǎn 司馬師纂 and others to lead the left.
Zhōng 忠 and Zuǎn 纂 fought unfavorably
and both withdrew,
saying:
"The enemy cannot yet be attacked!"
Ái 艾 angrily said:
"The line between survival and destruction
depends on this one action.
How can it not be attacked!"
He yelled at Zhōng 忠, Zuǎn 纂, and the others,
intending to execute them.
Zhōng 忠 and Zuǎn 纂 raced back to fight again,
achieving a great victory.
They beheaded Zhān 瞻 and Huáng Chóng 黃崇.
Zhān's 瞻 son, Shàng 尚, sighed, saying:
"Father and son have received great grace from the state.
Not executing Huáng Hào 黃皓 earlier
caused the state to be ruined and the people annihilated.
What is the point of living!"
He spurred his horse and charged into the enemy formation, dying.
Dù Yòu 杜佑 said: Dèyáng Xiàn 德陽縣 in Hánzhōu 漢州,
Dèng Ái 鄧艾 defeated Zhūgě Zhān 諸葛瞻 here,
and a *jīngguān* 京觀 (mound of enemy corpses) was erected.
Bài 敗 is pronounced *bù mài fān*.
The Hàn people did not expect the Wèi army to arrive so suddenly.
They had made no preparations for the defense of the city.
When they heard that Ài had already entered Píngtǔ,
the common people were in a turmoil,
all fleeing to the mountains and marshes,
beyond control.
The Hàn sovereign ordered his officials to convene a meeting.
Some suggested that since Shǔ and Wú
were originally allied states,
it would be advisable to flee to Wú.
Others thought that the seven commanderies of Nánzhōng,
The seven commanderies of Nánzhōng: Yuèxī, Zhūtí, Zāngkē, Yúnnán, Xīnggǔ, Jiànníng, and Yǒngchāng.
were easy to defend on their own,
and it would be advisable to flee to the south.
Guānglù Dàfū Qiáo Zhōu, however, believed:
"Since ancient times,
there has been no emperor who sought refuge in another state.
If we enter the state of Wú,
we would also have to submit as subjects.
Moreover, if governance is not different,
then the larger can swallow the smaller;
this is the natural course of events.
From this perspective,
it is clear that Wèi can annex Wú,
but Wú cannot annex Wèi.
If we are to submit as subjects,
is it better to be subject to a smaller state or a larger one?
What is the difference between the shame of being humiliated twice and being humiliated once?
If we surrender to Wèi now,
it is but one humiliation.
If we flee to Wú and become subjects,
that is one humiliation;
when Wú perishes along with us,
we will again have to submit to Wèi,
which would be a second humiliation.
Therefore, we should make plans early,
then they can be carried out.
Guǒ
means decisive,
or successful.
With disaster and defeat approaching,
the hearts of the officials
cannot be relied upon at all.
I fear that on the day we set out,
unforeseen changes may occur.
How could we even reach the south! "
Meaning that the hearts of the people had already scattered,
and after setting off,
they would disperse midway,
making it impossible to reach Nánzhōng.
"Now Ài is not far.
I fear he may not accept our surrender.
What then?"
Zhōu replied:
"Currently, Dōngwú has not yet submitted.
The circumstances are such that he must accept,
and having accepted, he must treat us with courtesy.
If Your Majesty surrenders to Wèi,
and Wèi does not partition land to enfeoff Your Majesty,
Zhōu requests to personally go to Jīngdū
Jīngdū
refers to Luòyáng,
the capital of Wèi.
Jìn Jǐngwáng's tabooed name was Shī.
The Jìn people avoided it,
and generally referred to Jīngshī as Jīngdū.
Shǔ was still discussing surrender,
but Qiáo Zhōu already used the Jìn people's taboo.
Alas!
He argued righteously. "
Everyone followed Zhōu's proposal.
The Hàn sovereign still wished to go south,
wavering and undecided.
Zhōu submitted a memorial, stating:
"The southern barbarian lands
normally provide nothing.
Meaning their people neither pay taxes for state use
nor provide labor for state undertakings.
Since Chancellor Zhūgě Liàng compelled them with military might,
they only complied when utterly destitute.
Now, if we go south,
we will have to resist enemies externally
and provide for ourselves internally.
Expenses will greatly increase,
with nowhere else to obtain resources.
The various barbarians will be depleted,
and their rebellion is certain! "
The Hàn sovereign then dispatched Shìzhōng Zhāng Shào and others to present the imperial seal and cords in surrender to Ài.
Běidì Wáng Chén angrily said:
"If our resources are exhausted and our strength is depleted,
and disaster and defeat are imminent,
then we should, as father and son, lord and subjects, fight a decisive battle outside the city walls,
and die together for the altars of soil and grain,
to face the former emperor.
How can we surrender! "
The Hàn sovereign did not listen.
On that day,
Chén wept at the temple of Zhāoliè,
first killing his wife and children, and then committing suicide.
Who would have thought that a ruler who renounced the throne would have a son like this!
Zhāng Shào and others met Dèng Ài in Luò.
Luò County belonged to Guǎnghàn Commandery, about eighty *lǐ* southwest of Chéngdū.
He wrote back, praising and accepting the surrender.
The Hàn sovereign dispatched Tàipú Jiǎng Xiǎn with a separate decree to Jiāng Wéi, instructing him to surrender to Zhōng Huì.
He also sent Shàngshū Láng Lǐ Hǔ to deliver the registers of soldiers and common people to Ài.
There were 280,000 households,
940,000 people,
102,000 armored soldiers,
and 40,000 officials.
When Ài arrived north of Chéngdū city,
the Hàn sovereign, accompanied by the crown prince, various kings, and over sixty officials,
arrived at the army gate, their faces bound and carrying a coffin.
Dù Yù said: Miànbù
means hands bound behind the back,
only showing the face.
Chèn
means coffin,
showing readiness to accept death.
Chèn,
pronounced chū jìn.
The Later Lord was forty-eight years old at the time.
Ài invited them in for a meeting;
he restrained his officers and soldiers,
preventing looting,
and comforted and settled the surrendered,
allowing them to resume their former occupations.
He immediately followed Dèng Yǔ's precedent,
and, acting on imperial authority, appointed Hàn Wáng Chán as acting Piàojì Jiāngjūn.
The crown prince was made Fèngchē, and the various kings Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
The Hàn officials were all appointed to Wèi official posts according to their rank,
some even serving as Ài's subordinates.
This was based on Dèng Yǔ's precedent of conferring titles on Kuí Xiāo acting on imperial authority.
Later, Ài was punished for this.
Piào,
pronounced pǐ miào.
Lǒngxī Tàishǒu Qiān Hóng and others took charge of the various commanderies in Shǔ.
Ài heard of Huáng Hào's treachery and wickedness,
arrested and imprisoned him,
intending to kill him.
Hào bribed Ài's attendants,
and thus ultimately escaped death.
Jiāng Wéi and others heard of Zhūgě Zhān's defeat,
but did not know where the Hàn sovereign had gone.
So they led their army east into Bā.
Bā
is Bāzhōng.
Hú Liè and others were dispatched to pursue Wéi.
When Wéi reached Qī,
Qī County belonged to Guǎnghàn Commandery.
Liú Xù said: Fēiwū County of Zǐzhōu was the land of Hàn's Qī County;
the Suí dynasty named the county after Fēiwū Mountain.
Shī Gǔ said: Qī
is pronounced qī,
also qiān sī.
He then ordered his soldiers to all lay down their weapons
and sent his credentials to Hú Liè.
He himself, along with Liáo Huà, Zhāng Yì, Dǒng Jué, and others, proceeded from the eastern route to Zhōng Huì to surrender.
The officers and soldiers were all enraged,
drawing their swords and striking rocks.
Seeing this,
how could the officers and soldiers of Shǔ be willing to submit to others?
It was their ruler who could not utilize them!
The garrisons
were the defending troops of the various garrisons in Hánzhōng established by Wèi Yán.
All their seals, cords, tallies, and parasols were temporarily returned.
The former Hàn emperor obtained Shǔ in the 19th year of Jiàn'ān during Emperor Xiàn's reign.
Wèi Wéndì ascended the throne in the 2nd year of Huángchū.
The state lasted for two generations and forty-three years before perishing.
9 The people of Wú, hearing that Shǔ had fallen,
then withdrew Dīng Fèng's and others' troops.
Wú's Secretary of the Central Secretariat, Huá Hé of Wújùn,
(Wèi had a Director and a Superintendent of the Central Secretariat,
but no Secretary of the Central Secretariat,
so this office was likely established by Wú.)
(Huá
is pronounced like 'hù huà'.)
(Hé
is pronounced like 'hù gé'.)
memorialized: "I have heard that Chéngdū did not hold,
Your servant's Lord was exiled,
the altars of soil and grain were overturned,
the land we relied upon was lost,
and the state that offered tribute was abandoned.
As a blade of grass, I secretly feel uneasy.
Your Majesty is sagely and benevolent,
your grace and favor extend far and wide in comfort.
Upon hearing this news,
you must surely be filled with sorrow and grief.
I cannot bear my feelings of distress and sadness,
and so respectfully submit this memorial to inform you!"
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says: "When the people of Chǔ destroyed Jiāng,
the Earl of Qín lowered his standards,
did not beat the drums when moving out,
and when several grandees remonstrated,
the Duke said:
'A state that was our ally has been destroyed,
how dare I not feel pity?
I fear for myself!'"
Shǔ was Wú's allied state;
with Shǔ's fall,
Wú was in a precarious situation.
Wú's ruler and ministers did not know fear,
so Huá Hé submitted a memorial to warn them.
When Wèi attacked Shǔ,
some people of Wú said to Zhāng Tì of Xiāngyáng:
"Since the Sīmǎ clan gained power,
great difficulties have repeatedly arisen,
the common people are not yet submissive.
Now they exert their strength in a distant campaign,
they will fail before they have time to rest,
how can they succeed?"
Tì replied:
"Not so.
Although Cáo Cāo's achievements covered the central plains,
the people feared his might but did not embrace his virtue.
Pī and Ruì succeeded him,
punishments were severe and labor was heavy,
they rushed east and west,
without a single peaceful year.
Sīmǎ Yì and his sons accumulated great merits,
removing their troublesome strictures and spreading their fairness and benevolence,
acting as their chief strategists and relieving their suffering.
The hearts of the people have returned to them for a long time now.
Thus, despite three rebellions in Huáinán,
their loyal supporters were not disturbed;
(In the first year of Jiāpíng under Emperor Shàolíng Lìgōng,
Wáng Líng rebelled;
in the first year of Zhèngyuán under Emperor Gāoguì Xiānggōng,
Guànqiū Jiǎn rebelled;
in the second year of Gānlù,
Zhūgě Dàn rebelled.)
The four quarters remained unmoved.
They employ the worthy and use the capable,
each exerting their utmost.
Their foundation is solid,
and their cunning plans are established.
Now, in Shǔ, the eunuchs monopolize the court,
the state has no proper governance,
yet they indulge in military affairs and abuse their power,
the people are weary and the soldiers exhausted,
they compete for external gains,
and do not attend to their defenses.
The strength of the two sides is not the same,
and their strategies are also superior.
Taking advantage of the danger to attack,
they will almost certainly succeed.
Alas!
Their success
is our sorrow."
The people of Wú laughed at his words,
but now they were convinced.
10 The people of Wú, considering that the Wǔxī Yi people of Wǔlíng bordered Shǔ,
and fearing their rebellion after Shǔ's fall,
appointed Zhōnglí Mù, Commandant of Cavalry, to govern Wǔlíng Commandery.
