Yù
was Shù’s son.
The matter of Dù Shù is seen in volume 73, during Míngdì Jǐngchū first year.
His wife and grandson were moved to Xīchéng.
Xīchéng county belonged to Wèixīng Commandery.
This was to establish a pretext for Jìn Wǔdì to pardon Ài’s grandson Zhuó.
Zhōng Huì’s elder brother Yù had once secretly told Jìngōng:
"Huì is cunning and unreliable,
he should not be given sole responsibility."
When Huì rebelled,
Yù had already died.
Jìngōng, remembering Zhōng Yáo’s merits and Yù’s virtue,
Zhōng Yáo had the achievement of pacifying Guānzhōng.
maintained their official ranks and titles as before.
Huì’s Gōngcáo Xiàng Xióng collected and buried Huì’s body.
Jìngōng summoned him and reprimanded him, saying:
"Previously, when Wáng Jīng died,
you wept at the eastern market, and I did not question it;
this event is seen in the previous volume, Jǐngyuán first year.
Now you again collected and buried him.
If I were to tolerate this again,
what would become of the royal law?"
Xióng replied:
"In ancient times, the former kings covered bare bones and buried rotting flesh,
their benevolence extended to decaying bones.
The Yuè Lìng states: In the first month of spring,
cover bare bones and bury rotting flesh.
Zhèng Xuán’s commentary says: Dried bones are ‘gé’,
rotten flesh is ‘zì’.
Lù Démíng says: Exposed bones are ‘gé’,
those with flesh are ‘zì’.
‘Gé’,
pronounced like ‘jiāng bǎi fān’.
‘Zì’,
pronounced like ‘cái cì fān’.
Zhōu Wénwáng’s benevolence reached even decaying bones.
Now that the king’s execution has been carried out,
the law has been fully satisfied.
Xióng, moved by righteousness, collected and buried the body;
teaching is also not lacking.
If law is established above,
and teaching is promoted below,
and this is used to instruct the people,
would this not be acceptable?
Why must Xióng be made to abandon the dead and defy the living,
to establish himself in the world?
If your distinguished self makes an enemy of dry bones,
meaning that Huì has already been executed,
and Jìngōng still considers dry bones an enemy,
not allowing them to be buried,
is this the magnanimity of a benevolent and wise person?"
Jìngōng was pleased,
and after a banquet and conversation, dismissed him.
2 In the second month,
on the day Bǐngchén,
the imperial carriage returned to Luòyáng.
3 On the day Gēngshēn,
Empress Míngyuán was buried.
4 Originally,
Liú Shàn had ordered Bādōng Tàishǒu Luó Xiàn of Xiāngyáng to lead two thousand soldiers to guard Yǒng’ān.
Family records: The Luó family were descendants of Zhuānxù,
enfeoffed in the state of Luó,
which is now Fángzhōu.
They were destroyed by Chǔ,
and their descendants took Luó as their surname.
Qiáo Zhōu’s Bā Jì states: In the sixth year of Chūpíng, in the reign of Hàn Xiàndì,
Yìzhōu Sīmǎ Zhào Wěi suggested dividing the counties of Bājùn from Hàn’ān downwards to form Yǒngníng Commandery.
In the sixth year of Jiàn’ān,
Liú Zhāng changed Yǒngníng to Bādōng Commandery,
with its seat in Yúfù county;
in the second year of Zhāngwǔ, in the reign of Shǔ Xiānzhǔ,
Yúfù was renamed Yǒng’ān.
The officials and people were alarmed and disturbed.
Xiàn executed one person who claimed that Chéngdū was in chaos,
and the populace then became stable.
When he received Shàn’s imperial edict,
he led his subordinates to mourn at the imperial pavilion for three days.
Wú heard of Shǔ’s defeat,
raised troops and moved west,
ostensibly for rescue,
but internally intending to attack Xiàn.
Xiàn said:
"Our court has fallen,
and Wú is supposed to be our 'lips and teeth.'
Instead of assisting us in our distress, they betray our alliance for profit;
this is extremely unrighteous.
Moreover, Hàn has already perished,
how long can Wú last?
How can I become a captive of Wú?"
He fortified the city and repaired armor,
announced an oath to his officers and soldiers,
and encouraged them with integrity and righteousness,
and none were not filled with indignation.
The Wú people heard of Zhōng and Dèng’s victory,
and that a hundred cities had no master,
and harbored ambitions of incorporating Shǔ.
But Bādōng held fast,
and their troops could not pass.
So they sent Fǔjūn Bù Xié to lead his forces west.
Xié
was Bù Zhì’s son.
Wú appointed him Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn.
He sent Cānjūn Yáng Zōng to break through the siege and go north,
to report the emergency to Āndōng Jiāngjūn Chén Qiān,
and also sent official seals and ribbons, and a hostage, to Jìngōng.
Xié attacked Yǒng’ān.
Xiàn fought with him
and greatly defeated him.
The Wú ruler was enraged
and again dispatched Zhènjūn Lù Kàng and others to lead thirty thousand troops to reinforce the siege of Xiàn.
At that time, Wú had appointed Lù Kàng as Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn,
and he commanded Xīlíng.
‘Shuài’
is pronounced ‘shuài’.
5 In the third month,
on the day Dīngchǒu,
Sīkōng Wáng Xiáng was appointed Tàiwèi,
Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn Hé Céng as Sītú,
and Zuǒ Púyè Xún Yǐ as Sīkōng.
6 On the day Jǐmǎo,
Jìngōng’s peerage was advanced to king,
and he was granted an additional ten commanderies.
In the third year of Gāoguìxiānggōng Gānlù,
Jìngōng was first enfeoffed with eight commanderies;
in the third year of Dì Jǐngyuán,
he was further enfeoffed with Hóngnóng of Tóngzhōu
and Fēngyì of Yōngzhōu,
making a total of ten commanderies.
Now another ten commanderies were added,
making a total of twenty commanderies.
Yǐ said to Xiáng:
"The Chancellor-King is revered;
Lord Hé and the officials of the court
'Lord Hé' refers to Hé Céng.
'Officials of the court' refers to all officials of the Wèi court.
'Cháo'
is pronounced zhí yáo fān;
the same below.
Today we should all lead the way in bowing to him,
without any hesitation."
Xiáng said:
"Although the Chancellor-King is honored,
he is essentially the Chancellor of Wèi,
and we are the Three Dukes of Wèi.
The King and the Dukes are only one rank apart.
How can the Three Dukes of the Son of Heaven casually bow to someone?
This would diminish the prestige of the Wèi court
and impair the virtue of the King of Jìn.
A noble person loves others with propriety;
I will not do it."
When they entered,
Yǐ bowed,
but Xiáng merely made a long bow.
The King said to Xiáng:
"Only today do I truly understand the depth of your regard for me!"
7 Liú Shàn (劉禪) moved his entire family eastward to Luòyáng (洛陽).
At that chaotic and sudden time,
none of Shàn’s (禪) high officials were able to accompany him.
Jiāng Wéi (姜維) was already dead;
Zhāng Yì (張翼), Liáo Huà (廖化), and Dǒng Jué (董厥) must also have died at the hands of the rebellious soldiers.
Shàn (禪) relied on Zhèng Xiàng (正相) to guide him appropriately,
ensuring his actions were flawless.
Yí (宜),
means appropriate.
Shì (適),
also means appropriate.
When Shàn (禪) first entered Luò (洛),
he met the Wei (魏) ruler and his officials,
and his etiquette was appropriate in each instance.
Alas!
If Zhèng (正) had tied his sash and stood in the court,
above, announcing and assisting the Han (漢) lord,
and below, speaking with guests,
with everything fitting and without fault or error,
would this not be the ultimate wish of a minister?
I regret knowing Zhèng (正) so late.
Initially,
Huò Yì (霍弋), the Administrator of Jiànníng (建寧) in Han (漢), was the Area Commander of Nánzhōng (南中).
Jiànníng (建寧)
was a commandery in Yìzhōu (益州) of Han (漢).
In the first year of Jiànxīng (建興) under the Latter Lord of Shǔ (蜀),
Jiànníng (建寧) Commandery was renamed,
with its seat in Wèi (味) County.
He wanted to rush to Chéngdū (成都),
but Liú Shàn (劉禪), believing the enemy had been pacified,
did not allow it.
When Chéngdū (成都) could not be held,
Yì (弋) wore mourning clothes and wept openly for three days.
All the generals urged Yì (弋) to surrender quickly,
but Yì (弋) said:
"Now the roads are blocked,
and we do not know the safety of our lord.
Such a great matter of leaving or staying
cannot be done lightly.
If Wei (魏) treats our lord with礼,
then to secure our territory and surrender will not be too late.
But if, by some chance, he is endangered or humiliated,
I will resist it with my death;
what does timing matter then!"
After receiving news of Shàn’s (禪) eastward relocation,
he then led the generals and governors of the six commanderies to submit a memorial, saying:
There were seven commanderies in Nánzhōng (南zhōng),
but here it speaks of six commanderies
because Yuèxī (越巂) had already surrendered to Wei (魏).
Jiàng (將),
is pronounced as liàng.
Shǒu (守),
is pronounced as shì yòu.
"Your servant has heard that life is granted threefold,
and one serves them as one.
Only where difficulty lies,
does one commit one's life.
Without parents, how can a bird be born?
Without a ruler, how can a bird live?
This is what is meant by 'life is granted threefold.'
Nán (難),
is pronounced as nǎi dàn.
Having nowhere to die,
we therefore commit ourselves
and dare not waver."
Zhì (質),
is as written.
He was appointed Commandant of Nánzhōng (南zhōng)
and entrusted with his original post.
On the day Dīnghài (丁亥),
Liú Shàn (劉禪) was enfeoffed as the Duke of Ānlè (安樂公).
The Jìn (晉) Records state: Ānlè (安樂)
belonged to the state of Yān (燕).
Lè (樂),
is pronounced as luò;
the same applies to the later instance of Lè (樂).
The King of Jìn (晉) feasted with Shàn (禪)
and had Shǔ (蜀) performances enacted for him.
Shǔjì (蜀技)
refers to Shǔ (蜀) music,
such as the Bāyú (巴渝) dance.
Wèi (為),
is pronounced as yú wěi;
the same applies below.
Jì (技),
is the same as jì (伎),
pronounced as qú qǐ.
Shàn (禪) laughed as usual.
The King said to Jiǎ Chōng (賈充):
"A person can be so heartless as this;
even if Zhūgě Liàng (諸葛亮) were still alive,
he could not have helped him long survive,
let alone Jiāng Wéi (姜維)!"
Another day,
the King asked Shàn (禪):
"Do you miss Shǔ (蜀) at all?"
Shàn (禪) replied:
"I am happy here,
and I do not miss Shǔ (蜀)."
Xì Zhèng (郤正) heard this
and said to Shàn (禪):
"If the King asks again,
you should weep and reply: 'The tombs of my ancestors
are far away in Mín (岷) and Shǔ (蜀);
my heart grieves westward,
not a day passes without longing.' "
Xībēi (西悲),
uses the language from the poem "Dōngshān (東山)";
this is a scholar's plucking phrases from texts.
When the King asked again,
Shàn (禪) replied as before.
The King said:
"Why does that sound like Xì Zhèng’s (郤正) words?"
Shàn (禪) looked in surprise and said:
"Indeed, just as Your Majesty commanded."
Everyone around him laughed.
8 In summer,
in the fourth month,
Wáng Zhì (王稚), the Commander of the Newly Attached, sailed across the sea into Gòuzhāng (句章) in Wú (吳).
The Commander of the Newly Attached
was likely a position created to lead a separate unit of people from Wú (吳) who had newly pledged allegiance.
A commander was appointed to govern them.
Gòuzhāng (句章) County belonged to Kuàijī (會稽) Commandery.
Xián (賢) says: The old city of Gòuzhāng (句章) is west of modern Mào (鄮) County.
9 In the fifth month,
on the day Gēngshēn (庚申),
the King of Jìn (晉) memorialized to restore the five ranks of nobility,
enfeoffing over six hundred people from the Rank of Cavalry Commander and above.
This was to reward the merits of pacifying Shǔ (蜀).
According to the Zhōu (周) system,
the ranks of nobility were divided into five grades: Dukes (公) and Marquises (侯) had territories of a hundred lǐ;
Earls (伯) seventy lǐ;
Viscounts (子) and Barons (男) fifty lǐ.
Qín (秦) abolished the five ranks of nobility.
Han (漢) ranked its marquisates by household count.
In the twentieth year of Jiàn'ān (建安) under Emperor Xiàn (獻),
King Cāo (操) of Wei (魏) established nominal titles for marquises to reward military merit,
and titular enfeoffments began from this point.
Although the five ranks of nobility were now restored,
they were also titular enfeoffments.
Qí (騎),
is pronounced as qí jì.
10 On the day Jiǎxū (甲戌),
the era name was changed.
It was changed to Xiánxī (咸熙).
11 On the day Guǐwèi (癸未),
Sīmǎ Yì (司馬懿), the Marquis Wénxuān (文宣) of Wǔyáng (舞陽), was posthumously declared Jìn Xuān Wáng (晉宣王);
and Sīmǎ Shī (司馬師), the Marquis Zhōngwǔ (忠武), was declared Jǐng Wáng (景王).
12 Luó Xiàn (羅憲) was attacked for a total of six months.
No relief arrived, and more than half the city fell ill.
Someone advised Xiàn (憲) to abandon the city and flee,
but Xiàn (憲) said:
"I am the city lord,
upon whom the common people rely.
If I cannot provide safety in danger
and abandon them in urgency,
a junzǐ (君子) does not do this.
I will die here!"
Chén Qiān (陳騫) spoke to the King of Jìn (晉),
who dispatched Hú Liè (胡烈), the Inspector of Jīngzhōu (荊州), with twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to attack Xīlíng (西陵) to relieve Xiàn (憲).
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
the Wú (吳) army retreated.
The King of Jìn (晉) allowed Xiàn (憲) to retain his old post
and added the title of Língjiāng Jiāngjūn (陵江將軍).
Shěn Yuē (沈約) recorded: Wei (魏) established the position of Língjiāng Jiāngjūn (陵江將軍)
as the first of the forty titles,
meaning to command across the Jiāng (江) River
to pacify Wú (吳) and Kuàijī (會稽).
13 The King of Jìn (晉) memorialized to have Sūn Yǐ (荀顗), the Minister of Works, standardize rites and ceremonies;
Jiǎ Chōng (賈充), the Central Protector of the Army, rectify laws and regulations;
Péi Xiù (裴秀), the Minister of Personnel, deliberate on the official system;
and Zhèng Chōng (鄭沖), the Grand Tutor, oversee and finalize them.
14 Wú (吳) divided Jiāozhōu (交州) and established Guǎngzhōu (廣州).
In the sixth year of Yuándǐng (元鼎) under Emperor Wǔ (武) of Han (漢),
the Baiyue (百越) were opened up,
and an Inspector of Jiāozhǐ (交趾) was established,
with his seat in Lóngbiān (龍編).
In the eighth year of Jiàn'ān (建安) under Emperor Xiàn (獻),
it was renamed Jiāozhōu (交州), with its seat in Guǎngxìn (廣信) County, Cāngwú (蒼梧).
In the sixteenth year,
the seat was moved to Pānyú (番禺) County, Nánhǎi (南海).
By this time, it was divided into two provinces:
Guǎngzhōu (廣州) had its seat in Pānyú (番禺),
and Jiāozhōu (交州) returned to its seat in Lóngbiān (龍編).
15 The ruler of Wú (吳) fell ill in his chamber,
unable to speak.
He then wrote a letter by hand to summon Prime Minister Púyáng Xìng (濮陽興)
and ordered his son Sūn ($#x29166;) to go out and pay his respects to him.
Sūn Xiū (孫休) grasped Xìng’s (興) arm,
pointed to Sūn ($#x29166;), and entrusted him to Xìng (興).
On the day Guǐwèi (癸未),
the ruler of Wú (吳) passed away,
receiving the posthumous title Emperor Jǐng (景帝).
He was thirty years old.
The people of Wú, seeing that Shǔ had recently fallen
and Jiāozhǐ was drifting into rebellion,
believed that Lǚ Xīng (呂興) was revolting.
They desired to have an adult ruler.
The Zuǒ Diǎnjūn (左典軍) Wàn Yù (萬彧) had once been the Wūchéng Lìng (烏程令),
and was on good terms with the Marquis of Wūchéng (Wūchéng Hóu) Hào (晧).
He praised
Hào's (晧) talent, insight, and decisive judgment, saying he was
"a peer of Chángshā Huán Wáng (長沙桓王);
he abides by laws and regulations."
He repeatedly spoke of this to Chéngxiàng (丞相) Xīng (興) and Zuǒ Jiāngjūn (左將軍) Bù (布).
Xīng (興) and Bù (布) convinced Empress Dowager Zhū (朱太后),
wishing to make Hào (晧) the heir.
Empress Dowager Zhū (朱后) said:
"I am a widow;
how can I know the concerns of the state?
If the state of Wú (吳) does not perish,
and the ancestral temples have support,
that is sufficient."
The era name was changed to Yuánxīng (元興),
and a general amnesty was issued.
Hào (晧),
courtesy name Yuánzōng (元宗),
was the son of Sūn Hé (孫和).
In the 16th year, eighth month,
on the Gēngyín day,
an edict ordered the Central Defender of the Army (Zhōng Fǔjūn) Sīmǎ Yán (司馬炎) to assist in matters of the Xiàngguó (相國).
Earlier, when Zhōng Huì (鍾會) was campaigning against Hàn (漢),
Xīn Xiànyīng (辛憲英) told her husband's nephew, Yáng Hù (羊祜):
"Huì (會) is unrestrained and arrogant in his actions;
this is not the way to long endure in a subordinate position."
Huì (會) requested her son, Lángzhōng (郎中) Xiù (琇), to serve as a Cānjūn (參軍).
Xīn Xiànyīng (憲英) worried, saying:
"Other days I worried for the state,
but today misfortune has reached my family."
Xiù (琇) firmly pleaded with the King of Jìn (Jìn Wáng),
but the King did not listen.
Xīn Xiànyīng (憲英) said to Xiù (琇):
"Go,
but be warned.
Amidst military affairs,
what can bring success,
is it not benevolence and clemency?"
Xiù (琇) eventually returned completely safe.
An edict
stated that because Xiù (琇) had advised against Huì's (會) rebellion,
he was granted the title of Guānnèi Hóu (關內侯).
In the 18th year, ninth month,
on the Wùwǔ day,
Sīmǎ Yán (司馬炎) was made Fǔjūn Dà Jiāngjūn (撫軍大將軍).
On the Xīnwèi day, an edict appointed Lǚ Xīng (呂興) as Ānnán Jiāngjūn (安南將軍),
and Dūdu Jiāozhōu Zhū Jūnshì (都督交州諸軍事).
Huò Yì (霍弋), Nánzhōng Jiānjūn (南中監軍), was remotely appointed Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ (交州刺史),
thus being able to conveniently select and employ senior officials.
Yì (弋) submitted a memorial dispatching Cuàn Gǔ (爨谷) of Jiànníng (建寧) to be Jiāozhǐ Tàishǒu (交趾太守).
Mèng Gàn (孟幹), Mèng Tōng (孟通), Cuàn Néng (爨能), Lǐ Sōng (李松), Wáng Sù (王素), and others led troops to assist Xīng (興),
but before they arrived,
Xīng (興) was killed by his Gōngcáo (功曹) Wáng
Tǒng (統).
The Wú Zhǔ (吳主) demoted Empress Dowager Zhū (朱太后) to Empress Jǐng (景皇后).
He honored his own mother, Lady Hé (何氏), as Empress Dowager (Tàihòu).
In the 21st year, winter,
tenth month,
on the Dīnghài day,
an edict appointed Xú Shào (徐紹), Wú Xiàngguó Cānjūnshì (吳相國參軍事) captured at Shòuchūn (壽春), as Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍),
and Sūn Yù (孫彧), Shuǐcáo Yuàn (水曹掾), as Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng (給事黃門侍郎).
Their family members who were here were all allowed to follow them,
not necessarily needing to return,
in order to widely demonstrate good faith.
Earlier, the King of Jìn (Jìn Wáng) married the daughter of Wáng Sù (王肅),
who bore Yán (炎) and Yōu (攸).
Yōu (攸) was made the heir of Jǐng Wáng (景王).
Yōu (攸) was highly talented and skilled,
pure, gentle, and fair,
and his reputation surpassed Yán's (炎).
The King of Jìn (晉王) loved him,
and often said:
"The empire
belongs to Jǐng Wáng (景王).
I have temporarily held the position of Xiàngwèi (相位).
After a hundred years,
the great enterprise should revert to Yōu (攸)."
Yán (炎) let his hair fall to the ground,
and his hands hung below his knees,
saying, "Does anyone read faces?"
He then showed them his unusual physiognomy.
Yáng Xiù (羊琇) thus became devoted to him.
Yáng Xiù (羊琇) was close to Yán (炎)
and made plans for Yán (炎),
observing what should be improved or removed in current policies,
and had Yán (炎) record them in advance,
to be prepared for the King of Jìn's (晉王) inquiries.
The King of Jìn (晉王) wanted to make Yōu (攸) the Shìzǐ (世子),
but Shān Tāo (山濤) said:
"To set aside the elder and establish the younger
is contrary to ritual and inauspicious."
Jiǎ Chōng (賈充) said:
"The Zhōng Fǔjūn (中撫軍) possesses the virtue of a ruler,
and cannot be easily replaced."
Hé Zēng (何曾) and Péi Xiù (裴秀) said:
"The Zhōng Fǔjūn (中撫軍) is intelligent and divinely martial,
possessing talent that transcends the age.
His popular esteem is already great,
and his heavenly appearance is such
that he is certainly not a subject's visage."
The King of Jìn's (晉王) mind was thus settled,
and on the Bǐngwǔ day,
Yán (炎) was established as the Shìzǐ (世子).
The Wú Zhǔ (吳主) enfeoffed his Tàizǐ (太子) Xiàn (僴) and his three younger brothers all as kings.
Initially, when the Wú Zhǔ (吳主) ascended the throne,
he issued benevolent edicts,
showed sympathy to scholars and commoners,
opened granaries,
relieved the poor,
and assigned palace women to those without wives.
At that time, everyone unanimously called him an enlightened ruler.
However, once he achieved his ambition,
he became crude, violent, arrogant, and excessive,
full of taboos and prohibitions,
and fond of wine and women.
Both high and low were disappointed.
Púyáng Xīng (濮陽興) and Zhāng Bù (張布) secretly regretted their actions.
Someone slandered them to the Wú Zhǔ (吳主).
In the eleventh month,
on the first day,
Xīng (興) and Bù (布) entered court.
The Wú Zhǔ (吳主) seized them,
exiled them to Guǎngzhōu (廣州),
and had them killed on the way,
exterminating their three clans.
He appointed his mother's father, Téng Mù (滕牧), as Wèi Jiāngjūn (衞將軍)
and Lù Shàngshū Shì (錄尚書事).
In this year,
the Túntián (屯田) officials were abolished.
Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, Juàn 69
Wèi Jì 1. It concludes with the year Xuányì Shètígé (rén-yín), totaling three years.
Year 2
(xīn-chǒu, 221) *Kǎoyì* says: The *Chén Zhì* states:
"In the first month,

(jiǎ-yín, 234) *Kǎoyì* says: In Táng Tàizōng's *Jìn Shū*, the biography of Jǐnghuái Xiàhóu Hòu states,
that the Empress died in this year.
It says:
"As Xuāndì held a position of great authority,
and all his sons possessed great talent and ambition,
the Empress knew that the Emperor was not a pure minister of Wèi,
and since the Empress was a maternal relative of the Wèi clan,
the Emperor deeply feared her,
and so she perished by poison."
However, at this time, Sīmǎ Yì was fully trusted by Míngdì,
and had not yet shown any signs of disloyalty,
much less his sons!
To simply because of her being a Wèi maternal relative,
to rashly poison his wife,
is completely inconsistent with the facts;
it is likely an exaggeration.
Otherwise,
the master himself poisoned her for some other reason.
Now, it is not accepted.
